en: We worship that Supreme Reality, which is the substratum of sound, Brahman, consciousness, and bliss, from whose transformations the letters, words, and sentences shine forth. 1.
The view of the Mahābhāṣya has also been elucidated by Bhartṛhari; having examined all treatises, the true nature of the sphoṭa is now being determined. (2)
Neither individually nor collectively, nor as objects of a single recollection, do the phonemes (varṇas) denote a meaning; rather, it is the sphoṭa that does so, and that is of two kinds.

In this context, indeed, the comprehension of meaning from words and sentences is established by the experience of all people and is accepted by all theorists. Among these, the individual phonemes (*varṇa*) do not denote the meaning, because if the meaning were understood from the first phoneme alone, the other phonemes would result in futility. Nor do they denote it when combined, because there is no possibility of combination for those that perish as soon as they are uttered and occur in a temporal sequence. Nor can they be the objects of a single simultaneous recollection, because in cases such as *nadī* (river) and *rasa* (taste), there would be no distinction between them since both would equally be the objects of a single recollection.

Therefore, one might argue that the *sphoṭa*—whether of a word (*padasphoṭa*) or of a sentence (*vākyasphoṭa*)—is manifested by the phonemes (*varṇa*), that it is partless (*anavayava*), unitary, eternal, and the denoter of meaning; to this, he replies: "Not by each [phoneme] individually. The *sphoṭa* of a word or the *sphoṭa* of a sentence is of two kinds. Among these, the proponent of the *padasphoṭa* maintains that the *padasphoṭa* alone is eternal, partless, the ultimate reality, and the substratum; whereas both phonemes and sentences are superimpositions upon it, being its illusory manifestations (*vivarta*). Thus, their differentiation is merely due to ignorance (*āvidyaka*).

The proponent of the sphoṭa of individual words maintains that the meaning of a sentence shines forth solely from the sphoṭas of the individual words through the power of expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) and other factors. However, the proponent of the sphoṭa of the sentence considers the sentence alone to be the eternal, partless substratum, while letters and words are its illusory manifestations (vivarta), and thus their distinction is merely due to ignorance (avidyaka).

In the view of the *sphoṭa*-proponents who maintain that it has parts (*sāvayava*), some consider the following: the letters (*varṇa*) themselves—though eternal and all-pervading—are the parts, being manifested by specific sounds (*dhvani*) known as "wind" (*vāyavīya-nāda*), which arise from the respective locations such as the palate. This is the distinction: in the partless (*niravayava*) view, it is the sounds (*dhvani*) themselves that manifest the *sphoṭa*; whereas in the view of having parts, it is the letters manifested by those sounds that manifest the *sphoṭa*. However, in reality, the view of having parts is not tenable.

To explain: are the phonemes (*varṇas*) parts of a whole (*avayavin*), such that they would be substances (*dravya*) like light according to the Bhaṭṭa school; or rather, according to the Tārkika school, qualities of space (*ākāśa*); or perhaps, following the view of the *Ekadeśīyas*, substances composed of wind (*vāyavīya*)? The first position is not tenable: for it is observed everywhere that the dimensions of parts are smaller than those of the whole (*avayavin*), whereas phonemes are [considered] maximally great (*paramamahat*); since that [smaller dimension] is impossible for them, they cannot possess the status of being parts.

The middle view is that since letters possess the quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*), they lack the status of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) due to their non-substantiality; consequently, because they lack the nature of being an inherent cause of a substance, they lack the property of having parts (*sāvayavatva*). Nor can they be [parts] in another sense—for those which perish quickly, occur sequentially, do not coexist, and are unconnected, cannot sustain a whole (*avayavin*); thus, they lack the status of being parts. Therefore, it is the very manifestation of the sentence (*vākyasphoṭa*), characterized by the division of phonemes and words as determined by cognition, which is superior; such is the *Tattvasamīkṣā*. 3.
If the permanence of phonemes is [established] by the force of recognition, why should impermanence not likewise be established by the force of cognitions such as their production? (4)

"For he who, out of delusion, might imagine a subverting factor even where none exists, being possessed by doubt in all worldly transactions, shall go to ruin.

In that regard, when many people pronounce a single [phoneme], there arise the distinctions of acute (udātta), grave (anudātta), nasalized (sānunāsika), and non-nasalized (niranunāsika). Because these contradictory properties are superimposed, there is a difference among phonemes due to this subversion. Nor should it be argued that the acute and other qualities are properties of the manifestors (*vyañjaka*) and not properties of the phonemes themselves; for if those were the manifesting air-currents, then since they are not audible, it would follow that their properties are likewise inaudible. To this, it is replied: [The reply follows: "It is said..."

Even when the sense organs grasp the substratum of qualities (guṇin), there is also the grasping of the qualities; otherwise, how could odors, tastes, and sounds be perceived by the olfactory, gustatory, and auditory organs, which grasp earth, water, and ether respectively? By this, other contradictory properties such as high pitch (tāratva) and so forth are also explained. Or, even if the quality and the possessor of the quality were both perceptible by a single sense organ, there would still be no fault; for since sounds are indeed audible like words, there is the perception of properties residing in them, such as accentuation (udātta) and the like.

Now, as for that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), it has as its object the universal *ga*-ness (*gatva*) and so forth, not the individual instances (*vyakti*) such as the letter *ga*. For this very reason, because a difference in the sounds is perceived, a difference in their speakers is inferred, as in: "Somaśarman is reciting, Viṣṇuśarman is not reciting. True; however, this effort to postulate a difference in the universal *ga*-ness while accepting a difference in the individual instances of the letter *ga*—and thereby denying its unity—is better applied to the individual instance of the letter *ga* itself. What is the use of this superfluous internal goiter (*antargaḍu*) of a postulated *ga*-ness? And thus they say:

"Therefore, that which is sought by the proponent will be obtained from the phonemes themselves; however, since the manifestation is obtainable from the sounds (nāda), the notion of [a single entity such as] 'ga-ness' and so forth is futile. Here, "obtainable through manifestation" refers to distinctions such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and others. Thus, when oneness is determined by the force of uncontradicted recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), this diverse cognition has as its object the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*), not the phoneme (*varṇa*). Furthermore, if there were a difference between the phonemes, the cognition would be "he uttered ten *ga*s," rather than "he uttered the letter *ga* ten times."

And thus the venerable Śaṅkarācārya said in the Śārīrakabhāṣya: "Indeed, it is the individual phonemes themselves that are recognized upon each utterance; for the cognition is 'the word *go* has been uttered twice,' and not 'two *go*-words have been uttered.'"

Although there is the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is that very letter *ga*," nevertheless, since difference appears through the force of various cognitions—such as "the *ga*-letter has arisen," "the *ga*-letter has perished," "a high-pitched *ga*-letter," and "a low-pitched *ga*-letter"—the object of this recognition is merely its belonging to that same class (*tajjātīyatva*), and not the non-difference of the manifesting individual. Nor should it be argued that, if this were the case, the cognition would be "this belongs to that class" rather than "this is that."

This very same flame of the lamp; I am eating those very same tamarind fruits; this very same medicine, drunk by others before, is now drunk by me as well—in such cases, there is a cognition of that same class (*tajjātīya*), because the form "this is that" (*so 'yam*) is observed, and because the distinction is not cognized through the reasoning "this belongs to that class, but it is not that. Nor should one dispute regarding the genus (*jāti*) of the phoneme *ga* (*gatva*) and so forth; for its establishment is based on the force of the inclusive cognition of the form of the phoneme *ga*—namely, "this is the phoneme *ga*, this is the phoneme *ga*"—and on the force of the inference of specific speakers, such as women or men.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total eradication of the very notion of birth. Nor should it be argued that, by the force of a perceptual recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in the form of valid knowledge, this cognition of production and so forth is merely an illusion and thus lacks a definitive ground for its exclusion; for, rather than postulating the invalidity of both cognitions, it is simpler to postulate the invalidity of only one—recognition—since parsimony (*lāghava*) serves as the decisive factor.
Therefore, in either view, even Brahmā himself cannot deny the clearly manifest Word-Brahman (*śabdaparabrahman*). ||4||
Even for eternal phonemes, when they are obscured by the manifesting winds or by sounds, there can be no cognition of the collection of phonemes. ||5||

Now, one might object: "Let it be that the phonemes (*varṇa*) are not subject to immediate destruction; even if they are eternal, how can there be a lack of simultaneity? To this, he says: "Even for those that are eternal... The word "even" (*api*) implies that for those that are eternal as well as for those that are all-pervading, a real (*vāstavī*) conjunction is over-extensive (*atiprasaṅginī*), because it would follow that the cognition of every meaning would occur from every [phoneme] at all times. Therefore, that [conjunction] must be described as following from experience (*anubhavānusāriṇī*). And since those [phonemes] are manifold, their coexistence (*sāhitya*)—in the form of manifestation (*abhivyakti*) as objects of that experience—is not possible.

Likewise, since there are many manifesting air-currents and sounds, even on the view that [the word] is eternal, there can be no such thing as a "collection" (samudāya) of these when they are separated by intervals. ||5||

The cognition of an object arises from the convergence of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of what was previously experienced; it does not arise from the nature of the object itself, because that would involve error, and because postulating another [cause] would be redundant. (6)

Now, it may be argued that this indivisible, partless *sphoṭa* which is accepted on the grounds that the cognition of meaning would otherwise be inexplicable, is not possible, because the cognition of meaning can be explained in another way. To explain: the impressions (*saṃskāras*) arising from the experience of each preceding letter—whose existence is inferred from the result of recollection—form a collection that acts as an auxiliary to the experience of the final letter; from that alone, the cognition of meaning is established. To this, he says: "The preceding... [and so forth].

It is the inherent nature of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) that it produces a memory of that very object from which its experience was born; however, in the production of the cognition of an object, this [impression] would act perversely. Furthermore, if the collection of impressions produced by the experience of phonemes were to cause the cognition of some other object, then every person, having experienced any single object, would know everything—an absurd consequence (*atiprasaṅga*).

And so, Vācaspati Miśra says in the second commentary (*Bhāmatī*): "For it is not observed that the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), which is synonymous with *bhāvanā*, has any capacity other than producing a memory whose object is the very same thing experienced at its own arising; for the latent impression produced by the experience of a cow does not cause one to remember a horse. By this [it is shown that] the latent impression produced by the experience of each individual letter does not cause one to remember [the word as a whole].

By this [argument], it is refuted that a single recollective memory (smṛti) in the form of a collective representation (*samūhālambana*) having all those letters as its object is produced by the aggregate of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) generated by the experience of each individual letter, and that such [memory], being conjoined with other letters, brings about the cognition of the meaning; for it cannot be said that, since the capacity to generate recollection is already established in such a form of latent impression, one should postulate a further capacity to generate the cognition of meaning on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*). For if one were to postulate a capacity even for a capacity, there would follow the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), as one would have to postulate a capacity even for the capacity of fire and so forth.

Furthermore, just as the capacity called *saṃskāra*, which is postulated because the effect characterized as memory cannot otherwise be accounted for, is not imagined to reside in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) or elsewhere, but rather in that very self (*ātman*) wherein its fruit—namely, the characteristic of memory—is inherent; likewise, it is appropriate to postulate the capacity to produce the direct perception of an object—which is postulated because the direct perception of an object cannot otherwise be accounted for—in that very self wherein its fruit exists, and not in some other locus where the capacity to generate memory might reside.

Nor should it be said that this [sequence] exists in the self (ātman); for if one were to postulate that with the experience of each individual phoneme there is one capacity to produce a memory whose objects are those respective [phonemes], and another capacity to produce the cognition of the meaning, this would entail the fault of excessive complexity (gaurava). Furthermore, by you who accept that sequence in the conscious self (cidātman)—which is the substratum of that [speech-sound] when qualified by the form of 'ga' and so on—you have also arrived at our own path; thus, we have no dispute. Moreover, for eternal and all-pervading [entities], there is no real sequence whatsoever. Sequence exists only as caused by perception; if that [perception] is one, how can there be a sequence? (7)

Now, it might be argued that the impressions (*saṃskāras*) deposited by each respective letter, acting together, produce a single recollection whose object is the entire sequence of letters; and thus, the letters, as they ascend upon a single recollection, become the denoters of a single meaning. In this way, there would be neither complexity (*gaurava*) nor a contradiction of their own nature. For, in this regard, is it being asserted that the impressions have no requirement for a homogeneous cause (*sajātīyāpekṣā*) in producing something of a different kind, or rather, that they have no such requirement in producing a single recollection having multiple objects?

The first [alternative] is not tenable; for the cognition "two" arises from two distinct experiences, each having as its object "this one" and "that one," and that [cognition] is produced precisely by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) generated by those two experiences. As the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda has stated: "In the case of all these objects, for all proponents [of this view], a mental cognition of a collective whole (*samuccaya-jñāna*) is observed, even though the cognitions [of the parts] occur in succession."

"If that [succession] were not admitted, then indeed, in the case of things perceived sequentially, the form of 'a hundred' and so forth would never arise; for that is a perception of a collective aggregate. This is not the final word. For in cases such as "those jars," we observe that the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding multiple objects have a mutual dependence within a single recollection directed toward many subjects. Thus, even if each impression individually produces a recollection of its own object, there is no contradiction in the fact that the impressions, when combined, produce a single recollection whose scope encompasses multiple phonemes.

This is observed: the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is the cause of recollection independently of the eyes and other senses, while the eyes and other senses are the causes of perception independently of that [impression]; however, in the case of recognition, the eyes and other senses do depend upon the mental impression. Nor should it be argued that if phonemes mounted upon a single recollection were the expressive agents, there would be no distinction between *nadī* and *dīna*, or *sara* and *rasa*, because of the absence of a rule governing the order of recollection, and consequently, there would be no difference between those uttered in no particular order or in a reversed order. This is not to be said.

For it is accepted that the capacity to convey meaning belongs to as many letters of whatever kind as are required for a given meaning to be understood. As it has been said: "Whatever number of letters, of whatever kind, and which have their capacities known to be effective in conveying a particular meaning, they are the very ones that convey that meaning in that same way."

By the phrase "of such a kind," it is stated that [the letters] have a single speaker and are sequential. Sequence (*krama*) is *ānupūrvī* (succession). And *ānupūrvī* is either the destruction of each preceding letter, or the cognition of each subsequent letter immediately following the cognition of each preceding letter, or the utterance of each subsequent letter immediately following the utterance of each preceding letter. And thus, only the letters that conform to this sequence will ascend to the cognition of the word (*pada*).

And so, although there is no distinction among [phonemes] existing within a single cognition characterized by recollection, nevertheless, with respect to their manifestation in either simultaneity or its opposite—succession—there is indeed a distinction for those phonemes uttered in sequence. To this point, he says: "of the eternal [phonemes]. For phonemes, which are eternal and all-pervading, neither temporal nor spatial succession can be a real regulator; for if one were to accept such succession based on their mere existence, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, this [succession] must be accepted as being conditioned by the cognition [of them].

If that [cognition] were of the nature of a single memory, then how could there be a sequence? For there would be no distinction whatsoever between phonemes mounted upon a single memory—whether they are manifested in a sequence, without sequence, or in a reversed sequence. ||7||

The phonemes, being objects of memory, do not possess a sequential order based on the sequence of their experience; since experience itself does not have this [sequential] nature, how much less could such a sequence belong to them? (8)

[Objection: But surely, since the experiences of each preceding phoneme possess a sequence, one must admit that this sequence is superimposed (*samāropa*) upon the phonemes themselves when they are apprehended through a single recollection; thus, the sequence is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). As the venerable authors of the *Mīmāṃsā-vārttika* have said: "The learned desire many means for determining a word—sequence, deficiency, excess, accent, letters, sentence, and the hearing of Vedic revelation or Smṛti. The meaning is that it is not only the conveying of a single meaning that serves as the ground for the designation of a "word," but sequence and the other factors as well.

In that regard, in the case of *rasaḥ saraḥ*, there is sequence (*krama*); in *karaḥ karañjaḥ*, there is the state of being newer or excessive (*nyūnatātiriktatva*); in *indraśatruḥ*, there is accent (*svara*); in *sā raṅgam āgatā nartakī*, there is sentence-meaning (*vākya*); in *parame vyoman*, there is Vedic revelation (*śruti*); and in *gṛbhṇāmi*, there is the traditional rule of Pāṇini, namely "the substitution of *bha* for *hṛ* and *grah* in the Vedas. Thus, the sequence of prior experience is the differentiator when a single recollection occurs.

And thus the venerable authors of the Nyāya-ṭīkā have also said: "The status of being the cause of the cognition of an object belongs not to the phonemes alone, but to those [phonemes] as qualified by sequence, deficiency, excess, and so forth"; with this in mind, he says: "Not in the perception... (nānubhūti...).

This recollection, produced by the experience of each preceding phoneme, has as its object only those phonemes [already experienced]. It does not take the experience of the preceding phonemes as its domain; how then could it [grasp] their sequence? Thus, even if the sequence is conditioned by the prior experience, it does not serve as a differentiator among the phonemes being recollected. Therefore, since the cognition of meaning is established through a recollection that apprehends the collection of phonemes, there is no need for an alternative explanation (anyathopapatti). ||8||
In the three distinct cognitions—"this is a word," "this is a sentence," and "these are phonemes"—only one clear manifestation (sphoṭa) is clearly experienced. ||9||

Now, it may be objected: "In the Prābhākara view, cognitions are self-luminous; therefore, that [cognition] which is the object of the memory must appear in that memory. True, but a cognition is not self-luminous, and thus the object of that [memory] is also not self-luminous, because it lacks its own form and because it is not an object of itself. If you argue that the aspect of the self (the subject) appears clearly as something distinct from the object-aspect of the cognition itself, then ask those who accept this view; we do not, for we maintain the theory of the perception of the threefold complex (*tripuṭī*).

Nor is it accepted even by them that the sequence of cognitions is self-luminous. Now, one might argue: "The postulation of a cause must follow the observed effect; therefore, even if not directly perceived, the sequence existing in reality must be stated as the differentiator. If the comprehension of the meaning is established from the very letters being perceived—as in the command "Bring the cow"—then one should not, in the absence of any evidence, postulate an invisible, partless essence called *sphoṭa* to the exclusion of these [letters]. This is because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for such a thing.

Furthermore, that comprehension of meaning which was stated [to occur] when the sphoṭa is not yet a means of valid cognition is undermined by its dependence on one another; for, while the comprehension of the sphoṭa would follow from the comprehension of meaning through the impossibility of that [meaning-comprehension] otherwise, the comprehension of meaning would likewise follow from the comprehension of the sphoṭa. To this he says: "This... I do not postulate a sphoṭa; rather, I perceive it as being directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*).

For instance, it is an experience established for all people that the single word "cow" (*gauh*) becomes a single sentence in the expression "bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), and this cannot be denied. In that case, one must admit that a single, undivided entity shines forth within the synthetic cognition (*anusamhāra-buddhi*) which is produced by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the apprehension of each preceding phoneme. Indeed, this cognition, which manifests as a single undivided object, cannot have as its object merely the phonemes themselves, whose natures are mutually distinct.

Because in the case of such a mental object (*buddhiviṣaya*), there is no inherence (*asamavāya*) of either unity or plurality in the entities presented therein. Nor should it be said that, just as trees are the objects of the cognition "forest," so too the phonemes (*varṇa*) alone are the objects of the cognitions "word" (*pada*) or "sentence" (*vākya*). This is because, in those cases, there is the apprehension of a single unitary cognition (*ekabuddhi*), the capacity to convey a single meaning (*ekārthapratyāyakatva*), or some such limiting condition (*upādhi*), whereas here [in the case of the word], no such condition is perceived. Here, the phrase "of the cognition 'word'" (*padamiti buddheḥ*) has been stated in order to support the view even of those who maintain that the word is merely the phoneme (*padasphoṭavādin*).

The view of the proponents of the *sphoṭa* (the primary theory) is that the *sphoṭa* itself, as a single entity consisting of nine parts (*navāṅga*), is the denoter of the sentence-meaning. Regarding this, the truth is as follows: one never has the cognition, "this is a sentence," nor "there are so many words," nor "there are so many phonemes. Among these, it has already been established that in the first case—that of the cognition grasping unity—some single entity being perceived is the cause, because of the oneness of that unitary cognition. Two other cases remain.

In this regard, if a sentence were composed of three words—such as "Devadatta, bring the cow"—which possess ultimate reality and a fixed temporal sequence, then when one says "Bring the cow, Devadatta," that sentence would be destroyed as a composite whole; consequently, the purposeful activity characterized by the comprehension of meaning produced by it would not occur, just as there can be no fetching of water from shards once a jar has been destroyed.

Likewise, if in the sentence "Devadatta, bring the cow," there were eight phonemes (*varṇa*) characterized by a specific sequence as the ultimate constituents of the sentence, then in the sentence "Bring the cow, Devadatta," where there are seven phonemes in a different order, there would be no comprehension of the meaning.

Therefore, having accepted that the division into phonemes and words is merely illusory (*avidyaka*), one must accept a partless, eternal *sphoṭa* as the essence of the sentence, which persists through all utterances and is conducive to the comprehension of meaning. ||9||

In this context, it is not appropriate for phonemes to be either eternal or non-eternal; rather, they are merely the illusory manifestations (vivarta) of that Brahman, just like the phenomenal world itself. 10.

Now, it might be argued: let the phonemes not be the objects of the cognition "this is a sentence"; however, how can the sphoṭa, which is the essence of the sentence, be the object of the universal human cognition "these are the phonemes," which possesses a manifold form? Nor should it be said that there is a cognition "these are the phonemes" with respect to the sentence, as there is [the cognition] "these are trees" with respect to a forest, or "these are threads" with respect to a cloth. For there is no cognition colored by the phonemes with respect to a sentence that is distinct from the nature of the phonemes or not inherent in them.

For it is observed that the intellect (buddhi), when colored by them, takes on their nature—such as "trees in the forest" or "threads in the cloth," which is the inherence of those [threads] in the cloth. Neither of these two cases applies here, because this [eternality] is not accepted [in the case of phonemes]. Therefore he says, "It is eternal. Here, in the case of the eternal *sphoṭa*, it is eternal. Furthermore, phonemes (*varṇas*) are all-pervading (*vibhu*); parts (*avayavas*) are not appropriate for them, because parts must be smaller than the whole (*avayavin*). Nor are they non-eternal, because it is impossible for a non-eternal whole to lack parts.

Therefore, these are merely transformations (vivartas) of that very manifestation. And thus, let the cognition not be of the nature of a valid means of knowledge (pramā) colored by the qualities of the object; rather, let it be of the nature of an error (bhrānti). Nor is there a rule that a cognition must be colored by an object either because of its identity with that object or because of its inherence in it; for even a conch-shell can be the object of a cognition colored by silver.

Therefore, the manifestation of that which is the ultimate reality—the substratum of the transformation (vivarta) and whose nature is luminosity—is not contradicted by its appearing as if colored by this or that transformation of phonemes (varṇa), though such transformations are imagined through ignorance (avidyā). Nor should it be said that there can be no transformation of phonemes because they are non-existent anywhere; for it is possible for even things that are non-existent anywhere—such as the manifold world of jars and so forth—to appear within the consciousness of Brahman, as has been explained at length elsewhere. Thus he says: "the manifold worlds" (prapañcāḥ). 10.
Just as a single face appears manifold in a jewel, a sword, and other such objects, so too does the one Self manifest diversely within the various bodies. 11.

Now, one might object: "If the eternal, partless *sphoṭa* is manifested by the phonemes (*varṇas*), then how can there be the comprehension of various distinct meanings from this [sphoṭa], which is itself devoid of distinctions? To this, he says: "Just as... (*yathā*).

Just as a face—though its position on the neck is fixed, its color such as fairness is fixed, and its dimensions such as breadth and height are fixed—is perceived in a jewel, a sword, a mirror, or the like, as if it were located in various places, possessed of various colors and dimensions, and as if it were divided even though it is undivided; so too, within the various *dhvanis* (articulations) which are distinct according to their respective causes of production, the *sphoṭa*, though it is one, appears as if it consists of various phonemes (*varṇas*), and though it is partless, appears as if it has parts, being perceived as if it were divided.

And thus, the difference between the denoted object, such as a jar, and the denoter, such as the word "jar," is merely conditional (aupādhika). For this very reason, they regard there to be non-difference between the word and its meaning. ||11||
Although the sphoṭa is distinct from the phonemes, having attained identity with them, it arises as the object of cognition; therefore, it is colored by those phonemes. (12)

Now, an objection: the cognition "cow" (gauriti-buddhi) apprehends only the phonemes *ga*, *au*, and *r* as previously experienced, and not a *sphoṭa* distinct from them; for if something different from the phonemes *ga* and so on were to appear, then the cognition would not be colored by the form of the phonemes *ga* and so on. Indeed, the cognition of a boar does not apprehend a boar colored by the form of a buffalo. Furthermore, if this cognition had an object that is a separate entity [from the phonemes], then the phonemes *ga* and so on would appear individually, just like the phonemes *da* and so on. To this, he says: "The *sphoṭa*."

Although the sphoṭa, which is distinct from the phonemes (varṇas), is manifested by them, it nevertheless assumes identity with each respective phoneme during its own recitation. Therefore, the cognition arises as colored by those respective phonemes, and not as colored by [the phoneme] 'da' and so forth. However, in the case of the boar and the deer, there is no relationship of locus and illusory manifestation; thus, there is no cognition of identity between these two. ||12||

When the final consciousness is accompanied by the cultivation of the impressions of each preceding experience, the reality of the jewel becomes clearly manifest, just as a crystal is clearly revealed. (13)

Now, one might object: since the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*) manifest the *sphoṭa* individually, the cognition of the *sphoṭa* arises from the very first sound; and since the cognition of the meaning is established by depending on that [cognition of the *sphoṭa*] alone, the subsequent sounds would be useless. To this, he says: "The preceding, the preceding... For even though these sounds manifest it individually, they are not capable of immediately causing the essence of the *sphoṭa* to appear in its entirety; rather, they cause it to appear in a form corresponding to themselves.

And thus, in the final cognition accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the manifestation of each preceding phoneme, the essence of *sphoṭa* shines forth most clearly; therefore, it was previously stated that there is no arising of the cognition of the object until after that [final cognition]. Consequently, the subsequent cognitions are not purposeless. Nor are the preceding ones, because in their absence, due to the lack of maturation of the impressions produced by them, there would be no assistance, and the mind, being otherwise occupied, would be incapable of manifesting that [sphoṭa].

As Bhartṛhari has said: "When the intellect—whose seed has been sown by sounds and which has reached full maturity through the continuous flow of the final sound—the word is apprehended. Just as for a gem-expert who examines a gem again and again, each successive perception of the gem penetrates the true nature of the gem's form; yet, these perceptions do not immediately manifest the reality that is distinguished from homogeneous and heterogeneous classes. Rather, it shines forth in the final consciousness, assisted by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by five or six such observations. (13)
Without a substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), the cognition of the superimposed (adhyasta) does not arise;
therefore, that the silver is a superimposition upon the mother-of-pearl is entirely consistent. 14.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the sphoṭa is slightly manifest in each preceding cognition of the phonemes, but becomes more clearly manifest in the final cognition? [Reply: This is not possible, because at the time of the final cognition, the preceding cognitions have already passed away, and at that time, the final cognition has not yet arisen; thus, there can be no assistance from the non-existent preceding [cognitions] nor from the non-existent final phoneme. Furthermore, once the indivisible entity—whether the word-sphoṭa or the sentence-sphoṭa—is grasped, nothing remains ungrasped within it such that its lack of manifestation could be due to the non-grasping of that [ungrasped part].

Nor is it a superimposition (samāropa), because of the absence of both a universal and a particular state; for a mother-of-pearl shell, when not apprehended as having the nature of a universal, cannot be the object of the superimposition of silver. Therefore, the synthetic cognition "this is a cow" (gaur iti) penetrates the forms of the phonemes that exclude one another and do not recur [in other instances]; it does not have a single entity permeated by the phonemes as its object. Hence he says: "it is not the substratum" (nādhiṣṭhānam).

The phonemes, such as *ga* and so forth, are also manifestations (*vivarta*); they are superimposed upon the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), which is of the nature of consciousness residing in the supreme locus. Therefore, when that [Brahman] is known, it is indeed the knowledge of the *sphoṭa*. However, because it does not convey meaning at that stage, it is called "unmanifest" (*asphuṭa*). But when it flashes forth clearly in the final cognition—which is conjoined with the ripening of the mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) formed by the accumulation of preceding and succeeding cognitions—then it becomes the cause for the comprehension of meaning. Because it is then most clearly manifested, it is designated as the "manifested *sphoṭa*" (*sphuṭa-sphoṭa*).

Alternatively, [the word] is grasped with slight uncertainty by the cognitions of the preceding phonemes, but it is grasped with complete certainty by the cognition of the final phoneme. For instance, when "kamala" is uttered, even though there is the experience of the phonemes *ka* and *ma*, the doubt as to whether it is the lotus (*kamala*) or something else, such as *kamaṇīya* (desirable), does not depart until the final phoneme, *la* or *na*, is experienced. Therefore, the state of being slightly uncertain is indeed the state of being doubtful; and the state of being completely certain is precisely the state of being more distinct.

For this very reason, other theorists of poetics, such as the followers of Dhvani, assert that *sphoṭa* is apprehended by the intellect and is a radiant manifestation devoid of sequential order and individual phonetic forms. By this, the objection that it is impossible for a *sphoṭa*—which is partless and devoid of all generalities and particulars—to have a manifestation that is both clear and indistinct, is refuted; for, in accordance with the necessity of the comprehension of meaning, its conceptualization as a single entity is merely a product of ignorance (*avidyā*). ||14||
Joy arises from the manifestation of truth, while it appears as a false description; just as the cognition of an elephant in a distant grove is merely the perception of trees. (15)

Now, if it is argued that since the phonemes (*varṇas*) have been described as illusory manifestations (*vivarta*), how can there be a valid cognition (*pramā*) consisting of the determination of the ultimate reality, the *sphoṭa*, by means of these which are of an unreal nature? For it is never observed that a determination of an ultimately real thing arises from something that is unreal. To this, he says: "The valid cognition of the real *sphoṭa*. The sense is this: just as, when a tree stands at a distance, a cognition of an elephant—though produced through the influence of certain defects and thus unreal—nevertheless gives rise to the valid cognition of the tree by way of prompting one toward it; so too, even from the appearance of phonemes which are unreal, there arises the valid cognition of the real *sphoṭa*. ||15||

The manifestation as distinct or indistinct, which is restricted to perceptual cognition, does not arise [in other cases]; if it were to arise, then that cognition would be nothing other than a cognition based on another means of knowledge. ||16||

Now, one might object: "Just as the preceding letters, being individually indistinct, cause the final letter—when accompanied by mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—to manifest the *sphoṭa* very clearly, why does the final letter, when accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by each of the preceding letters, not likewise produce a cognition of the meaning that is itself indistinct? Why postulate such a partless *sphoṭa*? To this, he says: "Perception... [and so forth].

In the case of the direct perception that "gauḥ" is a single word, it is possible for the sphoṭa to appear as both manifest and unmanifest due to a gradation in its manifestation; however, this is not possible in the case of the indirect cognition of the denoted meaning.

For instance, when a pearl has been separated from its oyster shell, there occurs for investigators first an indistinct perception, then a distinct one, then a more distinct one, and finally a most distinct one; this is established by the path of experience. However, regarding that inferable object situated within the oyster shell, such a gradation of manifestation is not established by experience, because a means of knowledge other than direct perception functions only to manifest the mere existence of the object to be known.

And thus, since cognition produced by another means of knowledge does not arise at all when its cause is absent, but arises only when the cause is present, it follows that it is clearly unmanifest; therefore, there is no equality of status (*samānayogakṣema*) between the manifest sound and the cognition of the object. By this, the objections regarding whether letters are the manifestors individually or collectively are also refuted. As it has been said: "Even that [entity] whose partless, manifest form is manifested by the cognitions of the letters is not exempt from this same critical inquiry."

Thus [the objection] is refuted; for since the cognition of the manifest and the cognition of the meaning are respectively perceptible and imperceptible, the letters cannot be equal in their capacity to manifest them. ||16||

When there is a persistence [of a certain property] in one thing and an exclusion of it in another, the latter is distinct from the former; such is the distinction among phonemes in cases like *nadī*, *dīna*, and *jara*. (17)

Now, one might object: "The meaning of the Nyāya-sūtra, 'That which ends in an inflection is a word' (*te vibhaktyantāḥ padam*), is that those very phonemes (*varṇas*) ending in an inflection constitute a word, and not something called *sphoṭa*; therefore, there is no essence of a word (*padātman*) distinct from the phonemes, known as *sphoṭa*. To this, he says: "In which... When X persists while Y ceases to exist, Y is distinct from X; for example, when the parts of gold persist, the bracelet, crown, and so forth cease to exist [as they are transformed].
While these phonemes (varṇas) thus persist, sphoṭas such as *padātman*, *āsana*, *nadī*, *dīna*, *jarā*, *rāja*, and so forth, emerge; therefore, they too are distinct from the phonemes. ||17||
Valid cognition does not arise as long as the word-meaning (pada) is not known; for all wise men accept that the known word-meaning is the instrument [of knowledge]. (18)

Now, even so, one might object that this cognition of oneness regarding a word does not establish it as a single entity through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but is merely a cause for conventional designation (*vyapadeśa*). Just as in the case of an army consisting of elephants, horses, and so forth, or a forest consisting of *campaka*, *kāśoka*, *kiṃśuka*, and other trees, certain adventitious conditions (*upādhi*)—such as a commander who destroys enemies or a particular location—give rise to the mere designations "army" and "forest," so too here, let there be an adventitious condition such as being the cause of the apprehension of a single meaning, or the description of a connection with a single meaning.

Nor should it be understood that being a single word (*ekapadatva*) is the cause for the cognition of a single meaning; for once that [cognition] has occurred, one speaks of "being a single word," which would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). This is because the determination of being a single word is not accepted as occurring prior [to the cognition]. Indeed, the comprehension of the relationship is not dependent upon the determination of words, since it is easily known that phonemes (*varṇa*), when they ascend into a single recollection (*ekasmṛti*), convey the meaning even in the absence of [prior] word-determination.

Furthermore, it is easy to grasp the convention for multiple phonemes that constitute the object of a single recollection; subsequently, the application of the term "word" (*pada*) occurs as a functional designation (*kāraka-śabda*). Otherwise, in all functional words (*kāraka-pada*), the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) would be unavoidable.

Therefore, on account of the appearance of verbal designation (*vyapadeśa*), it is impossible to say that the essence of the word (*padātman*) is clearly manifest (*sphoṭa*) as something distinct from the phonemes, appearing in cognitions born of the auditory sense—which manifest only multiple phonemes—and in memory, which arises from the impressions deposited therein and consists of a synthesis of the previously experienced phonemes, by way of suppressing the phonemes as they appear one after another. Furthermore, in the case of the cognition "the word *gauḥ* is one," the unity that appears there is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*); it does not sublate the inherent nature (*svābhāvika*) of the word itself, which appears as a plurality.

For this very reason, there is no contradiction between unity and plurality; thus he says "pramā" (valid cognition). Indeed, one does not understand the meaning from a word without having ascertained the nature and limits of that word—for instance, in cases such as "She has come to the stage," one who does not know the word *sā* (she) lacks the comprehension of the intended meaning. Therefore, one understands the meaning from a word only when the nature and limits of that single word are known; for all disputants consider a word, being already known, to be the instrument (*karaṇa*) for another person.

Likewise, the designation of a "single word" (ekapadatva) does not preclude the expression of a relation between a single meaning. To explain: it is not observed that isolated phonemes, which have not yet attained the status of a word, possess the capacity to convey meaning; nor would they possess such capacity even if uttered in a specific sequence. However, if unconnected [phonemes] were to convey meaning, then any meaning whatsoever might be understood from any source at all. Therefore, a relation must necessarily be asserted.

And that status of being a word (*padatva*) is possible for phonemes (*varṇa*) only by virtue of having attained such a state. Furthermore, that word-status does not arise through a sequential manifestation of such a form. If one were to postulate word-status based on a relationship and a designation, there would certainly be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*): word-status exists when there is a relationship and a designation; designation exists when there is a relationship; and word-status exists when there is a designation of the relationship. Moreover, it would result in a vicious circle (*cakraka*): word-status exists when there is a relationship; relationship exists when there is a designation of the relationship; designation of the relationship exists when there is word-status; and word-status exists when there is a designation of the relationship.

However, it is precisely the established nature of denotation that is being explained here. As for what was stated by the author of the *Līlāvatī*: "The cognition 'this is one word' is possible through the delimitation of having a single suffix (sup or tiṅ); in this regard, the factor to be accepted as the determinant of 'wordhood' (*padatva*) is the delimitation of having a single suffix, while the factor for 'sentencehood' (*vākyatva*) is the delimitation of having multiple suffixes. [This is the required translation.]

If there were no difference in the nature of *sphoṭa* itself, how could the diverse linguistic practices—such as "this is a word-sphoṭa" and "this is a sentence-sphoṭa"—be established? That cannot be the case, because it is impossible to state a single, recurring property that serves as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of "word-ness" (*padatva*) for both nominal stems ending in *sup*-suffixes and verbal roots ending in *tiṅ*-suffixes. Furthermore, since being either one or the other (i.e., being a stem or a suffix) lacks the status of a delimitor due to its complexity (*gaurava*), nor can it be argued that "being a suffix denoting number" is the recurring property.

Because there is no single, inclusive [property] that serves as a suffix; for since the etymological meaning of *pratyaya*—that by which an object is cognized—is common to bases (*prakṛti*) and so forth, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *ekaka*, where the suffix *ka* expresses the sense of "alone" (*eka*).

In the view that maintains the existence of word-sphoṭa (*padasphoṭa*), the word-sphoṭa—which is manifested by those respective letters ending in case-terminations and which generates the conventional usage of words—is itself what brings about the manifestation of the sentence-meaning through the power of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors. Therefore, in this theory of word-sphoṭa, there is no acceptance of the sentence as being an illusory appearance (*vivarta*). However, in the theory of an eternal, partless sentence-sphoṭa (*vākyasphoṭa*), there is no such defect, because the word—consisting of letters ending in case-terminations—is accepted as being an illusory appearance of that [sentence-sphoṭa].

Therefore, it is logical to consider that this cognition of the multiplicity of phonemes, being sublated by the non-conditional cognition of their unity, turns away from its [erroneous] objective support and takes the *sphoṭa*—the substratum itself—as its objective support. Thus we conclude. 18.
In this single manifestation as "cow," one might desire some limiting adjunct (upādhi); yet without that [adjunct], it would be neither one nor many. (19)

Furthermore, if the cognition of oneness regarding "cow" (*gauḥ*)—which is uncontradicted even for those who deny perception—were merely due to the delusion of a lack of faith in their own tenets or the epilepsy of confusion, then, because any arbitrary limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) could be imagined everywhere, the cognition of oneness would never be ultimately real. In the absence of that [oneness], and consequently in the absence of the cognition of duality and so forth which is based upon it, this entire world would become a mere void; therefore, he says: "Regarding 'cow'... For those disputants who hold such views, there is no entity whatsoever without that [oneness]. (19)
Now, according to the Nyāya view, the process of word formation (*padaprakriyā*) is as follows:

First, there is one moment (1) consisting of the production of the impression (*saṃskāra*) from the cognition of the first phoneme, coinciding with the destruction of that cognition. Then, there is another moment (2) consisting of the production of the cognition of the second phoneme from the production of that impression, coinciding with the destruction of the cognition of the first phoneme, and the production of the impression of the second phoneme from the cognition of the second phoneme accompanied by the impression produced by the experience of the preceding phoneme.

Although the production of a cognition occurs through the proximity of the cause of production and its destruction occurs through the proximity of the cause of destruction—and since that cognition belongs to the second phoneme, there is no causal relationship [between the first and second phonemes]—nevertheless, this [cognition] possesses the status of being a cause with respect to the production and destruction of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of each preceding phoneme.

Then, at the first moment [of the fourth stage], the impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of the second phoneme arises; simultaneously, the recollection of the two preceding phonemes, which was being generated by the two impressions born from the experience of those two preceding phonemes acting as auxiliaries to the experience of the [second] phoneme, comes into being—this constitutes one moment (1). Then, at the second moment, the recollection of the two phonemes arises; the experience of the other phoneme [the first one] perishes; the cognition of the second phoneme perishes; and then the recollection of the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) begins to arise—this constitutes one moment (4).

Then, at one and the same time: (1) the arising of the recollection of the convention (*saṃketa-smṛti*), (2) the destruction of the recollection of the two preceding phonemes, (3) the destruction of the experience of the final phoneme, and (4) the state of being about to arise of the comprehension of the word-meaning (*padārtha-pratipatti*). Then, at another [moment], at one and the same time: (1) the arising of the comprehension of the word-meaning, (2) the destruction of the instrument that produced it, (3) the state of being about to perish of the recollection of the convention, and (4) the state of being about to arise of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the word-meaning.

Then, there is the production of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) from that [last phoneme] (1); the destruction of the existence of the word-meaning cognition (2); and the destruction of the recollection of the convention (*saṃketa*) (3)—these constitute one distinct moment. Then, there is the destruction of the word-meaning cognition itself due to the [continued] production of the mental impression (4). Even though, in this process, at the very time of the recollection of the convention, the experience of the preceding phonemes has been destroyed by that recollection, and thus its capacity to cause the cognition of the word-meaning is impossible; nevertheless, since the entire sequence beginning with the experience of the final phoneme and ending with the recollection of the word is merely a conceptual construction (*vyāpāra*), there is no fault. Now, the process regarding the sentence (*vākya*).

The arising of the experience of the phonemes [of the word], the non-disappearance of the remembrance, and the simultaneous arising of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) and the reconnection of the word (*padapratisaṃdhāna*)—these constitute one moment (1). Then, the arising of those two [the impression and the reconnection]—which consists in the very nature of the reconnection of the word—is the awakening of the mental impression of the conventional usage; at that same time, there is the state of the remembrance of the relationship [between word and meaning] being about to arise, and the state of the mental impression [of the word] ceasing as it produces its various effects—these constitute one moment (2).

Now, this duration of time consists of the subsistence of the memory of the preceding phonemes, the destruction of the cognition of the final phoneme, and the process of recollecting the words; it is a momentary interval. Thus, through the force of the experience of the final phoneme accompanied by the cumulative collection of memories of each preceding phoneme, and through the force of the memories and experiences of those states that are in the process of perishing or have already perished, as well as through the auditory impressions (*saṃskāra*), there arises a single, diverse cognition in the form of both memory and experience which apprehends the final phoneme along with the preceding phonemes that have ceased. This very cognition is the cause of the comprehension of the sentence-meaning.

And thus the view of the Logicians (*tārkika*) has been demonstrated by the author of the *Bhaṭṭavārttika*: "Some say that this cognition, which possesses a variegated form and has both existent and non-existent phonemes as its object, is like the way a phoneme is grasped at every step within a word. In that regard, it has been explained more than once that in the formation of a word, the capacity to convey meaning does not reside in the phonemes themselves, but rather in a memory that takes as its object the collection of those phonemes; this memory is produced by the cumulative mental impressions (*bhāvanākūṭa*) formed by the experience of each preceding phoneme, and it functions through the mediation of the recollection of those phonemes.

The theory of the manifestation of sentences (*vākya-prakriyā*) is also not authoritative. This is because even from a collection of prior memories arising from the experience of each individual phoneme, there cannot arise simultaneously a manifold cognition in the form of a single experience of the entire sentence. As stated by the venerable Vācaspati Miśra in the *Tattvabindu*: "Nor can that memory, which is produced dependent on the impressions awakened by the [individual] phonemes, arise simultaneously with the [direct] experience."

Nor is the production of the phonemes [in sequence] logical, because the causal capacity for producing a cognition does not exist when there is no simultaneity of the causes. Thus, the masters of the *Tattvabindu* have stated its summary: "The perception of the phonemes, whether occurring in succession or beyond memory, does not bring about the comprehension of the sentence-meaning; nor is there memory [of them], because it depends on that [perception]; nor is there simultaneity between these two."

The meaning of this is as follows: at the time of the recollection of the preceding letter, there is no experience of the subsequent letter because it has not yet arisen; and at the time of the experience of the subsequent letter, the recollection of the preceding letter no longer exists because it has already passed. This is also stated by Vācaspatimiśra in the second commentary (*Tattvavaiśāradī*): "Furthermore, does this perception of a subsequent letter produce the cognition of the object by depending on the recollection of the convention regarding its own meaning, or without depending upon it?"

At the time of the recollection of the convention regarding the first letter, the hearing of the subsequent letters has ceased because they are momentary; thus, what recollection could it require? And at the time of hearing the subsequent letters, the recollection of the convention has not yet arisen; thus, what cognition of the preceding letters could it require? If there were no dependence on the recollection of the convention, then even for one who has never grasped the convention, the cognition of the meaning would result upon hearing the first letter alone. Therefore, it is established that the cognition of the meaning arises from the manifestation of the word, or rather, from the manifestation of the sentence.
For this very reason, it is stated elsewhere in detail that the origin of the world is from the Word (*śabda*). And for this same reason, it is said in the *Āgama* as well:

"May that Light, which the virtuous describe as the Brahman consisting of Word, which resides within the interior of consciousness, and which is the abode of the moon—the sovereign of speech—protect you incessantly.
Enough with this excessive detail.
May this garland of pearls from the well-spoken verses of various systems, strung together by Kṛṣṇa, shine upon the necks of both the learned who are free from malice and even the wicked. 1.
That which is experienced everywhere through the relationship of action and agent—that is the inner self (pratyagātman), the victorious glory consisting of the Brahman of sound (śabdatattva). 2.

The glorious word "Brahman" (brahmābhidha), which is the subject of the venerable Bhāṣya, has been elucidated by the learned Śrī Kṛṣṇatāta Śeṣa, in accordance with the consensus [of the tradition], as the manifestation of its true essence. ||3||
Whether it be defiled or adorned by learned men—who manifest both the existent and the non-existent, who extract the essence, and who are free from passion and hatred—let it be so. (4)
Thus ends the *Sphuṭatattvanirūpaṇa* composed by Śrī Śeṣakṛṣṇa.
Having bowed at the pair of feet of my parents and of Jānakī and Raghunātha, Mauni Śrī Kṛṣṇabhaṭṭa composes this *Sphoṭatattvacandrikā*. 1.

Among grammarians, the term *sphoṭa* is used for either words—whether denotative (*vācaka*), indicative (*lākṣaṇika*), or suggestive (*vyañjaka*)—which convey their respective expressed, indicated, or suggested meanings, or for the universal (*jāti*) residing in them. The word *sphoṭa* is both etymological (*yogika*) and conventional (*rūḍha*), like the word *paṅkaja* ("lotus"), according to the derivation: "that from which meaning bursts forth (*sphuṭati*). If one were to accept only the etymological sense, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to words that merely convey expressed, indicated, or suggested meanings.

Furthermore, the synonym for the signifier (*vācaka*) known as *sphoṭa* is not unestablished; for it is seen in the *Harivaṃśa*: "The nature of the letters is *sphoṭa*, while the nature of *sphoṭa* does not depend on the letters. Thus, there are five types of *sphoṭa*: the *varṇasphoṭa*, the *padasphoṭa*, the *vākyasphoṭa*, the *akhaṇḍapadasphoṭa*, and the *akhaṇḍavākyasphoṭa*. According to the view that the denotatum (*vācya*) is a genus (*jāti*) delimited by the capacity [to denote], and that the signifier (*vācaka*) is a genus delimited by the capacity [to signify], there are three types of *jātisphoṭa*: the *varṇajātisphoṭa*, the *padajātisphoṭa*, and the *vākyajātisphoṭa*.

Thus, there are eight types of *sphoṭas*. Just as in the *Ānandavallī*, for the sake of knowing the pure Brahman, the means employed is the teaching of the non-ultimate nature of Brahman through the five sheaths (*kośas*)—consisting of food, vital breath, mind, intellect, and bliss; or just as, for the sake of knowing the star Arundhatī, one is led to it by first identifying the non-ultimate star Sthūlālakā as Arundhatī; so too, for the sake of attaining the ultimate, indivisible realization of the sentence-meaning, these *sphoṭas*—consisting of letters, words, sentences, and the indivisible word-sphere—are the means. As it has been said: "The means [employed] for those in training are merely ways of coaxing children."

"Standing upon the path of untruth, one then strives for the truth. Thus, since neither the definition of a *pada*—namely, "a word consists of an inflected nominal stem (*su*) or a finite verb (*tiṅ*)"—nor the definition of a *vākya*—namely, "a sentence consists of that which has a single finite verb as its primary qualificand"—applies to a mere collection of phonemes, nor to a phoneme alone, nor to what consists of a base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*), nor to forms such as *pac*, *tip*, and so forth, whose expressive power (*śakti*) has not been grasped through grammatical analysis, there exists the *varṇasphoṭa* (the phoneme-sphoṭa) as the denoter.

Furthermore, those [elements] such as *visarga* and *ti* are inherent in the actual application (*prayoga*), whereas the *sakāra*, *lakāra*, and so forth are not postulated as such because they are not fixed. For instance, by means of *visarga* there is the recollection of *ru*, and by that, of *su*; likewise, by means of *ṇal* there is the recollection of *tip*, and by that, of the *lakāra*. Thus, the resulting complexity (*gaurava*) is quite evident. Moreover, for a grammarian who lacks knowledge of the original locus (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of understanding the meaning from the substitute alone.

Thus, the claim of the logicians—that the *sthāny-ādeśa* relationship exists only in the case of the substituend (*sthānin*) for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*), whereas it does not exist in the case of the substitute (*ādeśa*) due to its complexity (*gaurava*)—is refuted; for that would result in the opposite kind of complexity. This is the view held by the logicians regarding the nature of the sphoṭa. Grammarians (*śābdikas*), however, maintain that this is incorrect because there is no proof (*māna*), no occasion (*phala*), and because it contradicts the treatises (*grantha-virodha*). To explain: a word (*pada*) possessing expressive power (*śakta*) is fourfold—etymological (*rūḍha*), derivative (*yaugika*), etymological-derivative (*yogarūḍha*), and derivative-etymological (*yaugikarūḍha*).

"Ox," "cook," "lotus," and "horse-ear" are the examples in order. Among these, regarding the derivative example "cook" (*pācaka*), that word which consists of the parts *pac* and *aka* is not itself derivative; and although the whole (*samudāya*) is derivative, it is nonetheless not [itself] expressive (*śakta*). Thus, the claim that "an expressive word is derivative" is an unexamined statement.

When there is a specific capacity [for a word], its status as a *yaugika* (etymological) word consists in being a *pada*—whether a *subanta* (nominal) or *tiṅanta* (verbal)—which is a collection of a stem (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) whose meanings are indicated by grammar. This is stated in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to *rūḍha-yogika* (conventional-etymological) words, because in those cases the apprehension of the capacity for the specific [meaning] occurs [directly].

Likewise, the example of *gauraḥ* as a conventional (*rūḍhi*) word is also inconsistent; for the definition of a conventional word is that which, while lacking the cognition of the meanings of stems and suffixes as conceived by grammar, conveys meaning through their collection as a *subanta* or *tiṅanta*, such as *maṇi*, *nūpura*, and so forth, since it is not subject to the definition of conventionality [if it were merely etymological].

The state of being both etymological and conventional (*yogarūḍhatva*) consists in a word’s capacity to convey a collective meaning based on a prior consideration of the meanings of its constituent parts as determined by the technical treatises (e.g., *paṅkaja* and so forth). Since [the term *yogarūḍha*] is occupied by that [definition], it is appropriate that it be *yogarūḍha*. Furthermore, the distinction stated by the logicians (*tārkika*) regarding the term *yaugikarūḍha* is also untenable.

According to the logical principle that "a word uttered once conveys its meaning only once," the term *maṇḍapa* is distinct when it is conventionally fixed (*rūḍha*) to a specific type of house, and distinct when it refers to one who prepares a drink (*maṇḍayapānakartṛ*). This is because there is no evidence for accepting an additional distinction [between the two senses]. Likewise, the example "skillful in action" (*karmaṇi kuśalaḥ*) cited as an instance of conventional metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is also incorrect; for, according to the aforementioned reasoning, the quality of being conventionally fixed (*rūḍhatva*) applies to the sense of "skillful," while the quality of being etymological (*yaugikatva*) applies to the sense of "one who gathers grass" (*kuśādānakartṛ*).

The word *dvirepha* is indeed established in the sense of a "bee," because it is included among the synonyms for "bee" in the *Kośa*. For there is no inclusion of a term as a synonym when it is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*). Thus, the claim of the Logicians—that the word *dvirepha* has no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of "bee" due to the absence of a relation between its own denotative parts and the denotation of that sense—is refuted. Furthermore, since the aforementioned relation exists even in the case of Akrūra, their definition would suffer from over-extension (*ativyāpti*) there as well.

Alternatively, all phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves possess the nature of *sphoṭa*, as their expressive power is established by the *Ekākṣarakośa* (the Lexicon of Single Phonemes), and because this is likewise demonstrated in the *Mahābhāṣya* by the statement, "Phonemes are meaningful" (*arthavanto varṇāḥ*). Nor does it follow that, in cases such as *dhanaṃ* or *vanaṃ*, each individual phoneme would incur the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), because of the power residing in the aggregate (*samudāyaśakti*). This is because the power residing in the aggregate acts as an inhibitor toward any grammatical operation whose purpose is to destroy the specific sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) which serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for that very power's locus.

As for the claim in the *Bhūṣaṇa* that the word *sphoṭa* is used in its purely etymological sense—where *sphuṭati* means "that from which the meaning bursts forth" (i.e., a denoter)—this is not correct. For if corrupt words (*asādhuśabda*) were to possess the same expressive power (*śakti*) as correct words (*sādhuśabda*), they would be indistinguishable in their status as denoters and would consequently result in being called *sphoṭa*. Nor is this a desirable consequence, as grammarians do not accept it; furthermore, it would lead to the failure to include metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*) and suggestive (*vyañjaka*) words within the definition.

Furthermore, one should not fall into the error of thinking that because of the mention of "here" (*atra*) in the statement, "The word is the manifestor here in three ways," the manifestor exists only in the ear and not in the articulatory organs (*vyāpāra*). This is because those who maintain that the indivisible *sphoṭa* is manifested by the word accept [the manifestation] as occurring through the very act of articulation. Now, in the view of the Logicians (*Tārkika*), power (*śakti*) is the will of God; in the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, it is a distinct category (*padārtha*) in its own right; and by the Neo-Logicians, it is either the knowledge or the volitional effort (*kṛti*) of God. Since there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) among these, the view of the Mīmāṃsakas alone has been accepted.

If it is argued that "correctness" (sādhutva) belongs to both [the correct and the incorrect] and does not reside in the incorrect, otherwise, since the possession of expressive power (*śaktimattva*) would be the definition of correctness, it would follow that even incorrect words possess correctness because they are characterized by that very definition; furthermore, this is untenable because there is an absence of lexicons and other means for grasping the expressive power—[we reply]: No, for if there were no expressive power in those [incorrect words], comprehension from them would not occur. Nor is the view of the Logicians (*Tārkika*) tenable—that comprehension arises either from an error regarding expressive power or from the recollection of a correct word—because it is established by direct experience that comprehension occurs even for those who do not know the correct words, and because such a theory involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Nor can it be said that this [apprehension] is a cognition arising from error; for even in the case of mother-of-pearl grasped through the error of silver, there arises no cognition produced by an error regarding the capacity [of the object] to effect the practical activity associated with silver, since such a cognition would likewise fail to effect that practical activity. Furthermore, it is impossible to maintain the absence here of the Lord’s will, which has pure existence (*sanmātra*) as its object. Moreover, whose error of capacity could it be? It must belong either to the Lord, the agent of all practical activities, or to someone else. Not the first, because it is untenable for the Lord himself to be subject to error. Nor the second.

Because at the beginning of creation, there exists no other agent than God who could engage in the usage of correct, incorrect, and indeterminate words as the instigator and the instigated; just as the creation of objects that produce both merit and demerit has God as its agent, so too the creation of both types of words—correct and incorrect—has God alone as its agent. Thus, [the claim] that it is an error is utterly untenable.

Nor can there be an erroneous inference for a neutral observer; for since the causal complex capable of producing an inference exists equally for corrupt words as it does for correct words, and since there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka), it is impossible for it to be an error. If it is objected: "If one accepts that even corrupt words possess expressive power (śakti), then since 'possessing śakti' constitutes correctness according to the definition of the logicians, it would follow that these words are correct. Consequently, there would be no scope for the prohibition: 'One should not speak barbarously, nor should one use corrupt speech. This is not so.

Otherwise, there would be the consequence of grammatical incorrectness (*asādhutā*) for words that possess specific linguistic characteristics (*lākṣaṇika*). Nor is it simply the state of having a function (*vṛttimattva*); for if one were not to include either *śakti* (primary denotative power) or *lakṣaṇā* (indicative power), there would be excessive complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is a specific universal (*jāti*) that delimits the capacity to produce comprehension, while grammatical incorrectness (*asādhutva*) is that which delimits the capacity to produce transgression (*pratyavāya*). Alternatively, grammatical correctness is simply being understood through the grammar treatises, and grammatical incorrectness is being different from that.

And thus, by the Grammarian [Patañjali] stating, "A single word, correctly understood and properly employed, becomes a cow of plenty in the heavenly world," it is known that the word is understood through its derivation from a specific meaning via stem and suffix; and it is employed in such a specific sense. Therefore, for the word *goṇī* (ox-cart), correctness (*sādhutva*) resides only in the ox-cart and not in a cow. The argument that this is unjustified due to a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) is also not tenable.

For the principle that determines between two alternatives is indeed a logical reason (*yukti*), and in this context, it takes the form of the prior manifestation of knowledge. For this very reason, the teacher Vardhamānopādhyāya maintains that the knowledge of God (*īśvarajñāna*) is the *śakti* (power). The Grammarians (*śābdikās*), however, hold that power is the capacity to produce cognition (*bodhanakatva*). And that [capacity] consists in possessing a property that delimits the generative cause of beginningless cognition. As stated by Hari: "Just as there is an innate, beginningless fitness (*yogyatā*) of the sense organs toward their respective objects, so too is there for words an innate connection with their meanings, characterized by such fitness."

Competency (*yogyatā*) consists in the possession of a property that delimits the capacity to produce that [understanding]. Now, since verbal understanding does not arise for one who has not grasped the word-meaning relation (*śakti*), and since the grasp of the relation is a cause for verbal understanding, it would follow that the grasp of the relation occurs after the understanding, and the understanding occurs after the grasp of the relation; thus, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). This is because the relation is grasped through means such as a lexicon or the instruction of a teacher. Furthermore, even under the view that the relation is the will of God (*īśvarecchā*), the mutual dependence remains equal, as the understanding would occur after the grasp of the relation, and the grasp of the relation would occur after the understanding.

Alternatively, the power (*śakti*) is the beginningless relationship between word and meaning. However, it occurs to me that *śakti* is simply capacity (*sāmarthya*). Just as in the case of light, such as that of a lamp, the capacity for being perceived and for perceiving exists by virtue of its own nature (*svarūpasat*), and not because it is known; and just as in fire and the like, the capacity for burning exists by virtue of its own nature, and in the sense organs, the capacity for illuminating objects exists by virtue of its own nature—and this is what is effective, not the knowledge of it—so too in the case of a word, the capacity for being perceived and for perceiving exists by virtue of its own nature and is what is effective, not the knowledge of it.

Nor does it follow that there would be comprehension even when the capacity [of the word] has not been grasped; for, as in the case of sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) and other factors, this is because the absence of the grasp of *tātparya* (intention) acts as the cause for the absence of comprehension. If it is objected: "In the case of words with multiple meanings (*nānārtha*), the grasp of *tātparya* alone is the cause [of comprehension]," we reply: True. However, according to the view of the Grammarians (*Śābdika*), all words possess multiple meanings. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *vṛddhir ādaic* that "a word has many capacities" (*anekaśakteḥ śabdasya*). The analysis of the compound is: "one which has many [meanings], or whose capacity is manifold."

The established doctrine of the Naiyāyikas and others is that there is a difference in power (*śaktibheda*) corresponding to the difference in the delimiters (*avacchedaka*). The conclusion of the Grammarians (*śābdika*), however, is that due to parsimony (*lāghava*), the power of the word is one and the same. Nor should it be argued that this results in polysemy (*anekārthatva*); for such a fault applies equally to your own position as well. The only difference is this: in your view, [the meanings are conveyed] by different functions (*vṛtti*), whereas in my view, they are conveyed by a single function. Furthermore, there is no consequence of the abolition of the theory of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because that is precisely what is desired.

Just as you do not accept [the existence of *sphoṭa*], although it is established by all experience, because of parsimony (*lāghava*), and since you consider the consequence of the cessation of manifestation (*vyañjana*) to be non-defective; likewise, even though we [maintain the existence of *sphoṭa*], we achieve our goal through parsimony alone, for the consequence of the cessation of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is considered non-defective.

The meaning of that [statement] is simply this: when the purpose is accomplished by a single occurrence (*ekavṛtti*) of the entity (*vastu*), it is improper to postulate multiple occurrences; for the word "object" (*artha*) refers here to the occurrence (*vṛtti*). Furthermore, the phrase "others and others" is rooted in the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*). Nor should it be said that words have meanings not obtainable through other means; for its meaning is not that it is improper to postulate a primary denotative power (*śakti*) when it can be obtained through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), but rather that it is improper to postulate a denotative power when the meaning is already established through the condition of syntactic relation (*saṃsargamaryādā*).

Thus, while the Grammarians (Śābdikas) accept an additional power (*atiśaya-śakti*) in fire with respect to sound, the Logicians (Tārkikas), however, accept this power in sound but not in fire; such acceptance of a "half-old-woman" position (*ardha-jaratīya*) is improper. Nor should it be argued that since the phenomenon can be explained by the absence of the gem qualified by the absence of an excitant (*uttejaka*), there is no need to accept that [additional] power; for it is more appropriate to posit a relation to an additional power—which, though distinct, is simpler—than to accept a causal status (*kāraṇatāvacchedakatva*) based on a cumbersome qualified entity.
