Furthermore, according to the Grammarians (Śābdikas), identity-in-difference (*tādātmya*) is admitted even where there is difference characterized by qualities, substances, and so forth; for a substance is never perceived without its qualities, nor are qualities ever perceived without a substance. Thus, wherever inherence (*samavāya*) exists, there is the conventional usage of "identity-in-difference."

And thus, since it is impossible for the jar to exist prior to its quality [of color], it lacks causality with respect to that quality; therefore, by the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (*anyathānupapatti*), they accept that the qualified [entity] alone serves as the delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*). Consequently, it is maintained that the potsherd qualified by the quality [of color] is the cause of the jar qualified by that same quality.

However, the logicians (Tārkikas), because the qualified entity cannot be the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) of causality and because it is impossible for that which is qualified by a quality to be the cause, have accepted the production of a jar devoid of qualities. In that context, they have formulated a definition [of substance] as "that which is not pervaded by the characteristics of being a substratum of qualities, having color, and being a substance," and "possessing a genus that is co-extensive with substance-ness and resides in the same locus as qualities. This, however, appears to me to be incorrect. To explain:

Although the power (*śakti*) in fire is known through both positive and negative concomitance, the existence of a separate power has been refuted by accepting that the cause is simply the absence of the magnet (*maṇi*), qualified by the absence of an excitant (*uttejaka*). Yet, that same [separate] power is accepted in the case of sound. Likewise, having accepted that the qualified [absence of the magnet] is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) there, it is here denied; thus, like a sky-flower, the production of a qualityless jar is accepted. Since none of these are grounded in experience, all of this is merely an unworthy fabrication. This is the direction of the argument.

The grammarians (Śābdikas), however, maintain that there is a distinct power (*śakti*) residing in the space within the cavity of the ear, which is like fire for sound; or rather, it is the auditory space itself as qualified by that power. Thus, even though the drum-sound originates at a distance, the single auditory organ possesses the capacity to illuminate it—like a lamp—even while remaining in its own place. Consequently, the view that the drum-sound travels to the location of hearing according to the analogy of waves and ripples is not pleasing.

Otherwise, one would fall into the error of denying the experience expressed as "I am directly hearing the sound of the drum. Furthermore, it is cumbersome to postulate multiple sounds. Nor is it reasonable to claim that the auditory organ itself travels there, because movement is impossible for space (ākāśa), and because it would entail the absence of space within the cavity of the ear. Thus, the auditory faculty produces the direct perception of the quality alone.

Some, however, maintain that the gustatory and olfactory organs, like the auditory organ, produce the direct perception of their respective qualities alone. Others say this is incorrect. For instance, since sound and taste are qualities of space and earth respectively, and because direct contact (*sannikarṣa*) is possible through conjunction (*saṃyoga*), direct perception may indeed occur in those cases; however, in the case of taste and smell, the proximity is "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyukta-samavāya*). And since this requires a connection with a substance, there is no mutual connection [between the sense organ and the quality itself].

In that case, since there is no direct perception of a substance without the presence of sense-object contact, and since there is no possibility of a direct perception of a quality alone because a quality does not exist independently of a substance, it follows that these two [the eye and the tongue] produce the direct perception of a quality as qualified by a substance; they do not, however, produce the direct perception of a substance as qualified by a quality. This is because such a conclusion can be inferred from experience in exactly that way.

In the case of the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) and the tactile faculty (*tvagindriya*), however, there is the capacity to produce direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of both kinds: namely, either a substance qualified by its qualities or a quality qualified by its substance. A detailed exposition, however, should be sought in my *Tarkāmṛta* (The Nectar of Logic), which explains the meaning of words; it is not elaborated here for fear of prolixity. This is the direction [of the argument].

Let us return to our main subject. Even though an incorrect word (*asādhu-śabda*) possesses denotative power (*vācakatva*), it lacks the status of *sphoṭa* because it is not what is expounded by grammar. As for the individual phonemes (*varṇa*) contained within it, however, since their capacity is determined by monosyllabic lexicons (*ekākṣara-kośa*) and they manifest a distinct meaning, this is the "word-sphoṭa" (*pada-sphoṭa*), which will be analyzed under the section on word-sphoṭa. Furthermore, regarding words that are mere imitations (*anukaraṇa-śabda*), because there is an intention to distinguish between the object being imitated and the imitation itself, they convey an object in the form of that which is being imitated; thus, they possess the nature of *sphoṭa*.

[Objection: But surely, if imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is considered correct (*sādhu*) because it possesses correctness, then how can there be the linguistic usage of "sphoṭa" for the imitation of that which is incorrect? [Response: This is not so, because we do not accept that even the imitation of what is incorrect lacks correctness. For instance, when the Daityas ought to have said *he 'rayaḥ*, they instead said *he 'layaḥ*; yet in the statement, "Imitating that by saying *helayo helayaḥ*, they did not perish," there is no lack of correctness in that [imitation].

Likewise, regarding the statement, "Let it be for us either thus or not thus," when people utter the imitation *yavāraṇastalvāṇo bhavatu*, even though there is a sentence such as "there were sages named Yarvāṇas and Tārvāṇas" [based on that], no one at all accepts its lack of grammatical correctness (*asādhutva*). Therefore, the correctness of an imitation of what is incorrect is accepted by everyone. This is the direction [of the argument]: that phonemes (*varṇasphoṭa*) exist for the sake of communicating the indivisible sentence-meaning (*akhaṇḍavākyārtha*), which—like the food-sheath (*annamaya-kośa*) that is external to all—is for the sake of the knowledge of the pure Brahman. This is the general principle.

Thus ends the discussion on the *varṇasphoṭa* (the word-sound as a collection of phonemes). Now, the *padasphoṭa* (the word-sound as a unitary entity) is described; it is more internal (*antaraṅga*) than the *varṇasphoṭa*, just as the *prāṇamaya-kośa* (the vital sheath) is more internal than the *annamaya-kośa* (the physical sheath). Its internality consists in its being a direct constituent of the sentence, whereas the externality of the phoneme consists in its being a constituent of the word only by way of the word's production. The *padasphoṭa* is twofold: with parts (*sakhaṇḍa*) and without parts (*akhaṇḍa*), because the apprehension of the linguistic capacity (*śakti*) occurs precisely in the word through usage and other means.

In this regard, for the Naiyāyikas, who hold that a word is a meaningful unit (*śaktaṃ padam*), the *vākya-sphoṭa* consists of a collection of inflected words (*subanta*) and verbal forms (*tiṅanta*) such as "rāmaḥ" and "pacati," which are accompanied by their constituent parts. Now, the indivisible *pada-sphoṭa* is being defined. That [sphoṭa] is manifested by all the phonemes situated within a word; and its function is the communication of meaning—this is the established doctrine of the Grammarians (*śābdika*).

Nor is it the case that there is no denotative power (*pratyāyakatva*) in what is already known; otherwise, the statement "one knows the word" would result in the undesirable consequence of "one knows the meaning," which would contradict the Bhāṣya on the rule *aṇudit* (Pāṇini 1.1.69). The meaning of that [Bhāṣya] is not that there is no denotative power in what is known in a general sense, but rather that there is no denotative power in a phoneme (*varṇa*) that is known by means of a technical name (*saṃjñā*) such as "word" (*śabda*). This is because that [general rule] is restricted by the requirements of the specific context.

Thus, having raised the objection that there would be no transgression (anāpatti) for one who perceives a book in private due to the cognition of its meaning, the view of the Navyas—that even in that case there is a subtle manifestation (*sūkṣmābhivyakti*) of the word—is refuted; for it contradicts experience. As for what the Tārkikas and Vedāntins say in this regard—whether [the sphoṭa] is manifested by all the phonemes (*varṇa*), or manifested by some phoneme or other, or manifested by the final phoneme—it cannot be the first, because a conjunction of things that perish so rapidly is impossible. Nor can it be the second.

Regarding the claim that the sphoṭa is perceived through the word-sound (*śabda*), the letter *ṭa* is redundant. It is not the third [alternative] either; for since the cognition of meaning is established by the final letter itself, accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each preceding letter, what is the use of a sphoṭa? In this regard, there is no evidence for the instantaneous destruction of letters. Nor is the cognition "the letter *ga* has arisen" or "the letter *ga* has perished" a valid means of proof; for, as in the case of the statement "space was produced," such [cognitions] can be explained through manifestation and disappearance.

Furthermore, it is cumbersome to postulate the destruction of an infinite series of prior absences (*prāgabhāva*). Even if [the sphoṭa] were non-eternal, there is no possibility of its merging with the memory produced by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) generated from the experience of the phonemes. Nor is the second [phoneme] redundant; for when the word "paśu" is uttered, it serves a purpose by removing the doubt as to whether it is *paṭa-sphoṭa*, *uṭ-pada-sphoṭa*, or *payaḥ-sphoṭa*.

In the third case, just as a cloth is accepted as a distinct whole (*avayavin*) by me, even though the final conjunction—qualified by the conjunctions with dissimilar threads—is itself the cause of the effect that is the cloth; so too is it accepted by me [in this instance]. Nor can it be said that there is a distinct cloth because of such experience, for the same applies to the destruction of the cloth, and because of the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*). Furthermore, it is more cumbersome (*gaurava*) [to posit a distinct whole].

If it is asked, "But how is there simplicity (lāghava) in the case of the sphoṭa? listen: the sphoṭa is manifested by the sounds (dhvanis) alone. Thus, there is extreme simplicity because one need not postulate an infinite number of phonemes (varṇas), their prior absences, and their destructions; nor need one assert that sequential order (ānupūrvya)—which serves to produce distinct cognitions of meaning in cases such as *nadī*, *dīna*, *sara*, *rasa*, *jarā*, and *rāja*—is a cause, along with the final phoneme assisted by the latent impressions (saṃskāra) produced by the experience of the preceding phonemes. For you [the proponent of the sphoṭa], this must be asserted, whereas for us [the proponents of the phoneme theory], it is more cumbersome.

By this much of an introduction, having first refuted the fallacious objections raised by the Grammarians and others, I shall now explain the *sphoṭa*—which is distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), which is inseparable from the phonemes, and which, as it is said, "is the consciousness of all beings; my conviction is that the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) is [this]," and thus constitutes the form of the Word-Brahman.

It is also stated by another method: the indivisible word-sphoṭa (*akhaṇḍa-pada-sphoṭa*) is not something distinct [from the parts]. That which is called by the logicians (*tārkika*) and others a "derivative" (*yaugika*) or "conventional-derivative" (*yogarūḍha*) word—such as *pācaka* (cook) or *paṅkaja* (lotus)—is designated by us as the divisible word-sphoṭa (*sakhaṇḍa-pada-sphoṭa*), because the apprehension of the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) occurs there preceded by the synthesis of the individual parts through lexicons and other means. However, for one who lacks knowledge of grammar and apprehends the collective power solely through common usage, that very [word] is the indivisible word-sphoṭa.

As for those words that are conventional (rūḍha), such as *maṇi* (jewel) or *nūpura* (anklet), which you [the Naiyāyikas] claim are not [composed of parts], these are indeed accepted by all [schools] as indivisible word-sphoṭas (*akhaṇḍa-pada-sphoṭa*). This is because, in all such cases, the apprehension of the power (*śakti*) resides in the whole through usage characterized by the absence of knowledge of the meanings of the constituent parts. Thus, since conventional and etymological words, as well as divisible and indivisible sphoṭas, are synonymous, the dispute is merely over names; this is the direction of the argument. Consequently, the fallacious refutations of the logicians (*tārkika*) and others are struck down by a miscarriage of their own arguments; this is the direction of the argument.

There is no rule that only the logic of the logicians (tārkika) and others constitutes sound reasoning (*sattarka*), for even therein one frequently encounters unsound reasoning (*asattarka*) that is not supported by experience. For instance, it was previously stated that since the state of being an effect belonging to a qualified entity is established only through its cause, the production of a qualityless jar is illogical. Likewise, it has already been stated that because of the rule that color must reside pervasively throughout its substrate, and because the perception of a jar would otherwise be inexplicable, one must postulate a distinct "variegated" (*citra*) color.

Because there is no evidence for such a rule. Or, even if such a rule were granted, since the perception of a jar is established by the final sensory contact with the final part as delimited by its respective color—conjoined with the sensory contacts of those respective parts as delimited by their respective substances—there is the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating a distinct "variegated color" (*citra-rūpa*).

Thus, since the cognition of the qualifier is the cause of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*), the postulation of an indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*)—which does not apprehend the relation between the jar and "jar-ness"—is indeed improper, because such a cognition is impossible in instances such as "This is a jar. For the postulation of that [indeterminate cognition] occurs only in cases like "The man with a staff" (*daṇḍī puruṣaḥ*), where the relation is either eternal or a distinct relation such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), but not in cases like "This is a jar," because in those cases only a qualified cognition arises.

And thus, it follows that non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) does not have its own effect [to produce], which is a great deficiency. Likewise, the twofold division of time into "undivided" (*akhaṇḍa*) and "divided" (*sakhaṇḍi*) is also untenable; for that which is undivided would result in being incapable of serving as a basis for empirical usage (*vyavahāra*). Nor can it be argued that [time] is the cause by virtue of being the substratum of the world, according to the principle: "Time is considered the generator of produced things and the substratum of the worlds," because its causality is already established through the Lord (*Īśvara*) alone.

Nor should it be said that we have stated [in our own work] that space and time are not distinct from God when analyzing the categories of existence; for in that context, the non-difference of space and time specifically from God was asserted. And that [assertion] contradicts such scriptural passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman. Furthermore, by such scriptural texts as "From which these beings are born" and "In Him all is established," it is established that the status of being the creator of the world and the substratum of the world belongs to God alone, and not to time.

Therefore, the claim that time is the producer of produced things is incorrect; for it is improper to establish the non-difference between both [time and the seven categories] such as earth and so forth from Īśvara by means of their non-difference, since they are already established as distinct. Likewise, "limited time" (*khaṇḍakāla*) is also untenable. For limited time is indeed defined by the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of specific movements of the sun. And thus, since the specific movement of the sun is itself the limited time in reality, what is the point of postulating something over and above it? Consequently, limited time is nothing other than action (*kriyā*).

Thus, by those who maintain the theory of baking within the atom (*pīlupākavādins*), the destruction of the black pot and the production of the red pot are accepted as occurring within the atom itself. In that case, since the efficient causes such as the wheel and the stick are absent, how can there be production? If one were to accept [production] even without an efficient cause, then the status of the wheel, the stick, and so forth as efficient causes would be utterly destroyed.

Thus, resorting to a cumbersome and unestablished system of logic based on various such experiences is improper, as it consists of fallacious refutations against the simplicity-rooted theory of the indivisible *sphoṭa*. Having examined the indivisible *sphoṭa* of words because the knowledge of word-meanings is not the cause of the knowledge of sentence-meaning, the indivisible *sphoṭa* of sentences is now described. That [sentence-sphoṭa] is of two kinds, distinguished by being indivisible or divisible; among these, the indivisible one—which is distinct from the words and suggested by the indivisible parts—is established here due to its parsimony (*lāghava*).

And that [view] has been explained as the indivisible word-sphoṭa (*akhaṇḍa-pada-sphoṭa*). Furthermore, there is great parsimony (*lāghava*) in not having to postulate the causality of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*āsatti*). On the other hand, the divisible word-entity (*sakhaṇḍa-pada*) is well-known. Alternatively, in cases such as *hare 've* (O Hari, come), once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, the division of words (*pada-vibhāga*) becomes unavoidable; thus the distinction is that in one case there is the indivisible sentence-sphoṭa (*akhaṇḍa-sarva-vākya-sphoṭa*), while in the other there is the divisible [word]. And in this way, the objections [against the sphoṭa theory] are like a miscarriage. In that context, a "sentence" (*vākya*) is defined as that which has a single finite verb (*tiṅanta*) and whose primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*) is its meaning.

For example, as in "pacati bhavati" (he cooks, he exists). Even there, although the word *pacati* lacks a substantive (*viśeṣya*) [in its own right], there is no lack of definition (over-extension) because it lacks the status of being a primary substantive. However, the Logicians (Tārkikas), in order to establish the unity of the preceding and following sections of the text as a single sentence, have cited the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra: "A sentence is one because of the unity of meaning, provided that if it were divided, there would be mutual expectancy. They explain the meaning of the phrase "because of the unity of meaning" (*arthaikyāt*) by stating that for them, the unity of the sentence consists in the unity of the intended object of the purport (*tātparya*).

For that purpose, Vyāsa stated that perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) constitute a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*). [He held that] "whatever possesses a connection with another [word], that should be declared to be one sentence with it," but it is not appropriate to assume any arbitrary meaning, as that would be corrupted by faults. To illustrate: regarding the intent of recitation, in the case of the statement, "Just as Devadatta recites, so too does your son recite," there would result the undesirable consequence of this being a single sentence. And such a conclusion is not desired.

Because it would result in the application of an instruction that lacks a corresponding verbal expression. Thus, the mantra "I prepare a pleasant seat for thee; I fashion it well with a stream of clarified butter" (RV 1.22.15) is the text establishing the act of seating, as seen in the section on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The mantra "Sit upon this, O immortal one; take thy stand in the essence of the rice-grains, being well-disposed" (RV 3.6.9) is the text establishing the act of seating, as seen in the section on inference (*anumāna*). Just like the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the definition of the auxiliary elements of sacrifice (*yāgāṅga*) is the subject matter of the intended meaning (*tātparya*).

Thus, although inference depends upon perception, perception does not depend upon it; likewise, although that which establishes the existence [of a thing] depends upon that which establishes its non-existence, that which establishes its non-existence does not depend upon it. And in this way, the status of these two as parts of a single sentence is established. Nor is this an acceptable consequence, because it contradicts your own example cited in response to the argument "due to the unity of purpose" (*arthaikya*).

Furthermore, does this syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) pertain to words, or to sentences, or to books? It cannot be the first, because such unity occurs only between an action (*kriyā*) and its factors (*kāraka*), since mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is possible only between those two. This is because such unity arises only when there is expectancy for both, and it is impossible when there is expectancy for only one of them. Nor can it be the second, for syntactic unity occurs when a sentence that is established independently is connected with another sentence that stands in need of it.

And in the present context, *prakaraṇa* (context) refers only to the two "knots" (*granthi*) consisting of the composition of sentences, and not to the sentences themselves. This is because, in cases such as the definition "inference is the cognition produced by the consideration (*parāmarśa*) of the premises established through inference," there is no mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) between the perceptual sentence and [the inferential one], nor is there proximity (*āsatti*). Furthermore, the unity of sentences constitutes a *prakaraṇa*, according to its definition: "Context is the expectancy of one [sentence] for another."

If one were to accept that this [sentence] also constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), there would be a contradiction with the section on the relative strength of the means of proof—*śruti*, *liṅga*, *vākya*, *prakaraṇa*, and so forth—which establishes that *vākya* is weaker than *prakaraṇa*. Nor is it the third [alternative], because the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) between perception and inference is semantic (*ārthī*), not verbal (*śābdī*). Therefore, the composition of a sūtra here and the postulation of some arbitrary meaning is improper. As for the text of Śiromaṇi, it is established by the very principle that whatever possesses a connection is a single syntactical unit; such is the direction of the argument.

Let us return to the subject at hand. Since the apprehension of *śakti* (denotative power) occurs through sentences used in ordinary linguistic practice, it is the sentence alone that possesses the capacity to denote; thus, the meaning is manifested by the sentence (*vākya-sphoṭa*). Nor should it be argued that although the power resides in the sentence, it is nevertheless grasped in the individual words through the process of insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*udvāpa*). For if that were the case, the knowledge of the meaning derived from a sentence would become the cause of the knowledge of word-meanings, whereas the established consensus is that the knowledge of word-meanings is the cause of the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence. To hold otherwise would result in the collapse of all settled philosophical tenets.

The sentence-sphoṭa is twofold: divided (*sakhaṇḍa*) and undivided (*akhaṇḍa*). The undivided is further twofold: that which is distinct from the phonemes (*varṇātirikta*) and that which is not distinct from them (*anatirikta*). When the phonemes are not accepted because of their complexity (*gaurava*), and the undivided sentence-sphoṭa is manifested by the phonemes alone due to its simplicity (*lāghava*), then it is "distinct" [from the phonemes]. In this view, fallacious objections—such as the claim that [the sphoṭa] would be indicated by as many [phonemes] as there are phonemes—are refuted by a miscarriage of their very core.

However, when it is held that phonemes (varṇas) are not distinct from sounds (dhvanis), then in a sentence such as "Bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), the *vākya-sphoṭa* is indeed divisible (*sakhaṇḍa*), because it is possible to effect a division between the action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka*). In cases such as "O Hari! (*hare'va*) or "O Viṣṇu! (*viṣṇo'va*), once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, a division between the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the case-ending (*ākhyāta*) cannot be made; therefore, the *vākya-sphoṭa* there is indivisible (*anatirikta*). For a non-grammarian who lacks knowledge of the distinction between action and its factors, even a sentence like "Bring the jar" is likewise an indivisible, unitary *vākya-sphoṭa*.
In a word, phonemes do not exist; nor do words exist within phonemes. Between sentences and phonemes, there is no distinction whatsoever at all.

Thus, this is the manifestation of the meaning residing in a sentence that is distinct from an indivisible [unit]. The meaning is that just as there are no parts in a phoneme (*varṇa*), so it is here. Observe: in cases such as *mṛgo dhāvati* ("the deer runs") and *pacati bhavati* ("he is cooking"), one should understand, as before, that there is neither identity with nor difference from the indivisible essence. There is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the action of running, whose agent is the deer, with the action of seeing through the relation of being its object (*karmatā*). There is a syntactic connection of the action of cooking, whose agent is Devadatta, with the action of being in the present.

As it has been said: "Just as a single inflected noun (*subanta*) may be the qualifier of many finite verbs (*tiṅanta*), so too a single finite verb may be the qualifier of many nouns ending in *ktvā*, *kta*, or *tavya*.

Now, regarding the objection that in the view where the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is "the deer possessing an effort conducive to running" (with the deer as the subject qualified by the nominative case), the deer would incur the fault of requiring the accusative case because it is the object (*karman*) relative to the meaning of the root *dṛś* ("to see"); and furthermore, that if one were to supply the word "him" (*tam*), it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)—having raised these concerns, [the author] says: "Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, on the banks of the Pampā, a most virtuous crane."

The argument offered by some—that there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because, as in the case of *ityādi*, the meaning of the sentence functions as the object—is utterly baseless. This is because the capacity for agency (*kartṛtva*) belongs to that which is determined by the action of cleaning the teeth (*dantadhāvana*), and since that [agency] has already been expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), there is no evidence to sublate the internal refinement (*saṃskāra*) produced by the more immediate [action], even though there is an objectivity (*karmatva*) relative to the external meaning of the root (*dhātu*) at the time of its initial production. Furthermore, this is possible through [the consumption of] dog-flesh and the like.

This is because it is logically consistent with the example "He destroys hunger. Furthermore, even if there is no grammatical fault in this case under the view that the nominative-ending word is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the undesirable consequence arises that the sentence *pacati bhavati* ("he cooks and exists") would not function as a single syntactic unit (one sentence), because its meaning would then be "the existence [of Devadatta] which has as its agent the act of cooking whose agent is Devadatta alone."

Nor can it be argued that Devadatta possesses an effort conducive to cooking; for when the primary meaning is already established, the rule "when the qualified [subject] is sublated, the injunction and prohibition transfer to the qualifier" (asaviśeṣaṇe vidhiniṣedhau viśeṣaṇam upasaṃkrāmataḥ sati viśeṣye bādhe) would result in agency belonging to the action itself. Furthermore, there is no purpose for [assuming] a single sentence. Nor can the *nighāta* accent be the purpose, according to the rule "in a single sentence, the *nighāta*, the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, etc., must be stated," because that [rule] is excluded by the inclusion of the term *atiṅ* in the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*. This is true.

In the sense "the act of cooking, having Devadatta as its agent, has you as its participant," in the usage *devadattaḥ pacati te bhavati*, there would be no occurrence of the substitute [tvam] due to the absence of *samānavākyatva* (being within the same sentence). Furthermore, in the sense "there is one act of cooking having multiple Devadattas as its agents," the usage *devadattāḥ pacanti te bhavati* would also not occur; for if there were multiple agents, the rule *na bhavati* would require the plural ending (*bahuvacana*) here. Moreover, in the example *paśya mṛgo dhāvati*, there exists a purposeful result in the form of the *nighāta* (elision of accent).

Furthermore, the claim made by the logicians (*tārkika*) that the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is the object (*karman*) [of the act of cognition] is not tenable. To explain: is the sentence-meaning distinct from [the word-meanings] or non-distinct? It cannot be the first, because since it is not presented by a linguistic function (*vṛtti*), it is impossible for it to be connected as the object of the act of seeing (*darśana-kriyā*). This is because there is a rule that only that which is presented by a linguistic function can be the object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Otherwise, one would face the absurdity that even the ether (*ākāśa*), which is presented through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) from the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*), would become an object of verbal cognition. Nor can it be the second.

It is unestablished that the meaning of a noun can be construed with the meaning of a verbal root through a relation of difference (*bheda-sambandha*) without mediating the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhakty-artha*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of such a construction in sentences like "The rice cooks" (*odanaḥ pacati*). Nor is it the case that in such instances the meaning of the sentence is the object (*karman*), nor is the meaning of the noun its denotation (*vācyatva*). For otherwise, there would also be the undesirable consequence of such a construction in sentences like "The delicious rice cooks" (*ramaṇīya odanaḥ pacati*). Furthermore, in cases such as "Behold the Pampā lake" (*paśya lakṣmaṇa pampām*), there is indeed a syntactic split (*vākya-bheda*) due to the necessary ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the word "it" (*tām*).

Thus, the claim that the meaning of a sentence is the object [of the verb] has been examined and found to be unexpressed. Likewise, the statement in the *Vyutpattivāda*—that in the sentence "the blue pot comes into being" (*nīlo ghaṭo bhavati*), the pot is the locus of the coming-into-being whose agent is the blue [quality]—is also not tenable. This is because there is no evidence to refute the derivation of the meaning of a noun [as the subject], and because the cognition "the blue pot is the locus of coming-into-being" is indeed possible.

"For when an injunction or a prohibition concerns something qualified, they apply to the qualification provided there is a contradiction regarding the qualified object"—thus, the experience of "being" will occur only with respect to the qualification, namely, "blueness"; this is the general direction. In the same way, in cases such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) or "This is that Devadatta," the qualified and unqualified meanings should be understood as before.

The traditional teachers maintain that in the statement "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), because it is impossible for the consciousness qualified by omniscience and other attributes—which is denoted by the word *tat*—to be identical with the consciousness qualified by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—which is denoted by the word *tvam*—there must be a "partial renunciation and partial retention" (*jahadajahallakṣaṇā*) of their respective specific forms in order to establish identity. Now, what is the proof for the identity of these two? It cannot be the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of nouns, for does that [derivation] mean that there is only a relation of non-difference between the referents of two nouns, or that the referents of two nouns are themselves non-different? Not the first.

In expressions such as "the *āmikṣā* for the *vaiśvadeva*" (*satokam pacati vaiśvadevī āmikṣā*), there is deviation [from the rule of grammatical coreferentiality]. Nor is there non-difference, as in the case of "a jar and a cloth" (*ghaṭapaṭau*), because of deviation there as well. Therefore, when coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇya*) is improper; for that [preference] is rooted in parsimony (*lāghava*). The proof for this is the scriptural text establishing non-difference preceded by a censure of difference: "One goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity" (*mṛtyoḥ sa mṛtyumāpnoti ya iha nāneva paśyati*).

Furthermore, even in that case, one who perceives as if there were multiplicity attains death after death; however, one who does not perceive multiplicity in reality—since in the expression "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), the sense being conveyed is precisely difference—it cannot be argued that difference alone is understood, as in the case of the compound *rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king’s man) or the genitive compound *tasya tattvam* (his essence).

Even according to the Chāndogya, beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chānd. 6.2.1), and concluding with "That is the Self; that art thou, Śvetaketu" (Chānd. 6.8.7), identity is determined through the uniformity of the opening and the conclusion—a method that establishes the purport of the Veda. Furthermore, identity is ascertained by the scriptural text: "Brahman would desert him who knows Brahman as different from the Self" (Brhad. 2.4.6). In this view, there is no need for the resort to figurative interpretation (*lakṣaṇā*).

In reality, however, this is indeed the *sphoṭa* of the expressive sentence (*vācakavākyasphoṭa*). To explain: even though there is an impossibility of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between the two word-meanings as they are presented by their respective powers (*śakti*), there is no obstacle to the non-difference between the two substrata (*viśeṣya*) as presented by that same power. For example, in the case of "the pot is impermanent" (*ghaṭo 'nityaḥ*), although the property of potness (*ghaṭatva*), which is a single part of what is denoted by the word "pot," is not capable of being conjoined with impermanence, there is nevertheless a connection of impermanence with the pot itself, which is presented by the power of the word through its fitness (*yogyatā*).

Alternatively, the expressive power (*śakti*) resides only in the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), while the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). In this view, there is no defect whatsoever. Or again, just as in the case of words with multiple meanings (*nānārtha*), the primary denotation (*abhidhā*) is restricted by factors such as association (*saṃyoga*), so too, here, the primary denotation is restricted to the qualified object alone in accordance with the requirement of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*). Alternatively, let there be indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and let it be "indication where the primary meaning is abandoned" (*jahat-lakṣaṇā*). By means of that, there is merely the comprehension of the portion consisting of the qualifiers; however, its utility does not extend even to the qualified object.

This is possible because the presence of that [identity] can indeed be established; the same applies to the case of "this is that Devadatta. Nevertheless, the example given for *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (indication where part is abandoned and part is retained) is inconsistent—this is the direction of the argument. Likewise, in the sentence "one tree becomes five boats," the cognition is *sakhaṇḍa* (with parts), as before, even though there is a state of being divided (*khaṇḍaśattve*). "A meaningful element (arthavat) that is neither a verbal root (dhātu) nor an affix (pratyaya) is a nominal stem (prātipadika).

Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa states that the word *artha* here is understood in the sense of "that which is denoted" (*abhidheya*). Its meaning is that it refers specifically to that which expresses a general denotation; for if it were to refer to a specific denotation, the mention of roots, affixes, and indeclinables would become redundant. To clarify this, the word "general" (*sāmānya*) was employed. If one were to adopt the interpretation of "denoting a purposeful denotation," there would be the undesirable consequence (*atiprasaṅga*) of [applying the term *prātipadika*] even to things like a "wooden ladle" (*kūcī*) or a "swing" (*mañcī*), as these also denote something useful. Nor is such an extension desirable, because it would result in the undesirable consequence that such items would be eligible for usage as correct words (*sādhutva*).

The essence of this [word] consists precisely in its being produced by grammar; for even that which generates a verbal cognition of a valid means of knowledge possesses this quality. Nor should it be argued that the essence is merely the possession of a form delimited by the non-production of merit, since that is not present here; for it is precisely the state of being produced by grammar that indicates its true nature. Thus, the particle *eva* is employed solely to exclude anything other than that.

The venerable authors of the Bhāṣya state that the inclusion of the term "meaningful" (*arthavat*) here is for the purpose of designating a specific class of named items; its result is the prevention of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the technical name to meaningless clusters of sounds, such as "ten pomegranates, six cakes," or to other collections of phonemes within a word. Some maintain that since both types of rules (those concerning *samāsa* and those concerning *pada*) are formulated here, there is no fault whatsoever.

If it is argued that there is no fault even if such meaningless items are *prātipadikas*, and therefore the rule for "that which has meaning" (*anarthavat*) applies only to what is meaningful, we say: not so. For, when suffixes (*svādi*) are produced without distinction, it is accepted that there are restrictive rules (*niyama*)—one having the result of excluding the connection of those respective meanings with those respective suffixes, and the other having the result of excluding the connection of those respective meanings with other suffixes. [This applies] to the constituents of a collection formed by both meaningful elements and phonemes.

By the principle of expressing singularity for a whole through the dual or plural suffixes [of the whole], it is possible to convey the singularity of each individual constituent; therefore, there is no case-suffix for each [phoneme] individually. This should be seen very clearly in the *Bhāṣya* and *Tattvabodhinī* on the *HaYaVaRaTa* sūtra, during the explanation of the Vārttika: "Because the aggregate has a single purpose, the case-suffix does not occur after the individual phonemes," which occurs in the context of defining the meaningfulness of phonemes.

If it is asked, "What harm is there even if meaningless items were *prātipadika*s?", know that in cases such as *vanaṃ* and *dhanaṃ*, the substitution of *jaś* (nasals) and so forth would undesirably apply. However, the distinction is this: because the entire aggregate (*samudāya*) would not possess the status of a *prātipadika* independently, the suffixes (*vibhakti*) would not be heard [as they are]. Now, if the term "meaningful" (*arthavat*) is understood through the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of verbal roots (*dhātu*) and primary suffixes (*pratyaya*), then the explicit mention of "meaningful" (*arthavad-grahaṇa*) is redundant. Nor can it be an absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), because that would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) and entail the fault of a compound (*samāsa*).

If it is argued that similarity (*sādṛśya*) exists only when there is a meaningful purpose (*arthavattva*), we say: do not speak thus. For if one resorts to *paryudāsa* (exclusion), there arises the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of not understanding by what form the similarity consists. Even if "not denoting a non-existent" (*asattvāvacanatva*) were the basis, since similarity requires the possession of common properties (*prayojakadharmatva*), it would follow that only words such as *hiruk* and so on would receive this designation, because they possess those very properties. Nor should it be said that the similarity is based on the property of being a non-existence (*asattvībhūtatva*)—defined as the state of not being a denoter of a form that serves as a delimiter for connection with a *kāraka*—because [the definition] would be too narrow.

Since this very form [of the word] has been established as the basis for the various systems of Bhartṛhari and others—having disregarded gender, number, and so forth—and since it exists here [in the rule], the objection raised by those who claim that similarity is established by "meaningfulness" (*arthavattva*) alone—namely, that because they resort to the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of roots and affixes, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) will apply only to what is meaningful, and thus there is no need for the mention of "meaningful" (*arthavat*) in the rule—is rendered irrelevant. This is the introduction to the text "this being meaningful" (*ity arthavat*), as stated by Kaiyaṭa.

By this, the following [objection] is refuted: "The mention of *arthavat* (meaningful) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the rule *naÑ-ravi-yukta-anyapadārthe* is not eternal; thus, it is possible to reject the mention of case-endings (*vibhakti*) and grammatical relations (*kāraka*) in rules such as *uṣadheś-ca*. Even if meaningfulness is obtained through exclusion (*paryudāsa*), it was stated that this is for the sake of subsequent purposes; however, that too is answered by this very [argument].

The *Kaustubha* states that since meaningfulness is obtained through the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) [of meaningless elements], the inclusion of the term "meaningful" (*arthavat*) here is for the sake of what follows; however, it should be considered doubtful whether this is indeed the case. Furthermore, one should not argue that because the inclusion of "meaningful" in the preceding rule would otherwise be rendered purposeless, its status as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the application of the "rule of inclusion of the ending" (*tadantavidhi*) in the rule concerning *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes would be lost. For the absence of the "rule of inclusion of the ending" in the formulation of technical names (*saṃjñāvidhi*) is established by the explicit statement: "When a suffix is mentioned in a rule, there is no 'inclusion of the ending'."

Even if that [term *arthavat*] were meaningful, it is possible for it to function as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the rule of suffixal addition (*tadanta-vidhi*) by virtue of its capacity to establish the status of being meaningful (*arthavattva*) in that specific portion; nor is there any contradiction with the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *suptiṅ* (Pāṇini 1.4.14), for the Bhāṣya there states: "The term 'meaningful' (*arthavat*) carries over [from the previous sūtra]; and only that which ends in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffix is meaningful, not the *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffixes alone."

Furthermore, because primary derivatives (*kṛt*) and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) possess meaning, there is no deviation regarding the suffixes *tavyat* and others; thus, even though the continued application of the term "meaningful" (*arthavat*) would normally exclude it [the suffix], by virtue of the power of the formal declaration (*pratijñā*) that it is *svarita*, it functions as a qualifier—just as in the case of the summary [rule] regarding those possessing a specific meaning. By this, the view expressed in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *suptiṅantaṃ padam* (P. 1.4.14)—that [the declaration] is intended solely for subsequent purposes—is refuted. As for the declaration of its *svarita* nature, the very statement in the Bhāṣya, "In the declaration of the *svarita*, the term 'meaningful' (*arthavat*) is understood to carry over," is the authoritative proof.

As for the statement that the purpose of the previous sūtra is not fulfilled because that [result] is obtained simply by excluding verbal roots (dhātu) and suffixes (pratyaya), that is to be considered doubtful, as it contradicts the aforementioned Bhāṣya.

The exclusion of verbal roots (*dhātuparyudāsa*) in the rule *ahannityādi* is for the purpose of preventing the elision of the final *n*. Under the view that technical names apply according to their original enunciation (*yathoddeśapakṣa*), since the suffixes *tiP* and others, which are specifically prescribed, would supersede [the application of *prātipadika*], there would be no production of case-endings such as *su* even if the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) were present; nor would the elision of *n* occur. Thus, while the exclusion of verbal roots might appear unnecessary under this view, under the view that technical names apply at the time of operation (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the elision of *n* would be unavoidable because the specific suffixes would coexist with the status of being a nominal stem—which is brought about by the same rule prescribing the elision of *n*. Therefore, the exclusion of verbal roots is indeed necessary to prevent that.

Nor should it be argued that since the purpose is accomplished by the very prohibition of what ends in a suffix (pratyayānta-pratiṣedha), there is no need for the exclusion of verbal roots (dhātu-paryudāsa). This is because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule *na ṅasiṃbuddhyoḥ*; when the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is being prescribed, there is an absence of the prohibition "not [if] ending in a suffix" (*apratyayaḥ*) due to the characteristic of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*). As for the claim that there is an exclusion of what ends in a suffix by means of the characteristic of a suffix, that is to be reconsidered; for there is no application of the characteristic of a suffix in a case where the operation is distinct from that which ends in a suffix (*pratyayānta-bhinna-kāryatve*).

For this very reason, in the *Sūtraśeṣabhāṣya*, after stating that for the words *rājā* and *takṣā*, a prohibition would apply—namely, that they are not *pratyaya*s by virtue of the definition of a *pratyaya*—it was said, "Or rather, let there be a *paryudāsa* (exclusion). If even in the case of *paryudāsa* the aforementioned defect regarding the definition of a *pratyaya* were to remain as it was, then the passage beginning with "Or rather" (*athavā*) would indeed be inconsistent. In this context, it is impossible to say "not a root" (*adhātuḥ*). Why does [the rule] not apply here in the case of *ahan vṛtrāṇi*?

For in this way, there is no undesirable consequence even if that which ends in a suffix were considered a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Nor does the occurrence of the default singular number follow by virtue of its being a nominal stem (prātipadika), as is the case with words like *huṃ* or *phaṭ*; for the mention of *tiṅ* in the rule *sup-tiṅ-antaṃ padam* indicates that such [default] application does not arise here. Nor is there the undesirable consequence of elision (*luk*) by the rule *supo dhātv-pratyayayoḥ*, because that rule ordains elision only for a suffix that is co-occurrent with something other than an inflectional ending (*vibhakti*), based on its association with verbal roots (*dhātu*). However, in cases such as *paceraṃ sarvasmin* and *āṅ*, the elision of *na* does not occur due to the force of the specific utterance (*uccāraṇa-sāmarthya*).

This being the case, since the word *śreyas* would already be established as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by the rule *ādyudāttaśca*, and the elision of the case-ending (*sup-luk*) would be accomplished even without [the mention of] "nominal stem" in the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*, the inclusion of the term "verbal root" (*dhātu*) in that very rule indicates that a verbal root does not possess the status of a nominal stem. Thus, one might think there is no need for the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of roots. However, this conclusion is not final, because it contradicts the subsequent portion of the text. As for the statement in the Bhāṣya on the remainder of the Sūtra that, according to the aforementioned method, the exclusion of roots ending in suffixes (*pratyaya*) should not be made, that is to be considered with caution.

Regarding the term *apratyaya* (not being an affix), whether one adopts the view of *paryudāsa* (exclusion) or *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (simple negation), since it would not be included within the preceding [stem] (*pūrvāntavat*), its status as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would not obtain; consequently, neither the shortening of the vowel nor the application of the rule for nominal stems would apply. This is because the portion of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) [the letter *ṇ*] lacks the status of being part of the preceding [stem], and thus the mention of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) in the sūtra concerning shortening serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Otherwise, if that were not the case, the objection raised against the indicator would remain unanswered, and the passage from the earlier Bhāṣya would become irrelevant.

It should be discerned by the wise that Kaiyaṭa’s statement, which aims at refuting the earlier commentary (*bhāṣya*), is indeed merely erroneous, as will be explained immediately hereafter. Regarding the *bhāṣya*: "What is the purpose of [specifying] 'pratyaya' [in the rule]? [If it were not stated, one might ask: why does the designation *prātipadika* not apply to *kāṇḍe* or *kuḍye*? [To this, the answer is: the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyama*):

'The designation *prātipadika* applies only to that which ends in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffix, and only to that which ends in a suffix termed *pratyaya*, and not to anything else. And this [passage from the *bhāṣya*] is intended to refute the view that the term *pratyaya* functions as a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) [of suffixes].

For instance, in the term *apratyaya*, the word *pratyaya* occurs twice; in the latter instance, according to the view of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), although there is no application of the rule of "extension to that which ends with [the specified element]" (*tadantavidhi*) in the formulation of a technical designation (*saṃjñāvidhi*), the word is nonetheless considered meaningful because it conveys a sense independent of anything other than its own inflectional ending. Consequently, since the exclusion of *pratyaya* would otherwise be redundant, and because the intended meaning cannot be established otherwise, there exists a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) extending to that which ends with a *pratyaya*. Furthermore, that exclusion of what ends with a *pratyaya* need not be applied as a formal operation (*kārya*).

This is because of the adoption of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that [the suffix] *-taddhita* occurs only after a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix or another *taddhita* suffix. Here, by stating that the mention of *kṛt* serves as a restrictive factor, the refutation of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of verbal roots (*dhātu*) is also intended. For even if a root were to possess the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there would be no harm whatsoever. In the view that the technical definitions apply at the time of their enunciation (*yathoddeśapakṣa*), it is impossible to justify the application of case-endings (*sup*) to a root in examples such as *ahann* (from *ahan*), since the suffixes *tiP* and others would override (*apavāda*) it according to the maxim "that which applies when nothing else has already applied" (*yena nāprāpte*).

Even in the moment immediately following that elision (*lopa*), there is no attainment of that [suffix], because a general rule (*utsarga*) operates by avoiding the domain of its exception (*apavāda*). This is also because of the traditional maxim: "Having avoided the domain of the exception, the general rule takes effect. Nor is it the case that where there is an explicit statement of an exception, the general rule does not apply; for in this instance, there is no such statement of an exception. This is due to the principle illustrated by the "slayer of Devadatta" (*devadattahantṛ-nyāya*), which results in the complete immersion of the suffixes. Furthermore, the specific grammatical indications (*nirdeśa*) such as *tau sat* do not invalidate this principle.

When Devadatta is killed, there is no joy even when his killer is slain; however, when there is a superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of Devadatta’s being killed upon one who is merely intent on killing his daughter, there is indeed "revival" (*ujjīvana*) upon the killing of that [intended victim]. This is the body of the maxim. The words "those two" (*tau*) refer to the augment (*vṛddhi*) and the substitution of the homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*). Since in the case of one intent on killing, there is merely a similar contingency (*prasaṅga*) belonging to the same class as the effort to kill, and not an actual application (*pravṛtti*) directed toward the object of killing, that case does not fall within the scope of this maxim. Therefore, it is stated that this [maxim] serves to indicate its non-eternality (*anityatva*).

Otherwise, since the rule for *jaś*-substitution would have already achieved its purpose (*cāritārthya*) at the time the rule for *jaś*-substitution was about to apply, it could not be considered an exception (*apavāda*). For in that case, since [the *jaś* rule] would necessarily apply at the time the *jaś* rule is to take effect, its status as an exception would be established by the principle of *yenanāprāpta* (that which applies where another would otherwise have applied) merely through the absence of its own application within the scope of the other's operation. Otherwise, the giving of buttermilk (*takra*) intended for Kauṇḍinya would not set aside the giving of curd (*dadhi*) prescribed for one characterized as a Brāhmaṇa.

The author of the Dīdhiti and others maintain that because [the injunction] has fulfilled its purpose either prior to or after that [specific gift], there is no possibility of Kauṇḍinya receiving the curd. This is because, in the specific prohibition "curd is to be given to Brāhmaṇas, but not to Kauṇḍinya," the word "Brāhmaṇa" in the general rule "curd is to be given to Brāhmaṇas" refers to Brāhmaṇas other than Kauṇḍinya; thus, that sentence conveys the giving of curd as a gift to Brāhmaṇas other than Kauṇḍinya.

Furthermore, [if this were not the case], the rule *ṭābṛci* (Pāṇini 4.1.9) would not serve as an exception (*apavāda*) to *pādonta-rasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.8). This is because, in the alternative where that [exception] is absent, the present rule would find its scope of application (*cāritārthya*). Therefore, what has been stated [by us] alone is elegant. Even when there is a possibility [of coexistence], an exception does indeed take effect; thus, even the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *midaco 'ntyātparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.47) becomes consistent for this very reason. Some also maintain that, since the term *bhūvādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.1) presents itself without any other occasion (*niravakāśatayā*) during the prescription of verbal suffixes (*lavidhi*) and the prescription of *tiṅ* etc., there is no occurrence of *sub*-suffixes [in those contexts].

Nor is this [objection] unavoidable; for in the rule regarding the elision of *n* (nalopa-sūtra), the mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-grahaṇa*) is intended to refer to a nominal stem that possesses its own primary meaning (*sattva-pradhāna*). Thus, in cases such as *rāmān*, the elision of *n* does not occur due to the force of the specific injunction. This being the case, the fact that the mention of the *kṛt*-affix serves as a restrictive rule (*niyāmaka*) is also consistent. Kaiyaṭa, however, taking up the phrase "the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita*," states: "In this context, the mention of *taddhita* is for the purpose of restriction, while the mention of *kṛt* is for the purpose of prohibition; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the prohibition applying to the verbal root *aṭ* in forms such as *bhid-chid*."

As for what was stated in the *Manoramā*—namely, that the inclusion of the term *sāti* in the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* would otherwise be purposeless—that is to be reconsidered. For [the *sāti*] serves the purpose of including forms such as *soḍha*, *dūra*, *sama*, and *īṣat*. Otherwise, there would arise the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭarūpaprasaṅga*) of the form *ācakṣāṇ* when derived from the causative stem (*ṇijanta*) of the root *cakṣ* with the suffix *kvip*. Furthermore, the fault in this view is difficult to resolve.

In the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*, because of the inclusion of the term *sāt* and the inclusion of the term *vasi*, there is neither co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) nor non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) in both cases. In that regard, since the word *pratyaya* functions as a part [of a larger form], even if there were co-referentiality with the word *pratyaya*, Kaiyaṭa has stated that no fruit is obtained through non-co-referentiality, as he emphasizes its meaningfulness.

Taking up the phrase "gurucaraṇāḥ āhuḥ pratyayāntam na ca" (the venerable teachers say: "not that which ends in a suffix"), [the author] raises an objection: "But is not the exclusion of what ends in a suffix (*pratyayānta-paryudāsa*) redundant? For, although the mention of *kṛt* in the rule *kṛt-taddhita-...* serves as a prescriptive provision (*vidhāyaka*) to override the exclusion of verbal roots (*adhātu-paryudāsa*) in cases such as *liṅ-dhuk*, the mention of *taddhita* must instead serve as a restrictive provision (*niyamārtha*)—namely, that if a word ending in a suffix is to be a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it must be one ending in a *taddhita* suffix; thus, it would apply only to those ending in suffixes other than *taddhita*."

If it is argued that this is because the cessation of the designation *prātipadika* (nominal stem) is established [by the rule *kṛt-taddhita-samāsāś-ca*], then one must consider that even in cases such as *kartā* and *kārakaḥ*, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the cessation of the designation [of nominal stem]. This is because the mention of *kṛt* [in the rule *kṛt-taddhita-samāsāś-ca*] is superseded by the subsequent restrictive rule concerning *taddhita* suffixes.

Furthermore, they [the commentators] argued that even when considering the general sublation [of rules], it is not easy to maintain that the restriction regarding *taddhita* suffixes is sublated by the mention of *kṛt* suffixes alone; for if the restriction regarding *samāsa* were also sublated, it would follow that the sentence "mūlakenopadaṃśam" (with a radish as a side-dish) would be excluded. This is the intention of Dīkṣita. Here, a lack of satisfaction is implied by the mention of the word "name" (*nāman*), because the mention of *kṛt* suffixes serves the purpose of an injunction; nevertheless, there is no fault.

In the consideration of the general rule regarding sublation (*bādhyasāmānyacintā*), there is no sublation even of the specific restrictive rule (*taddhitaniyama*) for others. However, in cases such as *mūlakenopadaṃśam*, there is no fault because one relies on the governing heading (*adhikāra*) and, while continuing the application of the term "meaningful" (*arthavat*), intends the state of having a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). This very point has been accepted by the author of the *Kaustubha*. As for the statement that—since it is established by the mention of *sāti* in the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* that suffixes are not nominal stems (*prātipadika*)—the mention of the suffix *vap* in the preceding rule is for the sake of [indicating] that which ends in it (*tadanta*) by virtue of its capacity (*sāmarthya*).

That [objection] is not tenable; for the claim that [the mention of *ṅīp* and *āp*] indicates the absence of the status of being a suffix or a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) has already been refuted. Nor should one suspect that the mention of *ṅīp* and *āp* alone is the indicator of the absence of the status of being a suffix or a nominal stem, while the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes serves merely as an injunction (*vidhi*); for since the desired result is established by the *liṅgaviśiṣṭāparibhāṣā* (the paribhāṣā concerning words qualified by gender), [the mention of *ṅīp* and *āp*] lacks the force of an indicator (*ajñāpakatva*). If it is argued that "let there be a *bahuvrīhi* compound [in the rule] *apratyayaḥ* [meaning 'that which does not have a suffix']," this is not so; for if that were the case, the term *bahupaṭuḥ* would fail to receive its technical designation (*saṃjñā*).

This being the case, it is established that there should be no exclusion of the *pratyaya* (suffix) at the end. Regarding this, there is the Vārttika: "In this context, there is the contingency of multiple words [being treated as one] when they possess meaning. Therein, the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that which is both 'multiple' (*aneka*) and a 'word' (*pada*). This is in accordance with the interpretation that it applies even to a word consisting of multiple [constituent parts]. And here, it should be understood that the term refers to the aggregate as a whole; for if the term *apratyayasya* ("of that which is not a suffix") were applied [to each part], there would be the contingency of applying the rule to every individual word. Kaiyaṭa, however, has explained it as: "That in which there is more than one word is 'multiple-worded' (*anekapada*)," thus referring to the entire collection.

Nor does it follow that the whole [sentence] would result in being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Because of the rule stating "that from which a suffix is prescribed," even though the whole ends in a suffix, there is no fault, as it is not a word (*pada*) [in the technical sense]. Furthermore, since words such as nominal stems and individual words possess expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and compatibility (*yogyatā*), and their meanings are thus interconnected, they constitute a sentence; and because a sentence is invariably implied by its constituent parts, and because the specific meaning consisting of the connection between word-meanings is what is expressed by that [sentence], [the definition holds].

Otherwise, it would follow that [the sentence] could not be the object of a cognition produced by words. Nor can it be argued that even an unexpressed relation appears through the power of the sentence, because of the lack of uniformity (ananugama). For according to the opponents, since the sentence-meaning is unexpressed, the inclusion of the term "compound" (*samāsa*) in the rule would be entirely purposeless. And this is not an acceptable consequence, as it would lead to the absurdity of the text’s failure to introduce the statement: "The inclusion of the term 'compound' for meaningful aggregates is for the sake of restriction."

Regarding the objection that "if [the suffix] were meaningful, there would be the consequence of multiple words," this was raised as an example in the *Pūrvapakṣavārttika*. However, having set aside examples such as "ten pomegranates" (*daśa dāḍimāni*), it was stated during the occasion of explaining the subsequent *Vārttika*—which asserts that even a sentence is meaningful because it possesses meaning—that after citing the examples "Devadatta, bring the white cow" (*devadatta gām abhyāja śuklām*) and "Devadatta, you have sacrificed the black cow" (*devadatta gām ayāja kṛṣṇām*), it was said: "This sentence is indeed meaningful."

By the same logic, since *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes would also lack the requirement of "single-meaningness" (*ekārthībhāva*), they would attain the status of nominal stems (*prātipadika*); this would result in the inconsistency of the *Bhāṣya* passages concerning the restriction of nominal stems—which refute the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of suffixes and establish the rule for *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes. Furthermore, while the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) in the rule *atiṅ prātipadikam* serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) by that very logic, that logic itself is of no avail here, because [the application of] the rule would otherwise attach to every individual phoneme.

Thus, in this case as well, it is precisely the status of being a meaningful base (*prātipadikatva*)—which is otherwise untenable—that serves as the inferential mark for meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) in compounds and the like; therefore, the maxim beginning with "that which is meaningless" (*anarthavat*) is indeed appropriate. Nor is "meaningfulness" simply the capacity to convey meaning through the function (*vṛtti*) of the words constituting itself, rather than the capacity to convey meaning through a [single] function; for if it were so, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the term to meaningless aggregates such as "ten pomegranates" (*daśa dāḍimāḥ*).

For, if in a compound (*samāsa*) there were a manifold unification of meanings (*anekārthībhāva*), then—due to the grammatical maxim "a word-meaning connects with a word-meaning, not with a part of a word-meaning," which is based on the fact that the substratum of the relation of being the qualificandum as determined by the mode residing therein is not fully distributed (*aparyāpti*)—this maxim would be violated in cases such as *prāptodaka* (where water has arrived). Consequently, in compounds like *rājapuruṣa*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the king could be further qualified by attributes such as "more beautiful" (*sundataratva*). To prevent this, one would have to formulate a new rule stating "there is no application of qualifiers to what has undergone composition" (*vṛttasya na viśeṣaṇayogaḥ*), which would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

To prevent such undesirable applications as *rājapuruṣo’śvajaḥ* ("the king’s man and the horse-bred one"), a rule should be formulated stating that "there is no connection with a qualifier belonging to the same class (*sajātīya*) when [the compound] has a common substantive. Here, "belonging to the same class" means being denotable by a single word. By this, in cases such as *rājagopuruṣau* ("the king and the cowherd's man"), there is no exclusion from the scope [of the rule], because there is a different substantive. Similarly, to prevent [the application] in cases such as *rājapuruṣo bhāryāyāḥ* ("the king’s man and the wife's [man]"), a rule should be formulated stating that "there is no connection with another qualifier belonging to the same class. By this, in cases such as *rājadevadattapuruṣaḥ* ("the king and Devadatta’s man"), there is no exclusion from the scope.

Furthermore, this rule would have had to be formulated in order to prevent the use of the word *ca* in a *dvandva* compound. Likewise, the governing heading for the "Great Option" (*mahāvibhāṣā*) would also have to be introduced in order to prevent the use of words such as *krānta* in compounds like *niṣkauśāmbi*. Moreover, there is no contradiction with the section concerning the offspring of a Niṣāda and a Sthapati under the theory of "single-meaningness" (*ekārthībhāva*), because the final established position (*siddhānta*) remains unassailable in the absence of a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Nor can it be argued that, since the relationship between the capacity [of a word] and its being the cause of the knowledge thereof is as well-established as the relationship between *lakṣaṇā* (indication) and its being the cause of the knowledge thereof, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) alone is more appropriate; for if that were the case, since a non-ṭri-varṇika such as a Niṣāda who has acquired Vedic knowledge from a Stapati could perform sacrifices, there would be no need to postulate the application of a previously unknown Vedic study, nor would there be a restriction of the prohibition "women and Śūdras shall not study. This is because we accept the rule that when a *karmadhāraya* is possible in the Veda, no other type of compound is admitted.

Nor is there any excess [of meaning], because they are equal in status. Nor does it exceed [the scope of the rule] merely because it is already established, for the restriction is not made by us; rather, it is like the addition of another statement due to its being non-redundant. According to our own system (siddhānta), however, there is a relation of non-difference (*abheda*) between the meanings of two co-referential nominal stems (*samānādhikaraṇa-prātipadika*), because the entire collection of linguistic conventions (*vyutpatti-kadamba*) establishes that they are objects of a single, distinct presentation.

Ekārthībhāva (the state of having a single unified meaning) is the name for that [relation] which, despite the separate meanings existing at the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), consists in the capacity of the words grasped first to produce the presentation of a specific, unified meaning; this has been explained in detail by the authors of the various treatises.

For, according to the theory of independence (*vyapekṣā*), the statement in the Bhāṣya on the Sūtra—"In a compound, [the substitution of *ṣ*] is obligatory when the word *paśu* does not stand as the final member"—would be inconsistent. For in that context, since the definition of semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) as independence (*vyapekṣā*) is accepted in the preceding Sūtra, the option regarding the substitution of *ṣ* would apply only to the sentence (*vākya*), and not to the compound; however, because of the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) here, the recurrence of the option does not occur. And this [point] holds true in the view that favors independence (*vyapekṣā*).

In the view that words are derived (*vyutpatti-pakṣa*), since the rule *idudupadhasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.41) would have already established the substitution of *ṣ* permanently, the phrase *anuttarapadasthasya* (8.3.45) serves merely to prohibit that substitution [in specific cases]. In reality, however, it has been stated therein that this very view of derivation is intended for the sake of respect (*ādaraṇa*) so that forms such as *sarpiṣā* and *yajuṣā* may be established. But if the view that words are underived (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*) were accepted, then since the option provided by the rule *isusoḥ sāmarthye* (8.3.44) would apply, this present rule [8.3.45] would have to be for the sake of making it obligatory; and that is certainly not what the authors of the Bhāṣya intend.

Furthermore, regarding the example *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā*, there would be the undesirable consequence of an option (*vikalpa*) [regarding the substitution of *ṣ*]. And likewise, regarding the rule "of that which does not have another word as its prior member" (*anuttarapadasya*), what is the point? For in examples such as *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā*, there would be the undesirable consequence of an option. And so, taking the example *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā*—where the word *parama-* is not a prior member—once this [rule] has been applied, why does the previous rule [Pāṇini 8.3.44], "the substitution of *ṣ* is optional when *is* and *us* are in syntactic connection with a word ending in *a*" (*isusoḥ sāmarthye*), not apply here? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: "When a connection is intended between two things that reside in different words (*nānāpadārtha*), then the operation of *ṣ*-substitution should be applied; for these two [words] are joined together in that case. (Note: This passage addresses the distinction between *sāmarthya* as "syntactic connection" versus "semantic connection," arguing that the optionality of *ṣ* applies only when the connection pertains to distinct lexical items.)

In the commentary on the *Itivārttika*, having resolved that "there is no capacity for syntactic expectancy (*vyapekṣā-sāmarthya*) in the previous rule (*pūrvayoga*), as there is not here," one might further object: "What is the reason that the capacity for syntactic expectancy is relied upon in the previous rule, rather than 'becoming a single meaning' (*ekārthībhāva*), as is the case elsewhere? Anticipating this objection, [the author] states: "If there were only a single meaning, then in a sentence such as *sarpiṣkakaroti* or *sarpiḥ karoti*, the substitution of *ṣatva* would not occur; thus, what was previously stated would be inconsistent. This would be incorrect.

Moreover, it has been stated by the authors of the Bhāṣya in this very work with a voice that is clear as a bell: "In a compound, there is no mutual expectancy (vyapekṣā). Therefore, discerning people should consider how logicians can disregard the word of the Great Sage and yet maintain that there is mutual expectancy within a compound. If it is asked: "Granted that there is indeed 'single-meaningness' (ekārthībhāva) in compounds and the like, why then does a sentence not possess the status of a nominal stem (prātipadika)? The answer is: because the mention of the term "compound" in the rule *arthavat* [Pāṇini 1.2.45] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), according to the Bhāṣya.

Here, the intended meaning is a collection of meaningful items ending in case-suffixes (*sup*). This restriction applies to those of the same class; that is, for items of such a nature as are compounded, for items of such a nature as are compounded, and for items of such a nature as are compounded—namely, those ending in case-suffixes. This is because of the intention of the subsequent Bhāṣya. Otherwise, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of [applying this] even to words like *bahuvrīhi*. Although a compound may consist of items ending in primary suffixes (*kṛt*), it is stated thus because of their predominance.

Kaiyaṭa maintains that the term "meaningful" (*arthavattva*) in the rule *yuktasubantānām* (P. 2.1.6) is an elliptical expression for "meaningful [words] ending in case-suffixes," because we observe forms such as *aśvakrītī* and *atadī*—which are derived from nominal stems joined with prefixes (*gati*) or kārakas—under rules like *gatikārakopapadānām* (P. 6.2.139). Even though there is no homogeneity (*sajātīyatva*) between these and words ending in case-suffixes, the term "meaningful" here refers to those composite groups which, despite lacking independence, possess a meaning capable of being used in linguistic usage (*prayogārha*). This is because the word "meaningful" (*arthavat*) in the rule *arthavat* (P. 1.2.45) applies by extension to all such meaningful units.

In the case of [the rule] *gavityam*, since there exists usage of the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) even when it is not followed by *nit*, that [term] would indeed be excluded; however, there is no exclusion of the aggregate consisting of the base and the suffix (*prakṛtipratyayasamudāya*). This is because the suffix lacks meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) suitable for independent usage.

In the Bhāṣya on the *sarūpa-sūtra*, it should be understood that this very point is indicated by the statement "of nouns ending in case-terminations" (*subantānām*); some maintain this view. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of [the rule applying] only to a collection of *sup* and *tiṅ* suffixes, because of the restriction imposed by the rule "in the sense of repetition, [a verb] is frequently used with its object" (*jahikarmaṇā bahulamābhīkṣṇye*). Furthermore, even so, there is no possibility of the rule applying to a collection of *tiṅ* suffixes, as this is resolved by the restriction "a finite verb [is compounded] with another finite verb" (*ākhyātamākhyātena*).

As for the rule that in a composite [word], the preceding portion is a *pada* while the subsequent portion is not a suffix (*pratyaya*) and so forth—where the word "subsequent" (*uttara*) is used to exclude cases such as *janmavān*, and where there is no fault in cases like *rājaiyaḥ* because the intention is to exclude the absence of a suffix whose base is the preceding portion—this is questionable; for the fault is even more evident in examples such as *gavityayamāha*.

In a compound such as *vṛkṣaṇvasu*, since the initial constituent (*pūrvabhāga*) is a *bhavattva* (nominal stem), it lacks the status of being a "word" (*pada*) by virtue of its similarity to that [non-word] state; therefore, the result [of the definition of a word] cannot possibly be attained. Furthermore, the claim that the rule concerns a combination of elements that has not yet entered into the relationship of base and suffix is also questionable. For in cases such as *ekaikasmai dehi*, even when the treatment of a *bahuvrīhi* applies to the reduplicated word *eka* via the rule *ekaṃ bahuvrīhivat*, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the loss of the designation *prātipadika*.

For it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *kṣiyodīrghāt* that an extended application (*atideśa*) conveys an effect that is not incompatible with its own substratum.
