Nor is the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) seen in a *bahuvrīhi* prescribed by this very [sūtra]. Even so, this serves to exclude restriction (*niyama*). Furthermore, this is not a restriction belonging solely to the sūtra *arthavat* (P. 1.2.45), because there is an addition of further elements to the body of the restriction beginning with *saṃghāta* (P. 1.2.49) in order to prevent the non-cessation of the status of being a nominal stem—which is occasioned by being the end of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)—in cases such as *janmabhavān*.

Because it would lead to the consequence of futility (*vaiyarthyaprasaṅga*). Nor does it serve the purpose of extending the designation [of *prātipadika*] by implication (*atideśasāmarthyaka*), since its utility is already established through the extension of the designation [of *prātipadika*] from the masculine form itself, as in the case of *svanara-puṃvat*. Furthermore, in the alternative view, the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) is even more impossible, because it would entail a restriction (*niyamaprasaṅga*). Therefore, this restriction is not tenable. Moreover, if this were the case, since the status of the entire aggregate as a nominal stem would be absent, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of the suffix *su* (the nominative singular). Even if one resorts to the position that the doubling occurs in place of the original, the status of being a nominal stem is difficult to maintain due to the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Since the constituent parts (*sthāsin*) are *subanta* (ending in a case-suffix), the entire aggregate is also *subanta*. Furthermore, under the view that "secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) are added to nominal stems (*prātipadika*"), there would be the undesirable consequence of forms such as *paunaḥpunika* being established [as nominal stems]. Even if the status of being a nominal stem were prohibited for that which ends in a manifest suffix, this would be prevented by the present restrictive rule (*niyama*). Moreover, in reality, the position advocating double usage (*dvir-prayoga-pakṣa*) is weak.

Regarding the forms *paunaḥpunyam* and *paunaḥpunikaḥ*, if they were derived from the entire compound, there would be the undesirable consequence that the suffixes *ṣyañ*, *añ*, and *ṭhañ* could not be applied. For in that case, because the [first member] would not be a subordinate element (*anaṅgatvāt*), the elision of the case-ending (*lup*) would apply, and subsequently, due to the doubling (*dvitvam*), the entire compound would lack the status of being a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) and would lack the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); consequently, those suffixes could not arise. Furthermore, since the status of being a nominal stem is precluded by the restrictive rules governing compounds and primary derivatives (*kṛt*), this would lead to an inconsistency with the text of the *Dviruktakriyāstha* section. This flaw persists even in the view that the doubling occurs in place of the original word (*sthāne dvirvacanapakṣe*).

Nor can this restriction be maintained on the grounds that it is impossible to state the position that [the suffix] follows from the aggregate when a single case-ending (*ekavibhakti*) follows; for even that is established by the rule beginning with "subanta-prātipadikayoḥ" (Pāṇini 1.4.14). Thus, one should not strive for cleverness in proposing a restrictive rule that contradicts the rule stated in the authoritative treatises.

As for the objection that, because a compound (*samāsa*) has its case-ending elided, the mention of "compound" in the rule *kṛt-taddhita-samāsāś-ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.46) would contradict the statement by Miśra and others that this sūtra is merely an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the rule *artha-vad-ādi* (Pāṇini 1.2.45), and that one must therefore assume that in that context the word "compound" refers to something other than a suffix distinct from those ending in *kṛt*, *taddhita*, or compounds—this is to be considered doubtful. For since a compound is not itself a suffix, it is impossible for its mention to serve as a restrictive injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, the phrase *kṛt-taddhita* [in the rule] would otherwise be redundant.

They argue that in the rule *arthavad ādi...* (Pāṇini 1.2.45), the term *apratyaya* (non-suffix) was included specifically to exclude compounds such as *devānīya*, which consist of a base (*prakṛti*) and a suffix (*pratyaya*). This is because, even though a compound is something other than a suffix, it is not accepted as being "other than both a case-ending (*vibhakti*) and that which ends in a case-ending," since a compound possesses the status of being meaningful (*arthavat*) by virtue of conveying a meaning through the words constituting it. Therefore, they claim that [the mention of *apratyaya*] is redundant. However, this too should be examined.

This is of no consequence, because the technical designation *pratyaya* (suffix) is not applicable to those [elements] read under the heading *prāgdiśīya*, nor is the substitution of *tyadādyatva* (the replacement by *a* for *tyad* etc. applicable to them; therefore, the mention of *samāsa* (compound) here serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), and thus its inclusion is not redundant. Furthermore, even in the case of "sky-flower" (*khapuṣpa*) or "hare's horn" (*śaśaśṛṅga*), there exists a power (*śakti*) in the flower and so on with respect to the sky and the like—based on a connection mentally constructed and superimposed upon the sky and so forth—so the mention of *samāsa* is not for that purpose either.

Nor is it the case that the verbal cognition does not arise because the subverting cognition acts as an obstacle; for the ill fame of that lord of the earth, which was measured by a number exceeding a *parārtha*—ill fame that was like a cataract obscuring the measure perceived by the eye of wisdom—is indeed sung on the shore of the milk-ocean of the female tortoises by a multitude of mute beings born from the fear of the eight-headed [Rāvaṇa].

This is because, by the principle of *tumun* and so forth, that [suffix] functions as a substitute for the [infinitive] suffix *-tum*. And it has been stated by the authors of the *Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya*: "For verbal cognition indeed produces knowledge even with respect to an object that is absolutely non-existent. If it is argued: "Even so, how is the meaning of an *atasamartha-samāsa* (an appositional compound whose members are not semantically connected) established?"—know that its establishment follows precisely from the very means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*). Furthermore, one should not be deluded into thinking that because a sentence possesses expressive power (*śakti*), there can be no connection with qualifiers such as "blue" in cases like "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*).

Even regarding the aspect of the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), although there is a power (*śakti*) for that [compound], there is no loss of the respective powers of the individual words constituting it toward their own meanings. However, since a compound (*samāsa*) is not of such a nature, there is no connection with qualifiers and so forth within a single part of its meaning. Furthermore, because the sentence-meaning exists in a manifest form, there is no fault in the distinction between "bring the blue pot" (*nīlaghaṭam ānaya*) and "bring the pot" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), and so forth.

Furthermore, in cases such as *bahugomatka* and *bahevatya*, even under the view that the compound occurs before the case-ending (*vibhakti*), there is no contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is applied to a word ending in a case-ending" (*subantāt taddhitaḥ*). This is because those [suffixes] do not apply to a complete word (*paripūrṇa-pada*)—since they possess an additional meaning—and thus fall outside the scope of that maxim; consequently, there is no absence of the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) at the end of the compound, they say.

From the perspective of the actual entity (*vastutaḥ*), since the compound meaning "one who possesses excellence" (*samāsārthaka*) is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by virtue of its non-worldly (*alaukika*) formation, the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is easily obtained. This position is also accepted, as it has been established in the middle of the work that this view is supported by the authority of the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *praśaṃsāyāṃ rūpap* (Pāṇini 5.3.66). If it is argued that even if the qualified [compound] is a nominal stem, the secondary suffix occurs because it is a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), then there is nothing inconsistent in that view either.

The author of the Bhāṣya maintains that even meaningless elements possess the status of nominal stems (*prātipadika*) based on the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that "the two [words] *tvad* and *adhi*" are meaningless. Some also hold that they should be included by means of the particle *ca*, which serves to aggregate what has not been explicitly mentioned in the rule *kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca*. The fruit of this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is seen in forms such as *svadhara*. May all be auspicious! Having followed the path indicated by the Great Commentary (*Ākara*), I have sought gold; indeed, the Goddess of Speech has been obtained from the water-born lotus of my mouth, along with diamonds and strings of pearls.
Through the grace of the Lord of Serpents, I have acquired over a long period of time the skill in stringing together jewels, yet it is merely a thread for a meaningful purpose.
Thus ends the *Prātipadika-saṃjñā-vāda*, composed by the venerable Tārānātha of Goḍābolī. [Next:
The *Vākya-vāda*.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.

Now, what is this thing called a sentence (*vākya*)? According to the *Bhāṣya*, "A sentence consists of a single finite verb (*ekatiṅ*). Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*), however, maintain that "a sentence is a collection of words that generates a single cognition whose primary qualificand is the meaning of one finite verb. By this definition, there is no violation of the unity of a sentence even in cases such as "He cooks and [you] exist" (*pacati bhavati*) or "See, the deer runs" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*), despite the multiplicity of verbal roots (*kriyāpada*).

As stated in the Bhāṣya, "There is no sentence devoid of a verb," and because of grammatical rules such as "the verb *as* [is understood] after *bhavanti* in the first person," the supply of a verbal action (*kriyāpada*) is appropriate everywhere. Nor should it be argued that even if a verb is supplied, the meaning of the word ending in the nominative case (*prathamāntārtha*) is still the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the cognition; for in cases such as "Look, the deer is running," if the meanings of two nominative words were both qualificands, it would result in the undesirable consequence of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*).

If the deer were construed as the object (*karman*) in the act of seeing (*darśana-kriyā*), then a second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would result after the word *mṛga*. And if that second case were present, then by the grammatical rule "The suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* take the place of the *laṭ* [present tense] when not coreferential with the first case," there would be the substitution of *śatṛ* for *laṭ*, resulting in the sentence "One should see the running deer" (*dhāvantaṃ mṛgaṃ paśyet*). Consequently, the sentence "The deer, seeing [something], runs" (*paśyan mṛgo dhāvati*) would be destroyed. If one were to supply the word *tam* (the deer), there would be both a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) and unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Nor should it be argued that there is no harm in the difference between these two types of sentences; for if that were the case, the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* would become redundant, as there would be no instance of a *tiṅ* (finite verb) to be excluded by the term *atiṅ*. Furthermore, the natural application of the *nighāta* (tonal suppression) depends upon being part of a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*), since that [suppression] would be impossible in the absence of such unity. Nor can it be asked what verb should be supplied in the phrase "the ten incarnations of Hari" (*harer daśāvatārāḥ*); understand that the verb *bhavanti* ("they are") is to be supplied.

However, where there is unfitness [for the application of the rule], the present time—the meaning of the suffix *laṭ*—is not construed [with the verb], because it is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitatvāt*). Alternatively, *laṭ* is used in the sense of proximity to the present (*vartamānasāmīpye*). And this proximity takes the form of either the past or the future; for this very reason, Mukuṭa says: "The ten incarnations of Kṛṣṇa are victorious" (*jayanti kṛṣṇasya daśāvatārāḥ*). The Miśras maintain that in such instances as "The giver of water attains satisfaction; the giver of food attains imperishable happiness," there is no intention to express the meaning of *laṭ*.

Madhusūdana Ṭhakkura, in his *Kaṇṭhābharaṇoddhāra*, states that because the suffix *laṭ* signifies the present tense, and since proximity (*sāmīpya*) is a qualifier of the meaning of that suffix, [the expression "he cooks now"] is indeed a sentence. On this point, the Naiyāyikas maintain: even though an actionless state may exist, a sentence is of three kinds: a collection of nominal stems (*subanta*), a collection of verbal roots with suffixes (*tiṅanta*), and a collection of both nominal stems and verbal roots with suffixes. For example: "the three times," "he is cooking" (*pacati bhavati*), and "Caitra causes [him] to see" (*citraḥ paśyayati*).

However, "being a single sentence" (*ekavākyatā*) does not consist in the capacity to produce a cognition having a single primary qualificand (*ekamukhyaviśeṣyakabodhajanakatva*), because that [definition] would apply even to such cases as "Look, the deer runs" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*). For instance, in this case, the meaning of the sentence—the locus of the act of seeing whose object is the deer which is the agent of running—is manifested in the verbal action of "seeing" through the relation of objecthood (*karmatā-saṃsargeṇa*). And since the sentence possesses meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), there is no occurrence of the accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*) etc., which is triggered by a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Nor does it follow that there is a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

Furthermore, a sentence cannot be devoid of action; for instance, in the phrase "I am a snake" (*ahamasmi phaṇī*), some action must necessarily be supplied. Moreover, if [the pronoun] were to have the verb as its qualificand, then in examples such as "The man goes; prostrate at his feet" (*prayāti puruṣastasya caraṇāvabhivādaya*), there would be no reference to the man by means of the word *tasya* (his). This is because, otherwise, even sentences such as "These are the king's elephants and these are his horses" (*ete rājamātaṅgā ete tasyaiva turagāḥ*) would result in being grammatically incorrect. Thus they spoke at great length.

In this regard, we maintain the following: consider the sentence "The deer runs. Here, such a deer does not enter into a semantic relation as the object (*karman*) of the act of seeing. This is because it is an established principle that there can be no direct semantic comprehension (*anvaya-bodha*) through a relation other than identity between the meaning of a nominal stem (*nāmārtha*) and the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvārtha*). Otherwise, sentences such as "He cooks rice-grains" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacati*) would also result in being grammatically correct. Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because the deer qualified by running is the meaning of the entire sentence and thus lacks the status of being the meaning of a nominal stem.

If that were the case, the nominative case-ending (*prathamā*) following *mṛga* would not occur, because that [case-ending] also depends upon a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Furthermore, it is accepted by the followers of Patañjali (*phaliṣa*) that the sentence *paśya mṛgo dhāvati* ("See, the deer runs") forms a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatva*) precisely when there is no intention to express the running as the object of the act of seeing performed by the deer; yet that [unity] would be untenable under such an interpretation. This consensus of the followers of Patañjali has been clarified by Helārāja. For he says: "Just as one inflected word (*subanta*) may be a qualifier of another inflected word, so too they say that a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) may be a qualifier of another finite verb."

Having said this, the underlying intention is that there is no remedy [for the objection] when the act of running itself is intended as the object (*karman*). Otherwise, one would simply say, "See the deer running. Furthermore, since in the phrase "the three times are known," the connection with an action is possible, it would follow that citing a sentence devoid of an action as an example would result in an inconsistency. Moreover, even in cases such as "Listen, the cloud thunders," "Listen, the actor sings," and "See, the jar perished," the [proposed definition] fails to apply.
By this, the view that the objecthood (*karmatva*) resides solely in the meaning of the nominative case (*prathamā*) is refuted.

Furthermore, in this way, there would be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of number with the deer (*mṛga*). This is because the cause for a cognition whose qualifier is a number presented by a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is the presentation produced by a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*), which possesses the primary qualificandhood (*mukhya-viśeṣyatā*). Otherwise, in the example "The fame is white like a female swan" (*haṃsīva dhavalā kīrtiḥ*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the number also connecting with the female swan (*haṃsī*). And if one were to accept the absence of number-connection with the deer as being desired, then even sentences such as "Look, the deer are running" (*paśya dhāvanti mṛgāḥ*) would result in being grammatically correct (*sādhutva*).

Furthermore, from the observation of usages such as "The *paṭola* leaf destroys bile (*pitta*), its stalk removes phlegm (*kapha*)," and "Caitra has gone to the village; O Maitra, what does he do now?", it follows that by the word *tat* (that), there is a reference even to a qualifier. However, there is no reference to a qualifier that constitutes the very form delimiting the objecthood (*padārthatāvacchedaka*) [of the referent]. Therefore, in cases such as "These ten are the king's elephants," there is no inconsistency whatsoever. For this very reason, this is a general maxim (*utsarga*), not an absolute rule (*niyama*).

As it has been said: "Pronouns refer primarily to that which is most proximate [in the discourse]"; this is the general direction. This has already been analyzed below, and the remainder will be explained in the *Pada-pañcikā* commentary later on. Thus concludes the reflection of the venerable Mahopādhyāya, a jewel of the Maithila lineage. In this regard, the Naiyāyikas object: "In that case, even the nominative case-ending after the word 'mṛga' (deer) would not occur."

The meaning is this: if the deer qualified by the action of running were not the referent of the sentence, then because it would lack the status of being a noun-meaning (*nāmārtha*), the nominative case (*prathamā*)—which is dependent upon a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—would also not occur. To this, it is replied: in the statement "the deer runs" (*mṛgo dhāvati*), the nominative occurs first with respect to the agent who is the referent of the noun and possesses the number already expressed; subsequently, even though it is construed as part of the sentence-meaning in relation to another verb such as "sees" (*paśyati*), one cannot negate its initial status as a nominal stem. Therefore, who indeed is able to prevent the nominative?

As for the description of the intention of the Bhāṣya—that what is intended to be construed as the object (*karman*) in the act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa-kriyā*) is the deer’s running (*dhāvana*) characterized by eagerness (*utkaṇṭha*)—it has been stated: "Just as a single inflected noun (*subanta*) may be the qualifier of many verbs ending in *tiṅ*, so too a verb ending in *tiṅ* can be the qualifier of another verb ending in *tiṅ*."

Thus, both of these views presented by Helārāja are not sound upon critical examination. This is because of the rule that when two [words] express a co-referential meaning (*sahārtha*), the one ending in the suffix *prati* has the primary meaning; and because, according to the principle that "the presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the suffix is the cause for a verbal cognition delimited by the property of being a verbal cognition through the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) as determined by the mode-ness (*prakāratā*) residing in the meaning of the verbal root," there can be no syntactic awareness (*anvayabodha*) in which one verbal root-meaning is the mode and another verbal root-meaning is the qualificand, due to the absence of such a cause.

It is not the case that [the predominance of the action] is impossible. Nor should it be argued that, because of the statement of the distinguished sage Yāska—“Verbs (ākhyāta) have the action as their primary meaning, while nouns (nāman) have substance as their primary meaning”—the predominance of the meaning of the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*) in a verb must be abandoned. For the term *ākhyāta* is conventionally established (*nirūḍha*) only for finite verbs (*tiṅ*), and not for verbal roots (*dhātu*). The meaning of that [statement by Yāska] is that among the meanings of a verb—such as number, tense, and so forth—it is precisely the action (*bhāva*), which is the meaning of the verb distinct from number and time, that possesses predominance.

In reality, although the meaning of the word ending in the nominative case is primary, there is no contradiction in its being construed as a qualifier of the action of seeing through the relation of being the object of the deer’s intense running.

For the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) consists merely in being connected with that which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). In the case of "the deer runs" (*dhāvati mṛgaḥ*), the deer is the qualificand of the action of running, and the action of seeing is connected with it; thus, its mere state of being connected as a qualifier remains intact even for the action of running. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the statement of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, nor is there any contradiction with the statement of Helārāja. This is clearly established in the *Mīmāṃsā* in such passages as "The priests proceed wearing turbans" (*soṣṇīṣā ṛtvijaḥ pracaranti*) and "The priests proceed wearing red turbans" (*lohitoṣṇīṣā ṛtvijaḥ pracaranti*).

For instance, in the preceding sentence, even though turbans (*uṣṇīṣa*) are the means for accomplishing the desired end, they are construed as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). In that context, being a qualifier consists precisely in being related to that which is related to the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Since the priests are the qualificands of the turbans, the fact of being the means for accomplishing the desired end—which resides in them—is what the turbans are related to. However, in the subsequent sentence, there is no construction regarding the performance (*pracaraṇa*) by the priests qualified by the turbans—attained from the preceding sentence—as being the means for accomplishing the desired end; rather, it is only the redness (*lauhitatva*) itself [that is so construed].

Even in that case, it is because redness is understood to be connected to the property of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) through the mediation of the silent [injunction] by way of a succession [of meanings], based on the specific substratum in the form of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). As for the claim that one should say "see the running deer" simply because one sees it, that is not so; for when synonymous words are employed, the speaker's intention alone is the determining factor, and thus there is no undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*). If there were no intention whatsoever, one would not utter the word "deer," but would instead say only "see the running animal"; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

As for the argument that because the three times are known as such, there is no possibility of their connection with an action—and thus a sentence devoid of action would result in incoherence—that is not correct. For in the case of the question and answer sentences, "How many times? and "Three times," which do not require the action of knowing (*jñāna-kriyā*), it is possible for them to be devoid of action. Furthermore, as for the claim that [the definition] fails to apply even in cases such as "Listen, the cloud thunders," "Listen, the actor sings," or "The jar has perished, will perish, or is perishing," that too is incorrect.

"Indeed, when a prescription or a prohibition applies to something qualified, they shift to the qualifier provided there is a sublation of the qualified object"—according to this maxim, since hearing and seeing are sublated in the case of the qualified objects, namely, the roaring and singing clouds, the application of hearing and seeing shifts to the qualifiers, namely, the absence of roaring and singing. As for the claim that in cases such as "Listen, the cloud is roaring," because the act of hearing lacks the cloud as its object, this "object-ness" (karmatva) must be understood as residing solely in the meaning of the first case (the nominative), that is not correct.

By the maxim *saviśeṣaṇe hi* (for when there is a qualified [term]), even though the status of being the object of the act of raining is sublated in the case of hearing—since it is impossible for that [act] to have as its object a cloud qualified by roaring—the status of being the object of the act of roaring is possible for this [cloud]; thus, it has been correctly stated that the meaning of the nominative case is "object-ness. The distinction here is that when something is the referent of a word (*padārthatva*), it appears as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*). However, in reality, because of the rule that there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in a nominal suffix (*sub-vibhakti*), "object-ness" is not the meaning of the nominative case.

Furthermore, since the nominative case ending (*prathamā*) seeks only the meaning of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), and because there is no denotable object (*śakyārtha*) [in this context], it is impossible for there to be indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the form of a relationship with a desire (*śikya-sambandha*); such is the truth. This is because of the usage by the author of the *Mahābhāṣya*: "Conchs are heard, kettledrums are heard," and because of the usage by the learned: "The Pāñcajanya was heard resounding," as well as because the maxim "for when there is a qualifier" (*saviśeṣaṇe hi*) is universally accepted.

As for the objection that, if this were so, there would be no number-concord with the deer (*mṛga*), because the cause of a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the number presented by a verb is the presentation generated by a word ending in the nominative case as the primary qualificand—and otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of number-concord even with the female swan (*haṃsī*) in the example "The fame is white like a female swan," and if one were to accept the lack of number-concord with the deer, it would follow that sentences such as "Look, the deer are running" would also be grammatically correct—that is not tenable.

The meaning is as follows: in this way, in the perception [of the sentence], there is an auxiliary benefit (*upakāra*) by virtue of the fact that the running deer is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*). The sense is that "primary qualificandhood" (*mukhyaviśeṣyatva*) consists in being a qualificand precisely when there is an absence of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*). In that regard, the word "primarily" (*mukhyena*) need not be stated, because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as "Caitra alone is cooking."

Since the meaning of the particle *eva* consists in the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*), when it is construed with a single part of that meaning—namely, the qualifierhood of Caitra—the latter lacks the status of being the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣyatva*) required for the subjectivity of a word ending in the nominative case. Consequently, the sentence "Caitra cooks" does not have the same meaning as "Someone other than Caitra does not cook."

And thus, in the case of "Caitra alone cooks," in order to prevent the number from being construed with Caitra, it is appropriate to accept the following causal relation: for a verbal cognition whose qualifier is number, the cause is the presentation of a word ending in the nominative case as the qualificand, even when that presentation is brought about by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta).

In the verse, "O dark-thighed one, your fame, like another swan, plunges into the celestial Gaṅgā," if one does not admit the application of number to the object of comparison (the celestial Gaṅgā), then it would be untenable for the quality of being the locus of plunging into the celestial Gaṅgā—which is the meaning of the verbal suffix—and its number to serve as the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*).

In examples such as "Your fame is like a black swan" (*haṃsyeva kṛṣṇā te kīrtiḥ*), even though the excellence of the meaning is established, according to the school of rhetoricians, there would be no fault in the difference of gender and number—which causes a lack of aesthetic flavor—residing in the upamāna (standard of comparison) and the upameya (object of comparison). This is because of the rule that number is construed with the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) when it is something other than gender and tense; and since the pronoun *tat* invariably refers to the intended object of emphasis, whether it be the substantive or the attribute, depending on the context.
However, there is no apprehension whatsoever of the specific qualifier that serves as the delimitor of the property-ness (padārthatāvacchedaka) [of the object].
Thus ends the Vākyatattvavāda.
The Vākyaratnapradīpikā composed by Śrī Hariyaśomiśra.

According to the authoritative definition that "a sentence (*vākya*) is a collection of *su*-inflected words (*subanta*) or a collection of *tiṅ*-inflected words (*tiṅanta*)," if one takes either the state of being a collection of *su*-inflected words or the state of being a collection of *tiṅ*-inflected words—whether combined or individually—as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of a sentence, there would be a mutual lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). Furthermore, the definition "a collection of words" (*padasamūha*) would over-apply (*ativyāpti*) to such instances as "the cow, the horse, the man, the elephant. With this concern, he asks: "Now (*atha*). The understanding is that this well-known thing in the world, which is denoted by the word "sentence" and has become the object of inquiry, is what is intended.

The word *nāma* is a particle used as a sentence ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*). According to the *Bhāṣya*, "that which contains a single finite verb (*tiṅ*) is a sentence. If it were stated that "being a sentence consists in having the status of a finite verb (*tiṅ*) while there is oneness," then even the form *pacati* (he cooks) would result in being a sentence. If one were to resort to a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that in which there is one finite verb"—the resulting definition would be "a collection of words containing a single finite verb is a sentence. This would be over-extensive (*ativyāpti*), failing to exclude forms such as *pacati bhavati* (he cooks [and] exists). With this intention, he states the meaning [of the definition] as "one... [etc.]. By "by that" (*tena*), he means by the formulation of such a definition.

Regarding the phrase "and there is no contradiction in its being part of a single sentence" (*anvayaś cāsya naikavākyatāvyāghātaḥ*), this refers to the negation of that [contradiction]. In the case of *pacati bhavati*, the syntactic cognition (*anvayabodha*) is as follows: the action (*bhāvanā*) residing in a single substratum which is conducive to softening (*viklitti*); distinct from that, the action residing in a single substratum which is conducive to the production of a conjunction with a subsequent location, generated by momentum (*vega*), and characterized by a specific activity (*vyāpāra*) whose object is the visual perception; and [finally] that which resides in a single substratum distinct from the former. The phrase "no contradiction in its being part of a single sentence" means that there is no occurrence of multiple sentenceness (*anekavākyatā*) caused by the difference between two finite verbal endings (*tiṅanta*).

One might object: "Even in a sentence devoid of an action, there exists existence; therefore, the definition [of a sentence] does not over-extend to it. Anticipating this doubt, he states "nahi" and so forth, to show that since such a sentence contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) [in the definition].

One might object: "In passages such as *'prayāti puruṣastasyaikaṃ caraṇāvabhivādaye'* (I bow to one of his feet), since the pronoun *tasya* (of him) refers back to the word *puruṣa* (the person), we must accept that the meaning of the nominative case (*puruṣa*) alone is the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*). Therefore, the definition provided [by you] is incorrect. With this concern in mind, the opponent raises the objection starting with *astu* ("Let it be so"). The author replies starting with *paśyata mṛgaḥ* ("Look, the deer...").

Now, one might object: even if we accept that in sentences such as "paśyeṣa" ("see this!"), there is a cognition in which the meaning of the nominative case is the primary qualificand, why do we not accept—by supplying the word "tam" (him)—the following cognition: "The deer possesses an effort conducive to running, and [I] am the locus of the act of seeing whose object is the deer"? For if this were accepted, there would be no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) resulting from the generation of a cognition with multiple primary qualificands.

However, one might raise the objection: "Since the understanding generated is merely that 'I am the locus of a perception whose object-residence is a deer possessing an effort conducive to running,' and since there is no lack of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) because this [understanding] serves as the generator [of the final cognition], how can there be no way out here? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] replies: If one accepts the view that the meaning of a noun (such as *mṛga*, "deer") cannot be construed with the verbal root-meaning through a relation other than identity (*abheda*), then the usage of sentences such as *taṇḍulaṃ pacati* ("He cooks rice") would result in being grammatically correct [only if the rice were identical to the act of cooking], which is absurd. Therefore, it must be accepted that the meaning of a noun can indeed be construed with the verbal root-meaning through a relation other than identity, namely, the relation of being the object (*karmatā*). Thus, the deer is construed with the perception as its object.

Since it is untenable for the semantic representation (*upasthiti*) produced by a case-ending (*vibhakti*) to be the cause of a cognition whose qualifier is the word-meaning and which possesses a relation of difference (*bhedasaṃsarga*), [the author], with the intention that a second case ending (*dvitīyā*) must necessarily follow the word *mṛga* in order to convey the objecthood (*karmatā*) of the referent of *mṛga*, says: "of the deer" (*mṛgasya*), and so forth. He states the resulting conclusion therein: "And when there is a second case ending," and so forth, up to the end of the passage: "it would be 'see the deer running'."

One might object: "But surely there is no fault, for such usage does occur, as in 'Run after that deer! Anticipating this doubt, he says "And so" (*tathā ca*). [The response is: It would be like saying "See the running deer," but not "See, the deer is running"; thus, in that case, the cessation of that [usage] is undesirable. To this he says: "Because of the ellipsis of *tam*. That is to say, in that instance, the understanding of the deer alone as the primary qualificand is accepted by supplying the word *tam* (it); therefore, its cessation does not occur. Thus he states: "Because of the ellipsis of *tam*."

Anticipating the objection that there might be the undesirable consequence (iṣṭāpatti) of a split in the sentence (vākya-bheda), he refutes it with the words "na ca" (and not). "Tathā sati" means if there were such a split in the sentence. The meaning of the sūtra "tiṅṅatiṅaḥ" is that a finite verb (tiṅanta) is elided [by sandhi] when another finite verb follows it, provided it is not preceded by another finite verb.

One might raise the objection: "Even in the absence of being part of a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*), since there is no need for the exclusion of *tiṅ* [in the rule *atiṅ*], the possibility of its being a counter-example (*vyāvartyatva*) is established. Anticipating this, [the author] states that by the rule "The non-accentuation (*anudātta*), the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, and the substitutes for *idam* must be stated to occur within a single sentence (*samānavākye*)," the non-accentuation of one *tiṅ* ending would only apply when there is a single-sentence relationship with another *tiṅ* ending; thus, even in the absence of the mention of *atiṅ* in the sūtra, there would be no contingency of non-accentuation. To prevent that, the mention of *atiṅ* in the sūtra is necessary. He concludes by stating that, according to the natural sense of the non-accentuation rule, there is indeed no contingency of non-accentuation in the absence of a single-sentence relationship.

The meaning is that if there were no status as a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*) with another finite verb (*tiṅanta*), then because that [status] would be impossible, the occurrence of non-enclitic accent (*anighāta*) for what follows a finite verb would be untenable; thus, the mention of "not being a finite verb" (*atiṅ*) would be redundant.

Now, one might object: since the incarnations of Hari exist in the past and the future, there is an absence of the operation of verbal action (*kriyā*) therein; therefore, the definition [of tense] does not apply to them. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that even though the meaning of the present tense (*laṭ*) is not intended to be expressed, the usage of "not being" (*na bhavantī*) is possible—as in the phrase "know that they are not being" (*bhavantīlatvaṃ viddhi*). Thus, the understanding is as follows: there is an absence of an entity conducive to the act of becoming (*bhavana*), which resides in a substratum delimited by a plurality non-different from the ten incarnations related to Hari. This is because [the existence of those incarnations] is not intended to be expressed [as a current fact].

Even when there is an intention to express the sense of the *laṭ* (present tense suffix), by the rule "in proximity to the present, optionally as if it were the present," the cognition is that the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) resides in a time other than the immediate vicinity of the present. Thus he says: "In proximity to the present," and so forth. Precisely because the sense of the *laṭ* is not intended, and precisely because [the suffix] has the meaning of proximity, [he says] "or. [The example is] "Jayantī" and so forth. The cognition is: the *bhāvanā* conducive to excellence, residing in a time proximate to the present, which subsists in a locus delimited by a plurality non-different from the ten incarnations related to Kṛṣṇa.

For this very reason, the statement "mixed [with water] is not recommended" is cited by the author of the *Aṇubhāṣya*. Regarding the term "giver of water" (*vārida*): one must accept the following syntactic understanding—that there exists a present-tense *bhāvanā* (efficient force) conducive to the attainment of the object "satisfaction," which resides in a single substratum non-different from the giver of water. However, that is not possible because such a *bhāvanā* would have to be future-oriented. In this world, since the quenching of thirst in the giver of water is never observed without his own drinking, satisfaction must be said to belong to the next world; thus, the sense of the *laṭ* suffix (present tense) is not intended here. This is the underlying point.

"From this very [reason]" (*ata eva*)—Madhusūdana Ṭhakkura explains this in another place: "The word 'atha' (now) is being defined. One should understand that the commentary on the passage from the *Cintāmaṇi* beginning with these words is the work titled *Nyāyaratnāvalī*, and the commentary on that work by Pakṣadharamiśra is the work titled *Kaṇṭakoddhāra*, both authored by Madhusūdana. Regarding the phrase "the three times," the resulting cognition (*anvayabodha*) is that the times are non-different from those qualified by the property of being three (*tritva*).

In the case of "pacati bhavati" (he cooks while becoming), the subsequent cognition (*anvaya-bodha*) is that the action conducive to cooking has the state of becoming as its locus. In the case of "caitraḥ pacati" (Caitra cooks), the subsequent cognition is that Caitra possesses the action conducive to cooking.

The nature of being a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*) consists either in: (1) a word being co-occurrent with another word that generates a cognition possessing a primary qualificandhood (*mukhya-viśeṣyatā*) residing in its own referent, which is not determined by a modehood (*prakāratā*) residing in some other referent; or (2) a word being co-occurrent with another word that generates a cognition possessing a primary qualificandhood residing in its own referent, which is not determined by a modehood residing in any other referent. Since this definition exists even in cases such as "Look, the deer is running" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*), there is no deficiency in its status as a single sentence due to the absence of the requirement for the supply of a verb like "he sees" (*tam iti*). Thus, [the objection regarding] "Look" (*paśya*) is refuted.

Regarding the sentence "The deer runs, [I] see [it]" (*mṛgo dhāvati paśyāmi*), there is a single sentential unity. Now, one might object: since the cause of a cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of a noun and whose relation is a difference (or connection) is the semantic presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by an inflection (*vibhakti*), how can the running deer be the object (*karman*) in relation to the act of seeing? For in that case, there is an absence of a semantic presentation produced by that [inflection]. Therefore, the accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*) would be required; and thus, such a sentential fragment as *dhāvataḥ mṛgasya* [would be necessary]. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states that because such a fragment lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

He states that there is no occurrence of the second case ending because the cognition having that meaning as its qualifier is not pervaded by the delimitor of being produced by that [word]. This is expressed by the phrase "due to the absence of meaningfulness" (*arthavattvābhāvena*), which means due to the absence of any relation other than *śakti* (denotative power) or *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function) as defined by the meaning.

And thus, there arises a cognition possessing as its primary qualificandum (mukhyaviśeṣyatā) the referent of the word *sva* (itself), which is qualified by a locus-hood (āśrayatva) delimited by a self-linking relation (*svarūpasambandha*), which is non-different from a qualificandum-hood (viśeṣyatva) qualified by a mode-hood (prakāratā) residing in the act of seeing (*darśana*)—this mode-hood being delimited by the relation of objecthood (*karmatā*), which is non-different from a qualificandum-hood qualified by a mode-hood residing in the act of doing (*kṛti*)—this mode-hood being delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), which is non-different from a qualificandum-hood qualified by a mode-hood residing in the act of running (*dhāvana*)—this mode-hood being delimited by the relation of "favorability" (*anukūlatā*).

Now, one might object: "Since a sentence devoid of an action is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the threefold classification of sentences is inconsistent. Anticipating this doubt, he says, "Furthermore," and so forth. He demonstrates that there indeed exist sentences devoid of an action with the words, "For instance," and so on. This is because it is universally known—that is, established by the experience of all people. If it is objected: "Even here, it is possible to supply an action such as 'exists' (*bhavati*)," we say no; for there is a contradiction in applying the locus of a present existence to the past and future times.

Nor should it be argued that the present tense (*laṭ*) signifies proximity to the present, as in the case of [the word] *jayanya*. For proximity to the present consists of being past or future; thus, even if it were connected with an existence related to those past and future times, it is impossible for it to be connected with an existence related to the present. Furthermore, "proximity" cannot be defined in a way that is common to the present, by which an existence related to the present could also be included.

Nor should it be said that the sense of the *laṭ* suffix is both proximity to the present and the present itself; for a single word cannot simultaneously convey multiple meanings through both direct denotation (*śakti*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Nor can it be argued that, just as in the expression "the hamlet is on the Gaṅgā," where the co-occurrence of the hamlet and the boat necessitates the simultaneous presentation of both the current and the bank by the word "Gaṅgā" through two modes of operation, so too the *laṭ* should present both the present and its proximity. This is because, in the case of "the hamlet is on the Gaṅgā," the word "Gaṅgā" indeed presents both the current and the bank due to the requirement of connecting the hamlet and the boat. However, in the case of the *laṭ*, there is no such necessity for a dual presentation of the present and its proximity. Furthermore, the rule *vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavadvā* (Pāṇini 3.3.131) is intended to provide an option (*vā*) regarding the application of the suffixes, not to indicate that both meanings are simultaneously expressed by a single suffix. Thus, the view that the *laṭ* expresses both the present and its proximity is untenable.

Regarding the objection that there is a contradiction between two simultaneous functions, [the author] says "for here... and so forth, intending to show that this contradicts the ancient verses. To the question, "But surely in that case the meaning of the *laṭ* (present tense) is simply not intended to be expressed," he says "Moreover... and so forth.

In order to avoid the contingency of [the erroneous] validity of such cognitions as "this pot" or "that genus," it is necessary to accept that pronouns (*sarvanāman*) necessarily denote the principal element (*pradhāna*). Consequently, in the cognition "an activity conducive to going, residing in a single locus non-different from the person," since the person appears as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), there would be no reference by the word *tat* (in the phrase *taccaraṇau*) to that [person]. Therefore, one must accept that the cognition has the meaning of the nominative case (*prathamāntārtha*) as its primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*); thus, the action itself is the qualificand.

By the words "ityādi" (and so forth), [the author] explains that otherwise, if pronouns were to present qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), then since the cause for the cognition of a difference (*bheda*)—where the meaning of a noun is the qualifier (*prakāra*)—is the presentation produced by an inflection (*vibhakti*), there would be an impossibility of the connection of such a deer as the object (*karmatā*) with the act of seeing. Thus he says: "In the sentence 'Look, the deer is running,' etc."

The cognition of the case-role (*kāraka*)—namely, "the deer is that which possesses the activity (*kṛti*) specific to the meaning of the verbal root [√*dhāv*], which is produced by the nominal stem [‘mṛga’] whose meaning has been manifested"—arises from the knowledge of the sentence "the deer is running," assisted by the visual perception produced by the knowledge of the three-fold realm (*tṛśidhātu*). In the production of this verbal cognition—which possesses a qualificandhood residing in visual perception, as determined by a modehood residing in the deer (which is delimited by the activity of running, which in turn is delimited by the relation of objecthood)—the presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by the word 'deer' and so forth does not function as a cooperative cause.

Furthermore, the cognition produced by the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the sentence "The deer runs," assisted by the mental presence (*upasthiti*) of such [a deer], acts as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*). Thus, even if that deer is not the object of the mental presence generated by its name, there is no fault in the form of a violation of the rule—that the cognition of the meaning of a noun as the object (*karmatā*) within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) through a relation other than identity (*abheda*) is untenable—with this in mind, he says: "In that case, 'running,' etc."

That being the case, since the meaning of the sentence involves the deer—qualified by the act of running—as the object (*karman*) in its connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the phrase "even the first [case-ending]" implies that there is no prohibition against any general case-ending (*vibhaktisāmānya*). The undesirable consequence (*anartha*) would be that no case-ending whatsoever could follow the word *mṛga*. In this context, the reason for this must be supplied as "because it would not be a nominal stem (*apratipadikatvāt*)," in accordance with the text beginning with "of that too" (*tasyā api*).

Although this objection is irrelevant—since the word *mṛga-pada* is not a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) due to its being distinct from both a verbal root and an affix, and because it lacks meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) by virtue of denoting the non-existent nature of a "deer" (*mṛgatva*), which results in the failure of the grounds for its application—it is nevertheless the case that, just as in the sentence "the blue pot" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*), where the meaning of the verb *dṛś* (to see) is construed with the object, no case-ending is observed following such a sentence; so too in the present instance, the meaning of the verb is construed with the object.

The point is that even the nominative case-ending (*prathamā*) would not occur after the word "mṛga" (deer) when it signifies a deer qualified by the act of running (*dhāvana-kṛti-viśiṣṭa*). Now, one might object: "When a certain causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present, only that specific deficiency (*kātartha*) which is observed there should be applied as a consequence (*apādya*). Since in the sentence 'I see the blue pot' (*nīlaṃ ghaṭaṃ paśyāmi*), the understanding of the connection between the act of seeing and the objecthood (*karmatva*) of the blue pot is observed to arise from the knowledge of that very co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*), let there be no case-ending after the sentence 'Look, the deer is running' (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*), just as there is none after the sentence 'the blue pot' (*nīlaṃ ghaṭam*)."

The cognition that "the deer, who is the agent of running, is being seen" arises solely from the knowledge of the words ending in the nominative case; it does not arise in the absence of those specific case-endings. Therefore, [the opponent's claim] that the nominative case would not exist is groundless. To this, he says: "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*). And that syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is indeed untenable; the meaning is that if one accepts the cognition "the locus of the act of seeing the deer, who is the agent of running," then there is an inconsistency with the syntactic unity intended by the author (the *phaṇin*).

One might object: "How is it known that the connection of the deer’s act of running at full speed with the action of seeing is the intended scope of the speaker's meaning? Anticipating this doubt, with the intention of stating that "the understanding of a specific [meaning] arises from the commentary, for there is no lack of definition due to doubt," he cites the consensus of Helārāja, the author of the *Bhāṣyavivaraṇa*, by saying: "But the consensus of the commentators... etc.

Therefore, according to Helārāja’s clarification, the word *mṛgaḥ* (deer), being a nominal form (*subanta*), is not a qualifier of the act of seeing; rather, the running performed by the deer as its agent is the qualifier of the seeing. Following the word *eva*, the remainder of the sentence is: "it is construed with the action of seeing (*dṛśi-kriyā*) as the object (*karman*). Following the word *vivakṣāyām*, the remainder of Vākyapadīya 3.7.145 is: "when [the deer] is employed [as the subject], [one says] 'look, the deer is running'. *Na pratīkāraḥ* means not a refutation or rejection.

And thus, the point is that if such a deer were accepted as the object (*karman*) there, the very impossibility of its being an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) recognized by the grammarians would be the defect. Now, one might object: according to the rule—"The base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) express the meaning together, and between those two, the meaning of the suffix is predominant"—there exists a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) in the view that, for an expectancy-cognition whose qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) is determined by a mode-ness (*prakāratā*) residing in the meaning of the verbal root, the cause is the presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the suffix acting as the qualificandum. Thus, [the deer] cannot be the object.

If it is argued that because there is an absence of the semantic presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a suffix (*pratyaya*), the connection of "running" (*dhāvana*) with the verb is not possible, and therefore only the Naiyāyika position—which maintains that the deer alone is connected there—is correct, we say no. Precisely because of the aforementioned rule, the semantic presentation generated by a suffix is a cause for a cognition where the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) is the qualifier and [the suffix-meaning] is the qualificand. Consequently, the accusative case-ending is required for the presentation of the objecthood (*karmatva*). Otherwise, as he says [in the text], there would be the undesirable consequence of the collapse of the sentence "Look, the deer is running" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*).

The meaning of that [statement] is: "If one accepts the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) for the purpose of bringing about the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the objecthood (*karmatva*). And thus, such a requirement (*nyāya*) is fulfilled only in the case of words ending in *sub*-suffixes; however, in the case of words ending in *tiṅ*-suffixes, one must accept a semantic cognition (*anvayabodha*) where the verbal root-meaning is not the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Therefore, even when there is an intention to express the meaning of the present tense (*laṭ*), since it is possible to construe the present time within a cognition whose objects are past or future, he says "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*) to show that a sentence devoid of action would be logically inconsistent.

He states another fault in accepting a single cognition in which the meaning of the word ending in the nominative case is the primary qualificand: "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*). In the Nyāya view, regarding the sentence "Listen, the cloud thunders," the cognition is: "The locus of listening has as its object the thundering whose locus is the cloud. But that is not possible, because sound alone is the object of hearing, and the cloud is not the locus of that [sound]. In the Vaiyākaraṇa view, however, the cognition is: "Listening, which has as its object the thundering residing in a locus non-different from the cloud, has as its locus one that is non-different from you."

And that [interpretation] is indeed correct. In the Tārkika (Logician) view, the understanding from the sentence "Listen, the actor sings" is: "The locus of hearing has as its object the song, which has as its locus the actor. But that is not possible, because the actor is not the locus of hearing. In the Vaiyākaraṇa (Grammarian) view, the understanding is: "Hearing, which has as its object the song residing in a single locus non-different from the actor, has as its locus a single entity non-different from you. And that is precisely the actual state of affairs.

In the Nyāya view, the understanding of the sentence "The pot was seen before it perished" is that the locus of the perception has as its object a pot whose destruction occurred at a past time. However, this is not possible, because since the pot has already perished, its perception is impossible. In the Vaiyākaraṇa view, the understanding is that the perception—which has as its object a destruction occurring at a past time relative to a single counter-positive non-different from the pot—has as its locus a single substratum non-different from you (the speaker). And that [perception] is indeed valid knowledge (*pramā*).

And thus, according to the view of Nyāya, the sense is that there is simply non-pervasion (avyāpti) in various instances. By this, it is shown that [the objection] regarding the unfitness of expressions such as "hear, he roars" is refuted. Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the nominative": even if one accepts that in a sentence such as "see, the deer runs," the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*) of the cognition is the meaning of the word ending in the nominative case, there is no violation of the rule that a relation other than identity between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root cannot be the object of a relational cognition. Thus, there is no breach of the established principle.

The point is that if one accepts a sentence-meaning cognition (*anvayabodha*) of the form "I am the locus of the act of seeing which has as its object the first-case meaning residing in the deer who is the agent of running," then the deer—who is the agent of running—cannot be construed with the action of seeing through the relation of being the object (*karmatā*). Now, an objection is raised: if one accepts a sentence-meaning cognition whose primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*) is an action, then in cases such as "I salute the feet of the man who is going" (*prayāti puruṣasya caraṇāv abhivādaye*), there would be no reference by the pronoun *tat* (in the word *taccaraṇau*) to the man.

Since the meaning of the word ending in the nominative case (*prathamāntārtha*)—namely the person—is a qualifier of the denoted object (*ākhyātārtha*), it lacks the status of being the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣyatva*). Consequently, to avoid the undesirable consequence (*aprāmāṇya*) that sentences such as "this is a jar" (*ghaṭo 'yam*) or "this is its genus" (*taj-jātiḥ*) would be invalid (because the pronoun *ayam* could not then refer to the primary qualificand), one must not accept that the word [the pronoun] brings about the presentation of the primary qualificand. Therefore, one must instead accept a cognition in which the primary qualificand is the meaning of the word ending in the nominative case; with this in mind, he says: "Furthermore... (*kiṃ ca*).

Thus, if one accepts that the primary qualificand (mukhyaviśeṣya) of the understanding has as its subject the meaning of the nominative case-ending—as in "the deer, which is the object of the act of seeing and the agent of the act of running"—then why would there not be a connection with number [in that very locus]? To this, he says: "Even though it is presented by the verbal suffix," and so forth.

In this regard, the intended meaning is as follows: In the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), since the agent is not denoted because the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has "action" (*kṛti*) as its primary meaning, there would arise the undesirable consequence of such usage as *devadattena pacati* ("Devadatta cooks by means of himself"). To prevent this, the requirement that the number (*saṃkhyā*) must be construed with the "productive activity" (*bhāvanā*)—which is the meaning of the verbal suffix—is restricted to cases where the number is "not already expressed" (*anabhihitāyām*). However, if one does not accept the sense of the sūtra *kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā* ("the third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument") as belonging to the governing heading *anabhihite* ("when not [already] expressed"), then it is impossible to maintain that the number expressed by the suffix is construed with the agent or the object already denoted by the verbal suffix itself. Therefore...

It must be accepted that, for the sake of a relational cognition (anvaya-bodha) whose qualifier is a specific number (asaṃkhyā-prakāraka), the presentation (upasthiti) generated by a word ending in the nominative case (prathamānta-pada) is the cause, by way of the relation of primary qualificandhood (mukhya-viśeṣyatā-sambandha), which is defined as the state of being the qualificand residing in an object that is not intended as a qualifier of anything else.

And likewise, in the sentence "Look, the deer runs," there is the defect that the number cannot be construed with the deer because the aforementioned relation [of being the qualificand] does not exist; this is due to the fact that the deer, being a qualifier of something else, is not the object intended by the primary meaning [of the verb]. Now, one might object: even in the Grammarian's (Vaiyākaraṇa) view, since the deer is a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal suffix (tiṅ) through the relation of identity (abhedasaṃbandha), how can there be a construal of number with it? This is not so, because in that system, such a causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) is not accepted.

If it is asked what kind of causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) exists according to that view, it is as follows: "The verbal root (*dhātu*) is traditionally held to denote the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*), while the personal endings (*tiṅ*) denote the substratum (*āśraya*). Among these, the result is primary, the operation is primary, but the meaning of the *tiṅ* (the substratum) is a qualifier. In this context, the "result" is [the state of] being softened (*viklitti*) and so forth; the "operation," however, is the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), which is designated as a non-differentiated action because its nature is to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*). Having defined the meaning of the verbal root, he states the meaning of the *tiṅ*: "while [denoting] the substratum. The substratum of the result is the object (*karman*), and the substratum of the operation is the agent (*kartṛ*).

In this context, since both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) are obtainable within the verbal root (*dhātu*), the expressive power (*śakti*) of the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) does not reside in that [operation] portion. Having analyzed the meaning of the word, he analyzes the meaning of the sentence with the words "in the result," and so forth. The meaning is that the operation is the primary element, the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), with respect to the result such as the softening of the grain (*viklitti*).

The meanings of the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) are agent, object, number, and time. Among these, the agent is a qualifier of the activity (*vyāpāra*); the object, however, is a qualifier of the result (*phala*). Number is a qualifier of the agent when an agent-suffix is used, and a qualifier of the object when an object-suffix is used. Time, however, is a qualifier of the activity, but not of the agent or the object as number and result are; for if it were, there would be the undesirable consequence of using the form *pacati* ("he cooks") even for an agent whose activity has already ceased, nor would there be the undesirable consequence of using *pacati* during the stage when the result has not yet arisen even though the activity exists.

Thus, the causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) is established as follows: with respect to a cognition having a verbal suffix as its qualifier and a specific number as its mode, the cause is the presentation of the agent or object produced by that [suffix]. Consequently, in the sentence "Caitra cooks rice" (*caitraḥ taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), the resulting cognition is: "An activity occurring at the present time, which is conducive to the softening residing in the object that is rice, and which has an agent non-different from Caitra."

In the case of "caitreṇa taṇḍulaḥ pacyate" (The rice is being cooked by Caitra), the understanding is that there is an activity performed by Caitra at the present time, which is conducive to the softening residing in a single object non-different from the rice. And in this way, regarding the current instance "mṛgo dhāvati" (The deer runs), since the agent non-different from the deer is presented [by the suffix], and because of its existence, there is no impossibility of the number [singular] being construed with it; such is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "Since it has been accepted that the cause [of verbal cognition] is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the nominative case which resides in the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*), there is no impossibility of the number (*saṃkhyā*) being construed there. To this, he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*). The meaning of this is: "if one does not accept that such a presentation is the cause in relation to the primary relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*). And thus, in the view of the Logicians (*Tārkika*), there would indeed be an impossibility of construing the number there. He wards off the objection that the non-construal of number is acceptable by stating: "In 'the deer' (*mṛge*), etc., because of the consequence of grammatical incorrectness," up to the end.

If it is argued that the objection remains—that in the phrase "the person goes to that very [state]," the word *tat* (that) cannot refer back to the person—this is not so. For the word *tat* functions as a substitute for a qualifier, and since it is observed in some instances to refer even to that which serves as a qualifier, it is possible for the person, who is the qualifier here, to be referred to by the word *tat*. Thus he says: "Moreover... (*kiṃ ca*).

[Objection: "In that case, wouldn't there be validity even in such cases as 'this is a jar' or 'this is its genus,' since there too it is possible to have a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of jar-ness by means of that very word? To this he says: "But [in the case of] *paraṃ tu*... [He says] "not a reflective awareness. The point is that even if a reflective awareness of the mode of presentation (*prakāra*) brought about by the word is impossible through that word itself, there is no obstacle to a reflective awareness of a qualifier distinct from that [mode] by means of that word.

Now, if it is argued that in cases such as "these ten," since there is no obstacle to the word *tasyaiḥ* (by them) referring back to the king, it would follow that the pronoun (*tat*) applies to that [king]—the author states "by that" (*tena*) to concede this point. The meaning is that it is possible for a pronoun to refer back to a qualifier even when that qualifier is presented by a different mode than the one used for the substantive.

If it is objected: "But since it is the delimitor of the objecthood (*padārthatāvacchedaka*) of that [substance], how can there be a reference to it by the word *tat*?"—then, in the case of the statement "The leaf of the *paṭola* removes bile" as well, because the word *paṭola* is used metaphorically (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean "that which is related to the *paṭola*," the *paṭola* is indeed the delimitor of the objecthood; thus, there is no impossibility of its being referred to by the word *tat*.

Nor should it be argued that, because the compound (*vigraha*) and the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* must have the same meaning, one cannot accept a lakṣaṇā (metaphorical indication) for the first member in the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*; for if the word *paṭola* were restricted to the mere *paṭola* [plant] itself, it would lack the status of being the delimitor of the objecthood (*padārthatāvacchedakatva*), and thus its reference by the pronoun *tat* would be impossible. This argument does not apply here either, because in the present case as well, the word *rāja-* is restricted to the king alone and thus lacks the status of being the delimitor of the objecthood, making its reference by the pronoun *tat* impossible.

Now, from the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) "the leaf of the *paṭola*," a cognition arises in which the relation to the *paṭola* is the mode (*prakāra*). However, from the compound (*samāsa*) "the *paṭola*-leaf" (*paṭolapatram*), if one does not accept *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) there, a cognition would arise in which the *paṭola* itself is the mode. Consequently, the identity of meaning between the analytical sentence and the compound sentence—which consists in their generating cognitions with the same mode—would be violated. To prevent this, one must accept that the word *paṭola* has *lakṣaṇā* in the sense of "relation to the *paṭola*."

And if the word *paṭola* were thus the delimitor of the objecthood (*padārthatāvacchedaka*) [of the compound], there would be no comprehension (*parāmarśa*) of it by that very word [in the compound]. Nor should it be argued that, just as in the case of "the leaf related to the *paṭola*" (*paṭolasaṃbandhi patram*), in expressions such as "the *paṭola-leaf*" (*paṭolapatram*) and so on, there would be the consequence of the non-co-referentiality (*ananvaya*) of the meanings of the two nouns, because of the established rule that "the meaning of a noun [is co-referential] with the meaning of another noun" (*nāmārthayor iti vyutpatteḥ*).

In cases such as "The jar is not a cloth" (*ghaṭaḥ paṭo na*) and "Caitra goes like a horse" (*caitra iva aśvo gacchati*), since the semantic understanding is accepted through the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) between the referent of the word "cloth" and the negative particle (*na*), and through the relation of being located in itself (*svanipatatva*) between the referent of the word "Caitra" and the particle "like" (*iva*), it follows that there is no linguistic rule (*avyutpanna*) for the verbal cognition of the meaning of a nominal stem—distinct from a particle—to occur through a relation other than identity (*abheda*).

If it is argued that—just as there is a restriction on the rule [of grammatical agreement]—there can be no comprehension of the meaning of a noun (other than those already mentioned) through a relation other than identity with the denotation of another noun, and thus the restriction of the rule must be accepted because the traditional doctrine that "the analytical sentence (*vigraha*) and the compound (*samāsa*) have the same meaning" is itself the basis for this—then, since one must accept that the word *pāṭola* has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding its relation to the *paṭola* creeper, the *paṭola* would be the delimitor of the objecthood (*padārthatāvacchedaka*), and consequently, it remains impossible for it to be referred to by the pronoun *tat*. [Response: This is not so.

According to the view of the Ekadeśins (partialists), who accept that in the sentence "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), the jar also relates to the act of bringing by way of the relation of objecthood (*karmatā-sambandhena*), there arises—just as in the case of "the leaf of the *paṭola*" (*paṭolasya patram*)—a relational cognition (*anvaya-bodha*) where the *paṭola* is the qualifier, even though the cognition has the leaf as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*). Thus, just as in the latter case there is a cognition having the relation with the *paṭola* as its mode (*prakāra*), so too here there is a cognition having the *paṭola* as the mode.

And thus, since one accepts that the cognition [arising from] both the analytical (vigraha) and the compound (samāsa) has as its qualificandum a specific leaf characterized by the *paṭola* [creeper], there is no absence of the *paṭola* and other terms [in the compound] being the denotatum (*padārtha*), because there is no absence of their being the delimitors of the denotatum (*padārthatāvacchedaka*). Consequently, there is no impossibility of referring to them by the word "that" (*tat*) in such expressions as "the leaf of the *paṭola*.

And likewise, in cases such as "these ten are the king's elephants" (*daśaite rājamātaṅgāḥ*), the reference by the word "that" is possible because the king is not the delimitor of the denotatum. This is the intended meaning.

Alternatively, just as in the case of "paṭolasya patram" (the leaf of the *paṭola*) and "rājño mātaṅgāḥ" (the elephants of the king), where a cognition arises that has the meaning of the genitive case—endowed with its own inherent sense—as its qualifier, so too in cases such as "paṭolapatram" (the *paṭola* leaf) and "rājamātaṅgāḥ" (the king's elephants), even if one accepts a cognition where the leaf and the elephant are the qualificanda and the relation to the *paṭola* and the king is the qualifier by means of recollecting the elided genitive case, there is no violation of the rule that the meanings of two nouns are connected only through identity (*abheda*).

And thus, since there is no single delimitor (*avacchedaka*) for the denotatum (*padārtha*) of "paṭola" and so forth, it is possible for them to be referred to by that [single] word. However, in reality, because of the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that the meaning of a noun and its referent are non-different, and because there is no evidence for restricting [this rule], and because there is no necessity for the recollection of an elided genitive case, it is necessary to assume a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) toward the related object (*saṃbandhin*). Consequently, the state of generating a cognition with the same object (*samānaviṣayaka-bodhajanakatva*) constitutes the identity of meaning between the analytical statement (*vigraha*) and the compound (*samāsa*), but not otherwise.

That [the capacity of a compound to convey meaning] consists in its being a generator of a cognition of the same type [as that produced by the analytical expansion]. In the case of *āruḍhavānaro vṛkṣaḥ* ("the tree on which a monkey has climbed"), from the analysis *āruḍho vānaro yam* ("that on which a monkey has climbed"), the resulting cognition is: "the monkey is the agent of the act of climbing whose object is the tree. From the compound, however, the cognition is: "the tree is the object of the act of climbing whose agent is the monkey. The same applies to cases such as *prāptodako grāmaḥ* ("the village reached by water").

In that case, regarding the analysis (*vigraha*) "the water which has reached [the village]," the understanding from the analytical sentence is that the water is the object of the action of reaching; however, from the compound, there arises an understanding based on its internal structure (*ānvayabodha*) that the village is the object of the action of reaching whose agent is the water. Thus, because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the emergence of different modes of understanding in each instance, [the compound] cannot be the analysis. Furthermore, since a *bahuvrīhi* lacks an analytical sentence, it does not have the status of being an analytical sentence itself; for in the case of "citraguḥ" (one who has brindled cows), the statement "he to whom a brindled cow belongs" is an explanation of the meaning of the compound, but it is not the analysis (*vigraha*).

If it is argued that there is no analysis (*vigraha*) because the meaning is expressed by the very words being compounded, we say no; for it is not the case that there is no analysis at all there, since the analysis is precisely that which is understood from the sentence that initiates the compound. However, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, that [sentence] is not grammatically correct, because in that instance the analysis must be performed using only the words that are actually being compounded.

For this very reason, it is stated that a *bahuvrīhi* is necessarily a compound (*nityasamāsa*) in order to indicate that its analytical expansion (*vigraha*) is ungrammatical. For this same reason, its definition is given as: "an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*) is one without an analytical expansion (*avigraha*), or one whose analytical expansion does not contain its own constituent words (*asvapadavigraha*). In this context, an "analytical expansion not containing its own words" (*asvapadavigraha*) is a process of separation (*vyāpāra*) conducive to the comprehension of the meaning by means of other words that possess the same referents as the words constituting the compound.

One might object: "In expressions such as *rājapuruṣa* (the king's man), if one accepts that the word *rājan* (king) has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the related [man], then since there is a cognition of non-difference between the meanings of the words expressing the qualifier and the qualified, the rule 'a *karmadhāraya* occurs where there is a cognition of non-difference' would apply, resulting in the undesirable consequence of it being a *karmadhāraya* compound. This is not so, because the rule for a *karmadhāraya* applies only in cases where the two words expressing the qualifier and the qualified possess identical referents prior to the formation of the compound and convey a cognition of non-difference through their co-referential application (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). In the case of *rājapuruṣa*, this condition is not met.

And thus, the phrase "of the qualifier which is the delimiting factor of the denotatum" (padārthatāvacchedakarūpaviśeṣaṇasya) means "of the qualifier which is the delimiting factor of the denotative capacity" (śakyatāvacchedakarūpaviśeṣaṇasya).
