Consequently, since there is the possibility of referring even to a qualifier that is distinct from the delimiting factor of the denotative capacity, the point is this: in cases such as *rājamātaṅgāḥ* ("the king's elephants"), although the word *rāja-* has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of one related to the king, and although the king is the delimiting factor of the denotatum, he is not the delimiting factor of the denotative capacity; therefore, there is no impossibility of the reference.

Furthermore, according to the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), it cannot be argued that the compound *rājapuruṣa* has no denotative power (*śakti*) at all with respect to a person related to a king as its collective meaning. Nor can it be said that, since the king is the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the denotative power, there would be no subsequent reference (*parāmarśa*) to him; for the king does indeed function as a qualifier in that sense, being the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) in which the delimiting relation of the denotative power is fully instantiated (*paryāpti*). Thus, because he is a qualifier in that manner, there is no lack of justification for his being referred to by the pronoun *etat*.

For this very reason, at the point already mentioned, by the mere reference (*parāmarśa*) through the word "that" (*tat-pada*) even to the qualifier, there is no restrictive rule (*niyama*). The meaning is that there is no such rule that the reference must be exclusively to the primary sense (*mukhya-artha*), because a general rule (*utsarga*)—an injunction that operates when there is no sublation (*bādhaka*)—is sometimes set aside when a sublation exists; thus, there is no restriction. Regarding this, he cites the consensus with the words beginning "That has been said" (*tad uktam*). The remainder of the text, ending with "vimarśa" (in the form *vimarśa* with the suffix *añ*), is clear from the context of the treatise.

Having thus presented the view of the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas), he introduces [the following] in order to remove the objection raised against the Naiyāyika position—namely, that "if the meaning of the sentence were construed as the object (*karman*) in the act of seeing, then even the nominative case (*prathamā*) after the word *mṛga* would not occur"—by stating: "The claim that 'the nominative after the word *mṛga* would not occur' is meaningless. Thus ends [the section].

In the view of the Naiyāyikas, since the agent is not denoted because the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is the action (*kṛti*), one must accept the following: in order to prevent the undesirable consequence of such usages as *devadattena pacati* (‘Devadatta cooks by means of [himself]’), there must be a causal relation between the cognition of the qualifier—wherein the verbal suffix has the property of being a qualifier through the relation of being the qualificand—and the cognition of the object qualified by it; specifically, the cause is the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the meaning generated by a word ending in the nominative case, which has as its content an object that resides in the relation of being the qualificand within the intended meaning of the verbal suffix.

And likewise, in the case of "the deer runs" (*mṛgo dhāvati*), since the deer—which is the substratum (*anvayin*) of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) consisting of an effort conducive to running—is required to be connected with the number expressed by the verb-ending (*ākhyāta*) according to the rule that the number denoted by the verb must reside in the subject, it follows that the nominative case for the word *mṛga* (which presents the deer as the subject) is unavoidable. With this intention, he says: "In that regard, it is said," and so forth.

"The first objection—that the cited intention of the author of the Bhāṣya is contradicted and that the contradiction with Helārāja’s consensus is difficult to resolve—is not insurmountable; therefore, he says: 'As for what [was said]... Now, the maxim of Ajaya, namely that 'the stem and the suffix express the meaning together,' applies only when the suffix is a *sub*-ending. In cases such as *taṇḍulān* (accusative plural), where there is an internal cognition (*anvaya-bodha*) having the rice-grains (*taṇḍula*)—which are the meaning of the stem—as the qualifier (*prakāra*) and the objecthood (*karmatva*), which is the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*), as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), this [maxim] arises through the relation of being the qualificand."

Since there exists a presence [of the meaning] not produced by a second factor serving as a condition (pratyaya), the purpose of the utterance is fulfilled; therefore, in the case of a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), one must simply accept that the resulting cognition of syntactic relation (*anvayabodha*) has the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as its primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*). With this intention—namely, in accordance with the statement of the Sage Yāska, "The verb (*ākhyāta*) has the action (*bhāva*) as its primary [meaning]"—which intends a cognition of syntactic relation where the action denoted by the verbal root is the principal qualificand—he says: "And not... (*na ca*).

Regarding the statement "the verb (ākhyāta) has the action (bhāva) as its primary meaning," the word *ākhyāta* here is not conventionally established as referring to a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), because the authors of the grammatical treatises do not employ it in that sense, and even when they do employ it there, it is used in a secondary (metaphorical) sense; for the authors of the treatises are seen to use the term in its well-known primary application to refer to the finite verb forms themselves. Therefore, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*), considering the claim that "a word ending in a verbal suffix generates a relational cognition in which the action denoted by the root is the principal qualificand" to be the prattle of a deluded person, [interprets] the phrase "the verb has the action as its primary meaning" as follows: [The sentence is: "The verb has the action as its primary meaning. Here, the word *ākhyāta* refers to a word ending in a nominal suffix (*kṛdanta*) that generates a relational cognition in which the action denoted by the root is the principal qualificand. Thus, the proponent of the final view maintains this very point.

Since the meaning of the suffixes—other than number and time—is alone considered the "bhāva" (the primary meaning), and because the causal relation consists in the fact that the suffix is the cause for the verbal cognition whose qualificand is such a meaning, this [view] is based on a causal relation of this kind: namely, that the suffix is the cause for the verbal cognition whose qualificand is the meaning of the suffix, according to the principle: "The base and the suffix express the meaning together; of these two, the meaning of the suffix is the principal. Thus, it is by virtue of such a causal relation that [the suffix is the cause].

It is appropriate that the term *ākhyāta* (verb) occurring in the statement of Yāska should not be understood merely as a form common to both verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and nominal suffixes (*sup*). Since in examples such as *taṇḍulaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice"), we observe a cognition where the objecthood denoted by the accusative case is the qualificand, as well as a cognition where the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) denoted by the suffix is the qualificand, [Yāska] necessarily states: "the word *ākhyāta*."

[Objection: But surely, even this [quality of] running upwards becomes the object (*karman*) of the act of seeing (*dṛśi-kriyā*) by virtue of being the object of the resulting state; thus, there is a contradiction with that [definition]. To this he says: "But in reality... [Objection: But if this is so, then the status of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*), which consists in being connected through connection with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), is not accepted even by the Bhāṣyakāra for running upwards, but rather only for [the action] directly related to the act of seeing. Anticipating this doubt, he states the consensus of the Tāntrikas (the followers of the system), since such a status of being a qualifier is indeed accepted by them, saying: "And this is clear..."

According to the view of Pārthasārathi Miśra, since the meaning of an injunction consists in being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), in cases such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), there is an acceptance of the syntactic relation that the sacrifice is a means to a desired end; thus, in the subordinate injunction "he offers oblation with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), the syntactic cognition is that curd is a means to a desired end. This is either a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the meaning of the verbal root, or the syntactic cognition is that the state of having curd as its instrument residing in the oblation is a means to a desired end.

And likewise, in the present case, regarding the statement "The priests proceed wearing turbans," if one accepts the syntactic cognition that "the priests wearing turbans, who are subordinate members of the act of proceeding (*pracaraṇa*), are the means to achieve the desired end," then, upon the connection of the priests qualified by the turban with the status of being a means to the desired end, there follows the connection of the turban itself with the status of being a means to the desired end.

Similarly, in the case of the expression ‘lohitoṣṇīṣā ṛtvijaḥ’ (the priests with red turbans), when one accepts the form of the relational cognition that "the priests qualified by the red turban are the means for accomplishing the desired end"—which is a constituent part of the ritual performance—the fact that the redness itself is also understood as a means for accomplishing the desired end follows from its inherence in the turban which, in turn, is inherent in the priests. Thus, the point is that even in the present case, if the deer qualified by the action of running is the object of the act of seeing, then the running itself is also the object of the act of seeing; this remains entirely consistent with the Bhāṣya.

Even in the view of Bhaṭṭa, regarding the sentence "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), when the meaning of the sentence is accepted as "one should bring about the desired result by means of a sacrifice possessing Soma," there is no obstacle to the sacrifice qualified by Soma being construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the productive activity (*bhāvanā*). Since there is likewise no obstacle to Soma itself being construed as an instrument through the medium of the sacrifice, these [qualifiers] are indeed intended to possess the status of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇatva*) in the sense that they are construed while being themselves construed with the qualificand. Thus, in the cited example, both [the redness and the turban] are understood as: "One should bring about the performance by means of priests wearing turbans; [specifically], by means of priests wearing red turbans."

One should cultivate the practice [of understanding] by accepting the connection with the understanding of the subordinate element (*viśeṣaṇa*). Since it is accepted that the redness (*lohita*), which has become a subordinate element through its connection with the turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) by means of the officiant (*ṛtvij*), there is no contradiction in the fact that the nature of being a subordinate element—which consists in being connected to the principal element (*viśeṣya*)—is not obstructed. Likewise, even for the act of running (*dhāvana*), there is no contradiction in the fact that its status as the object (*karman*) in relation to the action of seeing (*dṛśi-kriyā*) through the medium of the deer is not obstructed by the connection. Thus, there is no inconsistency.

Nor should it be argued that in the Bhaṭṭa school’s view, in such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), the instrumentality belongs solely to the sacrifice and not to the Soma; for otherwise, since the fact that the sacrifice possesses Soma would not be established without another sentence following "one should sacrifice with Soma," the acceptance of a syntactic cognition (*anvaya-vibodha*)—namely, "one should bring about the sacrifice by means of Soma" (*somena yāgaṃ bhāvayet*)—based on an implied sentence would be untenable.

According to the Vārttika stating, "In an injunction (*vidhi*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*), the sacrifice is intended to be the instrument (*karaṇa*)," even in cases such as "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), where there is only an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), the understanding of the sentence-meaning is that "one should effect the desired result by means of a Homa characterized by curd."

Likewise, in this case as well, there is acceptance [of the qualified sacrifice as the instrument]. For if the meaning of the verbal root were accepted as the instrument independently of another sentence—such as "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*)—then the efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) having curds and the like as its instrument could not be obtained, and thus the injunction of the mentioned accessory (*guṇavidhi*) would be untenable. Therefore, since it is more reasonable to accept that the qualified sacrifice itself is construed as the instrument within the efficient-force, and that the qualifier is also construed as an instrument, it is improper to assume a separate sentence, as that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Intending to show that the nature of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*)—defined as being connected with that which is to be qualified (*viśeṣya*)—is well-established in Mīmāṃsā, [the author] states the definition of being a qualifier as "being connected with that which is to be qualified" in the passage beginning with "tathā hi" and ending with "svīkārāt. Therein, even in the subsequent sentence, [the connection] occurs through a mediated relation (*paraṃparā-sambandha*) consisting of "residing in that which resides in itself" (*svāśrayāśrayatva*); and this [connection] is linked to the qualified object, namely the *ṛtvij* (priest), by way of the turban (*uṣṇīṣa*).

And thus, it follows that for the redness (*lauhitya*), by way of the relation of being the substratum of its own substratum (*svāśrayāśrayatva-sambandha*), there is an inherence (*anvaya*) with the object denoted by the word *mṛga* (deer), which is the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) of itself; and [that redness] inheres in the property of being a means to the desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). Now, one might raise an objection with the following intention: if the deer, which is the substratum of the act of running, were to inhere as the object (*karman*) in the act of seeing, then one would not say "paśya mṛgo dhāvati" ("see, the deer runs"), but rather one would have to say "paśya dhāvantaṃ mṛgam" ("see the running deer"). With this in mind, he raises the objection: "yattu... (As for what [you said], etc.).

He provides the resolution with the words beginning "That is not so," based on the intention that since it is observed that in the usage of both the analytical (*vyāosa*) and the compound (*samāsa*) forms—such as *nīlaṃ ghaṭaṃ paśya* ("see the blue pot") and *nīlaghaṭaṃ paśya* ("see the blue-pot")—the speaker's intention alone is the determining factor, and since there is no lack of a determining factor for the difference in sentence meaning even when there is a twofold usage such as *ayam piśaṅgo mṛgo dhāvati* ("this tawny deer runs") and *dhāvantaṃ mṛgaṃ paśya* ("see the running deer"), the speaker's desire alone must be the determining factor.

If the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) is present, then even in a single usage such as "see the deer running," the desired consequence follows; therefore, by this much, there is no loss of the sense of "see the deer [who is] running. The point is that among synonyms whose meanings are non-different, when one is used, another cannot be prohibited by anyone from being used.

One might object: "When one sees a running deer, there is a difference in meaning between the two expressions 'paśyan mṛgo dhāvati' (seeing, the deer runs) and 'paśya mṛgo dhāvati' (see, the deer runs). In the former, the deer is intended as the object (*karman*) associated with the act of seeing; in the latter, the deer is intended as being connected to the act of seeing through its relationship as the object. Therefore, if one intends to express the deer’s connection to the act of seeing as its object, the construction 'paśyata mṛgo dhāvati' (O you who see, the deer runs) ought to be used. To this, he says: "In every way" (*sarvathā*). There is no inconsistency whatsoever.

The meaning is that there is no inconsistency whatsoever—such as a contradiction with the intention of the Bhāṣyakāra and others if the deer qualified by the action of running were construed as the object, the undesirable consequence of the suffix *śatṛ* in the word *dhāvatī*, or the undesirable consequence of a second case ending (*dvitīyā*) after the word *mṛga*. (Note: This passage addresses a grammatical objection regarding the analysis of the sentence "mṛgaṃ dhāvantaṃ paśya" [See the running deer]. The opponent argues that if the deer qualified by the action of running is the object, it would contradict the views of Patañjali and others; furthermore, it would lead to the incorrect application of the present participle suffix *śatṛ* instead of *śatṛn*, and a second case ending after *mṛga* instead of the first.)

Now, [the opponent] objects: "If *vākyatva* (sentencehood) is defined as being a collection of words that generates a cognition whose primary qualificand is the meaning of a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), then sentences are divided into three types—those consisting of a collection of finite verbs, those consisting of a collection of nominal stems ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*), and so forth—and examples are given in the order of 'the three times' (*trayaḥ kālāḥ*) and so on. However, in the case of 'the three times,' since there is no word ending in a finite verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), the definition fails to apply (*avyāpti*). To address this, by means of supplying the word *jñāyante* ('are known'), [the sentence is interpreted as] having as its object [a cognition] qualified by the number three, residing in a single substratum that is non-different from time."

Anticipating the objection that the definition of a sentence stated by the Grammarians—namely, "knowledge consisting in the cognition of the mutual connection [of meanings]"—is faultless because there is no contradiction even in cases such as "Look, the deer runs," where the action [of running] is construed as the object (*karman*) of the act of seeing (*dṛśi*), he restates [the opponent's view] in order to resolve it with the words "As for what [was said]... [The opponent argues: "In the case of 'The three times are known,' although your stated definition lacks non-pervasion (*avyāpti*), when the question 'How many times are there? is asked, the answer 'The three times' is indeed seen."

Regarding this, with the intention that the definition is under-determined (*avyāpta*) because there is no possibility of supplying a verb (*kriyādhyāhāra*) due to the absence of an instigator (*prayojaka*), he says: "Not so. This is because it is impossible for [the sentence] to be devoid of a verb. Nor should it be argued that the aforementioned definition is not under-determined, since even in the question and answer sentences—"How many times are the times? and "The times are three"—there is the possibility of supplying words such as "are known" (*jñāyante*).

The sense is this: when a question is posed with the desire to know the specific modes through which the property of time (kālatva) is manifested—asking "How many [types of] times are there?"—then, in order to satisfy that desire for knowledge, it is the sentence providing knowledge of those specific modes that is required; it is therefore improper to supply a verb that was not sought after.

Now, having accepted that the verbal cognition has the action as its primary qualificand (viśeṣya), if one instead accepts a cognition where the primary qualificand is the meaning of a word ending in the nominative case—as in "Listen, the cloud thunders," "Listen, the actor sings," and "The jar perished"—then [the following difficulties would arise]: in the first two cases, it would be impossible for the cloud (the locus of thundering) and the actor (the agent of singing) to be the objects of hearing; and in the third case, it would be impossible for the jar (which is the counter-positive of a past destruction) or the jar (which is the counter-positive of a destruction occurring at the moment of perception) to be the object of the verb "is seen" (dṛśya).

He restates the following objection in order to resolve the doubt that "one must indeed accept a cognition in which the action is the primary qualificand": "As for what was said, 'hear' (śṛṇu), etc. He says—refuting it with the words "For [prohibitions and injunctions] operate when accompanied by qualifiers" (*saviśeṣaṇe hi*)—that there is no inconsistency whatsoever, because the acts of roaring, singing, and perishing can be construed with the objects of hearing and seeing respectively.

Nor should it be argued that a qualification cannot function as a probans (sādhana) by relying on the maxim "the [qualification] does not [apply] when there is a qualified [subject]" (*saviśeṣaṇe hi*), because there is no evidence for such a maxim. This is because we observe such usage as "the heaven-dweller has perished" (*svargī dhvastaḥ*), "the crested one has perished" (*śikhī dhvastaḥ*), and "the crested one has perished" (*śikhī dhvastaḥ*). In these cases, since the destruction (the meaning of the suffix *kta*) cannot be construed with the heaven-dweller or the crested one—who, as the counter-correlates of that destruction, are themselves indestructible—the destruction must necessarily be construed with the crest and the heaven. Thus, the qualification functions as a probans.

Nor should it be argued that the word-generated presentation of the object denoted by the first-case suffix—which possesses a counter-positive such as destruction—is not a cause for the connection with the "tuft of hair" or "heaven," which are non-word-meanings (apadārtha), because the maxim states: "A word-meaning connects with a word-meaning, but not with a part of a word-meaning. For the connection of a word-meaning with a part [of another word-meaning] is also observed in certain instances.

If it is asked, "What is wrong [with this view]?"—it is because we observe such usage in examples like *śaraiḥ śātitapatraścaitrasyāgurukulam* ("Caitra’s teacher’s family has its leaves cut off by arrows"). If it is further objected that even in cases such as *ghaṭo nityaḥ* ("A pot is eternal") or *paśurapaśuḥ* ("An animal is a non-animal"), there would be no sublation (*bādhaka*) to the comprehension of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*)—namely, that [the pot] possesses potness which is the locus of eternality, or that [the animal] possesses animalness which is distinct from being an animal—and thus these too would have to be considered valid (*prāmāṇya*), we say: No.

Because the verb *iṣyati* (he desires) is expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*), even though a partial syntactic connection (*ekadeśānvaya*) is impossible, [the sentence] lacks validity because the term *ghaṭo nityaḥ* (the pot is eternal) lacks such expectancy for eternality. If it is objected: "In cases such as *svargī dhvastaḥ* (the heaven-dweller has perished), since there is no expectancy for a permanent [subject], how can there be a partial syntactic connection?", we reply: No. Since the comprehension of syntactic connection depends upon speaker-intent (*tātparya*), we accept a partial syntactic connection in this case because validity cannot otherwise be accounted for.

Nor should it be argued that even in cases such as "the jar is eternal" (ghaṭo nityaḥ), where there is an actual intention [to convey a meaning] and partial syntactic connection is possible, the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) would result; for when an intention exists, this is indeed accepted. For this very reason, where the syntactic connection of word-meanings is impossible, the authors of the treatises justify the matter by taking the expression to be primarily intended to denote the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna-nirdeśa*), according to the maxim: "An apparent inconsistency (*anyathānupapatti*) is stronger than anything else."

Furthermore, regarding the statement "the peacock is destroyed" (*śikhī dhvastaḥ*) and so forth, if one were to accept that the word *śikhin* (peacock) and others denote only the crest (*śikhā*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and that the resulting cognition is of the form "that which is distinct from the counter-positive of the destruction of the crest," then it must be said that the use of words that do not directly denote [the object]—such as "the crest is destroyed" (*śikhā dhvastā*) or "the heaven-dweller is destroyed" (*svarge dhvastaḥ*)—would be impossible. This is because of the maxim: "When one has control over the use of words, why should one employ a non-denotative term? For this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total disappearance of all words used in a secondary sense.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that there are two types of figurative usage (*lākṣaṇika*): the conventional (*nirūḍha*) and the purposive (*prayojanavat*). The conventional refers to words such as *kuśala*, while the purposive refers to expressions such as "a hamlet on the Ganges. In this context, [the word *svarga*] in the phrase "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) and so forth is neither purposive—because there is no perception of a purpose here, unlike the perception of coolness, purity, and so on in the case of [the word "Ganges"]—nor is it conventional, because that would entail the logical fault of assuming an intention (*tātparya*) without beginning (*anāditaḥ*), which is unnecessarily cumbersome (*gaurava*). Thus it must be stated.

Since authoritative usage such as "your voice is celestial" (*svargī dhvanistava*) is observed, the assumption of an initial intentionality (based on that usage) is itself authoritative; therefore, the presence of complexity (*gaurava*) is not a fault. Now, an objection: if one accepts that words like *śikhyā* (peacock-possessor) indicate merely the crest (*śikhā*), then because the crest would lack the status of being a qualifier—given that the primary qualificandum is the object presented by the word following the compound—the example would not be consistent with the maxim "for when there is a qualified [object]," and thus the application of the term *śikhyā* and so forth would be untenable. This is the point.

One must simply accept that [the word] conveys a substratum qualified by the crest-lock and so forth. And thus, since the relation of the property "having destruction as its counter-positive" occurs with respect to the crest-lock—which is but one part of the referent—the violation of the rule that "a referent is related to a referent" is indeed unavoidable; if this is argued, we reply: no.

In examples such as "Caitra’s teacher’s family" (*caitrasya gurukulam*), the qualification "when there is no expectancy" (*asatyām ākāṅkṣāyām*) is added to prevent over-extension (*vyabhicāra*). Similarly, in cases like "Heaven has perished from that" (*svarge dhvasto tataḥ*), the qualification "having an intention (*tātparya*) to convey a non-existent connection with a part" is necessary, because the rule "word-meaning [connects] with word-meaning" (*padārthaḥ padārthena*) must necessarily be observed by following the requirement for connection with a single part. Now, one might ask: what is the nature of the cognition here? If you say it is simply "the person possesses heaven whose counter-positive has perished," then even in a case where one who possesses heaven has perished, there would be the cognition "heaven has perished."

[Otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence [of the word] being used as a *karmadhāraya* compound (e.g., "the destruction of which is present"). If you argue that the cognition is "that which has a presently existing destruction as its counter-positive" (*vartamānadhvaṃsapratiyogī*), then, since the primary meaning is presented [in the compound], the subordinate member would become the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the principal member would become the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Consequently, even in cases such as "the pot is eternal" (*ghaṭo nityaḥ*), a syntactic cognition of the form "pot-ness residing in the pot is eternal" (*ghaṭavṛtti ghaṭatvaṃ nityam*) would be possible, leading to the loss of its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇikatva*). If you argue that it is "that which has a destruction qualified by its own origination as its counter-positive," then because the destruction-counter-positiveness itself would be understood as qualified by the substratum (*viśeṣya*), the loss of its status as a valid means of knowledge would again follow.

If it is argued that there is no lack of fitness because—just as in the case of a cognition of the "qualifiedness of the qualified" (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyabodha*), where the qualifier-determiner (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka*) relates to the qualified through a mediated relation (*paraṃparāsaṃbandha*)—so too in a cognition of the "qualifiedness in the qualified" (*viśiṣṭe vaiśiṣṭyam*), there is no obstacle to the present destruction relating directly to the qualifier while relating to the qualificand through a mediated relation; [we reply: that very relation is simply not known, such that it could be connected with the qualificand.

To this it is replied: the relation [intended] is that of having a substratum non-different from itself (*svābhinna-āśrayatva*), which is the relation belonging to the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Nor should it be argued that even in cases such as "the jar is eternal" (*ghaṭo nityaḥ*), there would be validity because there is no sublation when "eternal" is construed with the jar through the relation of having a substratum non-different from itself. For, according to the maxim—"When a superimposition has occurred, one seeks its cause; it is not that a cause exists first and then a superimposition occurs"—one must simply resort to the mere justification of grammatical usage, such as the expression "the sound of the *svār* vowel," even if it lacks formal validity.

In cases such as "the crystal is red," since the redness in the crystal appears through a mediated relation (*paraṃparā-sambandha*), there is no room for [the definition] to apply if it were restricted to being a conjunction with its substratum; otherwise, even statements like "the sky is red" would result in being considered valid [cognitions]. Therefore, because there is an absence of usage by experts regarding expressions such as "the sky is red" based on a mediated relation qualified by having a subject characterized by the nature of being a crystal, [that definition does not over-extend].

And likewise, in the present context, the relation in question is that which is characterized by having the person as its locus (anuyogika) and being qualified by having a locus identical to itself, as defined by the counter-positive of destruction; this is because of the usage of learned authorities such as "The self is destroyed," whereas the relation characterized by having a jar or the like as its locus and being qualified by having a locus identical to itself is not the relation defined by eternality, because there is no usage by learned authorities such as "The jar is eternal."

And thus, when there is a sublation of the injunctions and prohibitions through direct connection with the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) itself—given that the particle "hi" (for/indeed) introduces a qualification—the conclusion is that there is no direct connection with the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), but rather the final determination rests upon an indirect connection (*pāraṃparya-sambandha*) with the qualified object. This is the meaning.

In this regard, listen: even in the case of the cognition "the cloud thunders," when one accepts the understanding that [thundering] is the object of hearing and has the cloud as its substratum, there is no possibility of the cloud being directly related to the act of hearing. Therefore, while the thundering—as the qualifier—is directly related to the hearing, the cloud cannot be the object of hearing through direct relation. Rather, the cloud qualified by the thundering is related to the hearing through the relation of "having as its substratum that which has itself as a substratum" (svāśrayāśrayatva). Thus, the cloud qualified by the thundering becomes the object of hearing through this indirect relation.

There is no lack of logical connection due to the impossibility [of such a relation], nor does it follow that there would be a failure to hear the sound whose function is roaring. Now, one might object: "Even so, if one accepts the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the nominal referent—the counter-positive of destruction—with its own substratum (the self) through the relation of being non-different from itself, then the rule of word-formation (*vyutpatti*) stating 'the syntactic connection of two nominal referents' would be violated. This is not so; for, just as in the case of particles (*nipāta*), here too the scope of the rule of word-formation is restricted.

Nor should it be argued that while the contraction of the scope [of the rule] for the particle *na* situated in the *leḍ* (imperative) tense is established by both parties, such is not the case here; for even this contraction is established by both parties due to the absence of any other possible application (*gatyantarābhāva*).

Nor should it be argued that the maxim *na ca saviśeṣaṇe hī* (for when there is a qualification, [the rule does not apply]) is not universally valid; for in cases such as *svargīdhvaṃsataḥ* ("one who has heaven's destruction"), since the word denoting the substratum (*dharmin*) is understood as intending only the property (*dharma*), one accepts the cognition "heaven is the counter-positive of destruction. Since the rule *nāmārthayoḥ* (between the meanings of two nouns) is thus restricted, and the rule *padārthaḥ padārthena* (a word-meaning [connects] with a word-meaning) can likewise be restricted, it would be improper to accept a mediated (*paraṃparā*) relation for the cognition of connection by resorting to such a restriction. This is what must be said.

In expressions such as *svarga-dhvastaḥ* ("Heaven has perished"), the mention of the substratum (*dharmin*) would otherwise be redundant. Thus, when there is an intention to express the connection with the substratum being distinct from itself (*sva*), the usage is *svarga-dhvastaḥ*; whereas when there is an intention to express the connection with the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) residing solely within itself (*sva*), the usage is *svarga-dhvastaḥ*. These two usages arise according to the difference in the speaker's intention between common people and the authors of the technical treatises.

Now, the word "śabda" (sound/word) is being defined. Since we observe such usages as "this object has been heard" (*śruto 'yam arthaḥ*) or "the conch is heard" (*śaṅkhaḥ śrūyate*), in the cognitive apprehension that "therein, the word is the object of definition," although the act of defining lacks an object insofar as it is a process conducive to knowledge, the status of being the object of definition for the word is accepted by taking its status as the object of the knowledge produced by that [act of definition]. This is even in cases such as "this object has been heard," where the object does not possess the status of being the direct object (*karman*) of the verbal root *śru* (to hear).

The status of being the object (*karman*) of the verbal root *śru* (to hear) with respect to an object is established solely by virtue of that object being the object of the cognition produced by the sound which is the sense-object of hearing. In the expression "the conch is heard" (*śaṅkhaḥ śrūyate*), although the conch itself lacks the status of being the object of that [cognition], the status of being its object is nevertheless accepted for the conch as the delimiter (*avacchedaka*) of the conch-blowing, since the conch-blowing is the object of that [cognition].

In this regard, consider the statement "the cloud thunders" (*itthaṃ na śṛṇu garjati meghaḥ*). Even though the cloud qualified by the act of thundering is the locus of the thundering that becomes the object of hearing, if one were to accept that [the cloud] is the primary object of the act of hearing, then the thundering would have to be considered the primary object and the cloud merely a secondary object (*gauṇakarmatva*). However, with the intention of using such a construction to convey the desired meaning—namely, that the thundering itself is the object of hearing—there is no obstacle to obtaining that intended sense. This is the point intended when it is said that [the restriction applies] "to the qualifiers, such as the absence of thundering and singing."

It was stated [by us] that this is because hearing, seeing, and so forth are possible, but not with the intention that only roaring and the like constitute the object (*karman*) of the verbal root *śru* (to hear). For if that were the case, one would fall into the position of the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*).

[Objection: But surely, even in such elliptical constructions as "Listen to the thundering of the cloud" (*meghagarjanaṃ śṛṇu*) and "Behold the running of the deer" (*mṛgadhāvanaṃ paśya*), the thundering and so forth possess the status of being the object of hearing; and since the cloud is the locus of that thundering which has become the object, it is possible to intend its status as the object of hearing through a mediated succession (*paraṃparayā*). Likewise, it is possible for the deer and its running to be the objects of seeing. [Response: This is not the case for those of straightforward intellect who rely on such indirect formulations as "The cloud thunders" (*garjati meghaḥ*) or "Behold, the deer runs" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*).

If it is argued that this [usage] brings beauty, we say no; for we observe that in those whose hearts are permeated by the impressions of the science of poetics (*sāhitya-śāstra*), aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) arises precisely through the employment of a devious path. Now, one might object: consider the sentence "The deer runs" (*mṛgo dhāvati*). Since there is no cognition of a relation other than identity between the meaning of the verbal root and the meaning of the noun, and since such a construction would be ungrammatical—just as the usage "Rice cooks" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacati*) is not accepted as valid—it follows that a relation of "objectness" (*karmatā*) cannot possibly exist between the deer and the action, and thus the proposed analysis is untenable. Anticipating this doubt:

Regarding the claim made by some that the meaning of the nominative case following the word *mṛga* (deer) is "objecthood" (*karmatva*), and that this objecthood is construed with the deer through the relation of "being located in" (*ādheyatā-sambandha*), while it is construed with the act of seeing through the relation of "not being the qualifier of" (*anirūpakatva-sambandha*), listen to this in order to refute it: [the author] restates what was said by Upādhyāya-vaṃśamaṇi—that in sentences such as *megho garjati* ("the cloud thunders"), there is no possibility of such a construction because the objecthood expressed by the nominative case following the word *megha* cannot be construed with the act of hearing (*śravaṇa*). Thus he says: *yattu...* (As for what [some have said]).

In the phrase *apāstam* ("cast away"), one should understand that the word *etena* ("by this")—which serves as the reason—is heard [in the commentary] as the basis for the explanation: "because there is an absence of the status of being the object (*karmatva*) of the cloud. By adopting either the "pigeon-on-the-roof" maxim (*khalekapotanyāya*) or the "entry of the king's servant" maxim (*rājapuruṣapraveśanyāya*), the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is accepted such that: first, the act of roaring (*garjana*) possesses the property of being the substratum (*āśrayatva*); second, the cloud possesses the property of being the substratum of that roaring; third, the cloud possesses the status of being the object (*karmatva*) of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*); and finally, the cloud—qualified by the property of being the substratum of the roaring—possesses the status of being the object.

He refutes [the opponent's view] with the words "that is not so," based on the following reasoning: even if one accepts that the status of being an object (*karmatva*) residing in such a cloud is intended to apply only to the qualifying portion—by virtue of the maxim "when a qualified [entity] is mentioned, it is the qualifier that is intended"—nevertheless, the status of being a secondary object (*gauṇakarmatva*) remains uncontradicted even in the case of the cloud. He explains this by stating: "even though the status of being an object is not contradicted"; the meaning is that even though the primary status of being an object is not contradicted in the case of the cloud as qualified by roaring.

The meaning is as follows: because it is impossible for the act of roaring to be the primary object of the verbal root *śru* (to hear) through its own inherent connection, even the appearance of the cloud—qualified by the act of roaring—as a secondary object (*gauṇakarma*) of the root *śru* is only tenable when one intends to express that the roaring itself is the object of that [hearing]. Thus, there is no possibility of understanding the act of roaring as the object of the verbal root *śru*.

Regarding the literal reading: "Even when the activity of the cloud [rain] is obstructed by the activity of the wind in the month of Śrāvaṇa, the connection with the activity of thundering is impossible. In this case, if the activity of the first [word, *megha*] were connected with thundering, it would not be the case that the meaning appears as "the cloud qualified by thundering," but rather [it would appear that] the thundering is connected [to the cloud]. However, that is untenable; for it is proper that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—namely, the cloud—be connected with the meaning of the first [word], whereas since thundering is not the meaning of the nominal stem, it is unfit to be so connected, according to the established rule: "The meanings of nominal stems are connected with the meanings of other nominal stems" (*pratipadikārthānām*).

And thus, in the case of "the deer runs" (*mṛgo dhāvati*), because there is no possibility of the word *mṛga* being construed with the suffix *-ghañ* (which denotes the action itself) through a relationship other than identity between the meaning of the verbal root and the meaning of the nominal stem, you accept that the nominative case following the word *mṛga* has the sense of the object (*karmatva*). However, this is not correct in instances such as "the cloud thunders" (*meghaḥ śṛṇoti garjati*), because it is impossible for the cloud (*megha*) to be the object of the verbal root *śru*. Therefore, by the maxim "even when the garlic is eaten, the disease is not cured," your refutation of the *vaṃśamaṇi* [the bamboo-jewel logic] is ineffective.

With the intention that this is indeed correct, he says: "It has been correctly stated that the meaning of the nominative case is simply 'being an object' (karmatva). Furthermore, here [in this system], being free from faults means only that it is not seized by the criticisms mentioned regarding the *vaṃśamanu* [tradition]; it does not mean absolute faultlessness, because it will be shown later that even the well-formed case-endings (*suvibhakti*) are seized by the criticisms to be stated. Similarly, being free from faults here means only that it is not seized by the criticisms already mentioned; it does not mean absolute faultlessness, because it will be shown later that even the well-formed case-endings are seized by the criticisms to be stated.

This is because, just as there is an injunction for the genitive case in the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* [Pāṇini 2.3.65] to denote the object (*karman*), there is no such injunction for the nominative case to denote the object. Furthermore, since the nominative case must be accepted as having expressive power (*śakti*) in some instances—otherwise, one would have to resort to an unintended metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—it cannot be maintained that the nominative lacks such power entirely. Nor should it be argued that the nominative case possesses expressive power regarding gender (*liṅga*) and so forth, based on the injunction: *prātipadikārthaliṅgaparimāṇavacanamātre prathamā* [Pāṇini 2.3.46].

This is because that sūtra intends only to express the fact of being the primary [referent] (*prathamā-vyañjakatva-mātra*). Now, one might object: in the sentence *paśya mṛgo dhāvati* ("See, the deer runs"), since the deer is connected to the act of seeing by way of the relation of being an object (*karmatva*), what is the difference in its being the meaning of the nominative case (*prathamārthatva*) compared to its being an object? Nor can it be said that the distinction lies in avoiding a contradiction with the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*)—namely, that the connection between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verb is untenable unless through a relation other than identity—for if that were the case, there would be no distinction [in the present instance].

Since the cognition of a particular kind is established by experience whenever a particular causal complex (sāmagrī) exists, that cognition must be produced by that very complex; thus, in the case of the co-utterance "He cooks rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because the cognition whose qualificandum is the cooking having rice as its object has not been experienced [prior to the sentence].

In the sentence "paśyā mṛgo dhāvati" ("Look, the deer runs"), since it is established by experience that there is a verbal comprehension (*anvayabodha*) in which the act of seeing has the deer as its object (*karma*), one must accept a verbal comprehension in which the deer is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) related to the state of being an object (*karmatā*). Therefore, he says "padārthavṛtti" (residing in the word-meaning), because even if such a grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) is not accepted, there is no fault [in our position].

The point is that in the case of the cited example, since the cognition has as its qualificandum the act of seeing qualified by having the deer as its object, it is possible to account for this even if the deer is not the qualificandum of the act of seeing qualified by the state of being its object; for it is impossible to accept the view that the meaning of the nominative case is construed with the act of seeing through the relation of objecthood, as this would contradict grammatical convention (*vyutpatti*).

Now, one might object: if, in the absence of a specific grammatical rule, one were to accept figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for a case-ending in the sense of another case-ending, then even in the sentence "taṇḍulaḥ pacati" (the rice cooks), it would be possible for the nominative case to figuratively signify the object; consequently, a single unified cognition could arise in which the act of cooking is the qualificandum and the state of being the object is the qualifier, just as in the case of "taṇḍulam pacati" (he cooks the rice).

And likewise, regarding the statement "The hearing of the *Bhārata* is the work of Vyāsa," even here, without the grammatical rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65), there would arise a cognition of the relation of the object (*karmatva*) and so forth—namely, that "the hearing whose object is the *Bhārata* is the work whose agent is Vyāsa. Since it would be impossible to justify this through a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the genitive case in the sense of "object-ness" and so on, the rule [of Pāṇini] would be rendered useless. With this intention, he says: "But in reality, in the case of a case-ending... (*vastutaḥ tu vibhaktau*).

[Objection: Surely, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) possesses *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) precisely in accordance with the intended meaning; and as for the grammatical rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti" [Pāṇini 2.3.65], it is for the purpose of precluding the second and third cases, so it is not redundant. To this, he says: "Furthermore... (*kiṃ ca*). [The phrase] "because of the impossibility of the primary meaning" (*śakyābhāvāt*) means that since the sūtra [Pāṇini 2.3.46] beginning with "prātipadikārthaliṅgaparimāṇavacanamātre" is understood as indicating the primary intention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and so forth regarding those meanings, and since the nominative case (*prathamā*) expresses a specific meaning, *lakṣaṇā*—which consists of a relation to the primary meaning—is not possible. This is the sense.

Now, consider the following: in cases such as *megho garjati* ("the cloud thunders"), since the direct objecthood (*sākṣātkarmatā*) of the thundering—which has the cloud as its agent—is impossible through connection with the meaning of the verbal root *śru* ("to hear"), one might first accept the connection of the thundering with the cloud and then, by way of that, accept its connection with the meaning of the verbal root. To this, he replies with the example *śaṅkhāḥ śrūyante* ("conch shells are heard") and so forth, on the grounds that "it is better to avoid the mud from afar than to wash it off"—that is, distance itself is preferable. Thus he says: "In cases such as *śaṅkhāḥ śrūyante*... [and so on].

The meaning is that conchs being blown are heard; the meaning is that kettledrums being sounded by their noise are heard. And thus, conchs qualified by the act of blowing are the substrata of the objecthood of hearing; there is an operation conducive to hearing residing in an object delimited by a plurality non-different from conchs qualified by the act of blowing; and likewise, kettledrums qualified by sound are the substrata of the objecthood of hearing.

The meaning is as follows: if one accepts the cognition of the sentence "śabdam aviśiṣṭabherī-abhinna-bahutvāvacchinna-karmavṛtti-śravaṇānukūla-vyāpāraḥ" (the sound, which is non-different from the drum, qualified by plurality, residing in the object, having an activity conducive to hearing), then—by the maxim *saviśeṣaṇe hi* (for when there is a qualification)—one must necessarily accept that the status of being the object (*karmatva*) of the root *śru* (to hear) resides in the sound (*śabda*) which is itself the qualifier of the conch. Consequently, there is no obstacle to accepting such a cognition even in cases like "śṛṇu garjati meghaḥ" (listen, the cloud thunders), according to the aforementioned maxim.

[Objection: In cases such as "the conchs are heard," since the word "conch" (*śaṅkha*) must necessarily possess a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the blown conch and so forth, one might argue that even by accepting such a *lakṣaṇā* for the word "conch," the direct connection with the objecthood (*karmatva*) denoted by the verbal root *śru* (to hear) remains possible; thus, the maxim "for when there is a qualified [object], [the operation applies] to the qualification" does not apply here. How, then, can the present case be resolved by that maxim? To this, he says: "The sound of the Pāñcajanya was heard," and so forth.

For in that case, there is necessarily a comprehension of the syntactic relation (*anvaya-bodha*) in the following manner: "The act of blowing, which is conducive to a past audition, resides in a single object that is non-different from the *pāñcajanya* shell, which serves as the locus for the sound characterized by the aforementioned qualifiers. Thus, [the *pāñcajanya*] is the locus of the sound characterized by the aforementioned qualifiers and serves as the locus of the objecthood of the past audition whose agent is Janaka. Therefore, because the *pāñcajanya* possesses its qualifiers, when the objecthood of the audition is restricted to it, those qualifiers [are also understood].

The point is that even if one accepts the view that in a sentence with a qualifier (*saviśeṣaṇa*), the primary meaning is a cognition whose qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) is the first-case-ending noun, the same principle (*nyāya*) can be applied to resolve this case as well.

Now, an objection is raised: in the sentence "Look, the deer is running" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*), there is a relation between the deer and the objectness (*karmatā*) residing in the deer, which is non-different from the qualificandumness (*viśeṣyakatā*) that is itself non-different from the qualificandumness delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) residing in the effort conducive to running (*dhāvanānukūlakṛti*). This [qualificandumness] is further non-different from the qualificandumness delimited by the relation of inherence residing in the effort conducive to running. [This is how the structure of the cognition is described.]

The resulting cognition arises as follows: "He is one who possesses the state of being the locus of the act of seeing, which has as its object the deer (the agent of running), and which is characterized by a primary qualificandhood residing in the referent of the word 'you'—this qualificandhood being delimited by a relation of self-referentiality, which is itself delimited by a relation of self-referentiality residing in the locus of the self [the speaker], which is non-different from the qualificandhood delimited by a relation of self-referentiality residing in the referent of the word 'deer', which is non-different from the qualificandhood delimited by a relation of self-referentiality residing in the referent of the word 'running', which is delimited by a relation of self-referentiality residing in the act of running. This is the understanding that occurs.

Thus it has been introduced. Listen: in the sentence "The cloud thunders," there is [the cognition] delimited by the relation of being the self-nature residing in the substratum of thundering, which is determined by a qualifierhood delimited by the relation of being the locus of the cloud; this is determined by a qualifierhood delimited by the relation of being an action non-different from the qualificandhood residing in the cloud; and this is determined by a relation delimited by being determined by a selfhood non-different from the qualificandhood. The hearing—[is thus established].

One must accept that the resulting cognition possesses a primary predication residing in the meaning of the word [the shell], which is qualified by a relation consisting of its own nature as distinct from the particularity determined by the particularity residing in the locus [the hearing], and is further delimited by the relation of its own nature; specifically, the cognition is: "The locus of the hearing, whose object is the cloud characterized by thundering, is the self," or "The conch, which is the locus of the sound, is the locus of the hearing whose action has already occurred. Such is the cognition of the relation between the meanings of the words that must be admitted.

And that [cognition] is sublated in cases such as "one should sprinkle with fire," just as the instrumentality of fire in the act of sprinkling is sublated; for in the case of hearing, since the object characterized by [the quality of] thundering is sublated, it is impossible for thundering to be construed as the instrument in hearing by way of its dependence on its substratum (the cloud). If this is argued, we say no.

Even though there is a sublation of the status of being the object (*karman*) of the root *śru* (to hear) when applied directly to the cloud qualified by thundering—since the cloud itself does not possess the act of hearing—there is no obstacle to the cloud being understood as the object through the relation of "possessing thundering which is its own substratum. Thus, by taking the cloud qualified by thundering as the subject (*dharmin*), it is possible for its qualifier, the thundering, to be construed with the meaning of the root *śru* via the aforementioned relation. [Objection: But surely, even in the view of the Logicians (*Tārkika*), in cases such as "Listen, the cloud thunders," the principle applies that "when a qualified entity [is mentioned], [the operation applies] to the qualifier" (*saviśeṣaṇe hi...*).

Even if one were to establish the state of being a logical subject (*yogya*) through reasoning, there would still be no connection of number with the cloud and so forth, despite their being presented by the word "garjati" (thunders), because such a connection is not observed. For instance, in cases such as "caitraḥ pacati" (Caitra cooks), although the agent—the primary substratum of the activity (*kṛti*) denoted by the verbal suffix—is Caitra, the connection of number with the cloud, which is the substratum of the act of thundering, is not seen; this is because the cloud, being a qualifier of the act of hearing, lacks the status of being the primary substratum.

This is because the non-distinction [of the subject] from the other [term] results in its being the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Otherwise, in the case of the sentence "Caitra goes like Maitra," in the resulting cognitive apprehension (*anvaya-bodha*)—namely, that "Caitra, who is the locus of similarity as determined by Maitra, possesses an effort conducive to going"—the number conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) would have to apply to Maitra as well, since he too is presented by the word ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta-pada*) therein. However, such an application does not occur.

It should not be argued that, by accepting that one [word] is not the cause for the cognition of the connection of the qualificand with another qualifier, there is no risk of such a connection occurring in the present case of Maitra, because the aforementioned type of presentation (upasthiti) is absent due to the absence of the specified relation. Listen: even in cases such as "The cloud thunders," since the aforementioned relation is absent regarding the cloud and so forth, the undesirable consequence of the number expressed by that [verb] not being connected would be unavoidable.

Nor should it be argued that—just as there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) for the singularity conveyed by the singular number in the expression "Devadatta sleeps well" (*devadattena supyeta*), even though that singularity is presented [by the word], so too there should be no connection for the singularity presented by the singular number in "the cloud thunders" (*garjati*), because it is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitatvāt*)—for such an argument would lead to the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of using expressions such as "Listen, the clouds thunder" (*śṛṇu garjanti meghāḥ*). With this intention, he restates [the objection] starting with "As for what was said... and ending with "...because it would result in grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). In the phrase "fame shines" (*kīrtiḥ... bhāti*), the verb "shines" (*bhāti*) is to be supplied (*adhyāhāra*). The phrase "because it would result in grammatical correctness" means...

The meaning is as follows: since the number [of the deer] is not intended to be expressed in the statement "The deer run" (*dhāvanti mṛgāḥ*), even though the singular number is present [in the verb], there is no connection of that [singular] number with the plurality of the deer; therefore, such a sentence lacks the status of being semantically incompetent (*apārthakatva*).

It is not accepted that the semantic requirement for the understanding of number—wherein the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyātārtha) is construed with the subject—is that the presentation (upasthiti) generated by a word ending in the nominative case, related to the primary qualificandhood (mukhyaviśeṣyatā), serves as the cause for the cognition of the number's relation to the qualificandhood. For if that were the case, then in instances where a deer or similar entity functions as a qualifier of the action of seeing (dṛśikriyā) in its capacity as the object (karmatā), there would be no such presentation related to that [qualificandhood], and thus the construal of the number would fail to occur; furthermore, this would lead to the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of sentences such as "the deer run" (*dhāvanti mṛgāḥ*) being unaccounted for.

Rather, it is accepted that the presentation [of the object] through the relation of being a qualificand (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*) is the cause for the cognition of its connection [with a property]. And thus, since the presentation of that [object] through the relation of being a qualificand exists in the deer (*mṛga*), there is no impossibility of connecting singularity [to it] in such cases as "The deer is running" (*mṛgo dhāvati*); for the singularity conveyed by the singular verb form in "is running" (*dhāvati*), which is intended to be expressed, is not sublated in the deer. Furthermore, there is no possibility of unfitness in such cases as "The deer are running" (*dhāvanti mṛgāḥ*), because [the plurality] is indeed fit.

He resolves [the objection] with the following intention: "It need not be stated that [the term 'mukhya'] applies only to that [primary sense]. Now, one might object: "If the primary status (*mukhyatva*) is not included within the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) when the relation of cause and effect is defined as previously stated, then in the case of the expression 'as white as a swan' (*haṃsīva dhavalā*), there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the number [of the pronoun] applying to the female swan (*haṃsī*) as well. To this we reply: No, for in that case, if one accepts the application of the number to the female swan, it results in what is actually desired (*iṣṭapatti*).

Furthermore, because there is a deviation [of the definition] in cases such as "Caitra alone cooks" when the primary status is not attributed to the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), it is rightly said that one need not mention "primary" (*mukhya*). With this intention, he says: "because of the deviation in cases such as 'Caitra alone cooks'. He clarifies the deviation regarding what was previously asserted—namely, that the cognition of that [object] is caused by the relation of being a primary qualificand—by means of the passage beginning with "the exclusion of connection with another" (*anyayogavyavaccheda*).

In this regard, in another case, there is first the absolute non-existence of identity (*tādātmya*); where there is the absence of identity for that [entity], there is its difference—by this rule, it follows that difference resides in the locus of difference. Thus, difference is the substratum, and difference is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); the meaning of the particle *eva* is the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*).

Just as in the expression "Pārtha alone is the archer," the word *pārtha* [denotes] the locus of the exclusion (*bheda*) which is the meaning of the particle *eva*, and that exclusion possesses the property of being the delimitant of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*). In that context, by means of the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā-saṃbandha*), there is the exclusion of Pārtha; by means of the relations of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatā-saṃbandha*), there is the locus of that exclusion; and by means of the relation of inherence (*ādheyatā-saṃbandha*), there is the locus of that [exclusion].

If difference were the counter-positive (pratiyogin) of itself as defined by its own nature through the relation of self-definedness, then, because that [self-defined] absence would not exist within the difference itself, there would be no connection with number; furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of such expressions as "the deer run" (dhāvanti mṛgāḥ). Rather, it must be accepted that the cause for the cognition of its connection is the presentation of that [difference] through the relation of being the qualificand (viśeṣyatā).

And likewise, if the relation were the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there would be no cognition of that [relation] as being a deer; consequently, in cases such as "the deer is running," the expression of singularity would be untenable. This is because the singularity intended to be conveyed by the singular verb ending in "is running" would be contradicted if applied to multiple deer, or else, in cases such as "the deer are running," the very possibility of the expression would be lost due to its lack of fitness. With this intention, he provides the solution: "In that case, it need not be stated that [the relation] is primary (*mukhya*)."

One might object: "If the primary status [of the relation] is not introduced into the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) when the causal relation is defined as stated above, then in the case of 'white like a swan' (*haṃsīva dhavalā*), there would arise the undesirable consequence that number (*saṃkhyātva*) would also reside in the swan. To this it is replied: No, for if one accepts that number resides in the swan in that instance, it is a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*). Furthermore, in cases such as "Caitra alone cooks" (*caitra eva pacati*), if the primary status were not introduced into the qualificandhood, there would be a logical inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*).

And thus, with the intention of showing that it was rightly said that "it cannot be stated that [the agent] is not denotable," he says: "because of deviation (vyabhicāra) in cases such as 'Caitra alone cooks'. He clarifies the deviation from the thesis that would occur if one were to accept that the cause for the cognition of that [agenthood] is the presentation [of the agent] through the relation of being the primary qualificand (mukhya-viśeṣyatā-sambandha), by means of the passage beginning with "anyayoga-vyavaccheda" and so forth. In that context, "otherness" (anya) refers to something else; "connection" (yoga) refers to its identity (tādātmya); and "exclusion" (vyavaccheda) refers to the absolute absence (atyantābhāva) of that [identity] in that [other thing].

According to the rule that "where there is the non-existence of identity with something, there is difference from it," it follows that difference resides in that which possesses difference. Thus, difference is the locus, and the meaning of the particle *eva* (only) is that difference is the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*).

For example, in expressions such as "Pārtha alone is the archer," the word *pārtha* [denotes] the exclusion (*bheda*) which is the meaning of the subsequent particle *eva*. This exclusion is the locus (*āśraya*), and its counter-correlativity-delimiting property (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) is as follows: there, Pārtha [is related] to the exclusion by way of the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā-sambandha*); the exclusion [is related] to its locus by way of the specific relation of qualifierhood (*viśeṣaṇatā-viśeṣa-sambandha*); the locus [is related] to the exclusion by way of the relation of being contained therein (*ādheyatā-sambandha*); and the counter-correlativity of the exclusion [is related] to itself by way of the relation of being self-defined (*sva-nirūpitatva-sambandha*). [This is established] by way of the relation of its own nature (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

In the qualifier "archerness" (*dhanurdharatva*), which is the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of that [absence], there is a connection with Pārtha by way of identity (*tādātmya*). Thus, there is a relation of being the locus of a qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*)—which is non-different from a relation of being the locus of a qualificandum determined by a mode residing in the locus, itself determined by a relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*)—residing in Pārtha. And so forth.

That which possesses a primary subjecthood (*mukhya-viśeṣyatā*) residing in Pārtha, which is determined by a qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) residing in the state of being an archer (*dhanurdharatva*), which is non-different from a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by a qualifierhood residing in the property of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*), which is non-different from a qualificandhood residing in the self-nature (*svarūpa*) relation, which is non-different from a qualifierhood residing in difference (*bheda*), which is delimited by a relation of non-distinction (*asaṃbhinna-sva-nirūpitatva*), which is determined by a qualifierhood residing in the state of being a qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) that is non-different from the qualificandhood residing in the
