Thus, the resulting cognitive apprehension (anvayabodha) is established as: "Pārtha is distinct from that which is delimited by the property of being an archer, which serves as the deliminator of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of the difference residing in someone other than Pārtha. Similarly, in cases such as "Caitra alone cooks," the resulting cognitive apprehension should be understood as: "Caitra is one who possesses an effort conducive to cooking, which serves as the deliminator of the counter-correlativity of the difference residing in someone other than Caitra."

And thus, even when there is a distinction [of the locus] such as "in the field," because there is no relation between the qualificand residing in the qualifier and another word ending in the nominative case—due to the absence of the cognitive presentation (upasthiti) [of that other word]—the cognition of the connection with singularity does not arise; therefore, the deviation [from the rule] is indeed manifest. Intending this, he says: "in a part of the meaning of the particle *eva*," and so forth. "In a part" means in the distinction (*bheda*).

Because there is an absence of being the object of a presentation (upasthiti) generated by a word ending in the nominative case; because even when there is a relation of being the qualificand residing in the other qualifier, there is an absence of a presentation generated by a word ending in the nominative case; and because when there is a relation of being the qualificand residing in the other qualifier, there is an absence of a presentation generated by a word ending in the nominative case. To explain how, in this context, Caitra possesses the status of being a qualifier in the difference [expressed as] "Caitra is not cooking," he says: "Caitra-anyo na pacati" (Caitra, who is other than the one who cooks, does not cook).

The meaning of "Caitra does not cook" (*caitraḥ na pacati*) is simply that Caitra lacks the effort conducive to cooking which is delimited by the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in someone other than Caitra; it does not mean that Caitra lacks the effort conducive to cooking while being possessed of the effort conducive to cooking by someone other than Caitra. Consequently, there is no contingency of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*) due to a difference in the qualificands. This is because the meaning of "Caitra alone cooks" (*caitra eva pacati*) is identical to that [of "Caitra does not cook"].

Raising the objection that if one does not accept that the cognition of that [object] is the cause of its manifestation through the relation of primary qualificandness (*mukhya-viśeṣyatā-sambandha*), then by what relation could it be the cause there, he states "And thus" (*tathā ca*) to explain that it is the cause through the relation of qualificandness common to both primary and secondary [objects].

If one does not accept that the cause for the presentation [of the meaning] is the relation of primary qualificand-ness (*mukhyaviśeṣyatā-saṃbandha*) [between the two], then in the case of "Your fame is like a female swan," there would arise the following verbal cognition: "That which possesses the state of being the locus of plunging into the heavenly Ganges, which is related through similarity as defined by a female swan that is the locus of singularity. In that case, since both the number and the state of being the locus of plunging would be common attributes (*sādhāraṇadharma*) of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), expressions such as "Your fame is like a female swan" (*haṃsīva kṛṣṇa*) would be grammatically correct; however, [this is not the case]. Regarding the female swan...

If one does not accept that [the suffix] *anvak* is used with numerals, there would be grammatical incorrectness (*asādhutva*). Furthermore, even when there is a difference in gender and number residing in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), the sentence would not be incorrect; thus, because there is no deviation from this rule, the description in the treatises of the Alamkāra school—that a difference in gender and number residing in the standard and object of comparison is a determinant of defectiveness due to its causing a lack of aesthetic flavor (*vairasya*)—would not be possible. Therefore, he says: "In such cases as 'upamāne' etc."; and the reason why there would otherwise be no defectiveness is stated at the end.

The reason why it is appropriate to accept [the number] in the simile—given that the number is not accepted as inhering in the female swan (*haṃsī*) which serves as the object of comparison, and given that it is not accepted as inhering in the number denoted by the verb (*ākhyāta*) because it would otherwise be untenable due to lacking a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*)—is stated here.

Now, one might ask: "What is the fault if there is an absence of common properties between the *saṃkhyātā* (the subject) and the *stu* (the object of comparison)? To this, he says: "Like a swan," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the occurrence of ungrammaticality" (*asādhutvāpattau*), the ellipsis is to be supplied as: "even when there was previously identity of gender and number between the words expressing the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*). Thus, by showing that identity of gender and number leads to ungrammaticality, a counter-example (*vyatireka-vyatireka*) is demonstrated. [The meaning is: "Defectiveness" (*duṣṭatvam*)—that is, the state of being determined as defective—would not occur.

And likewise, since number possesses the property of being a substrate for the substratum-ness [of the universal], the same fault would arise in its absence; therefore, the intended meaning is that it is appropriate for number to be the cause here through a relationship of a qualifier common to both the primary and secondary [referents].

If "being the primary [subject]" (*mukhyatva*) were not included in the definition of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*), then the unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*) of number (*saṃkhyā*) connecting with the *haṃsī* (the female swan) would also arise; however, since it has been stated that "it [number] connects only with the primary," this objection is warded off by the acceptance of the very point [of connection] implied by the sense. Furthermore, if "being the primary" were included in the definition of being the qualificand, one would incur the charge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). On the contrary, if one does not accept the connection of number with the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), there would be no defect; thus, having raised the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*), [the author] concludes that the relation of being the qualificand is common to both the primary and the non-primary.

That its status as a cause [of verbal activity] has been established; now, by means of that very connection, he states another proof for its being a cause of verbal activity, beginning with the words "for the meaning of the verb is something in addition to the numbered time," and so on. This is because of the rule that number must be construed with that which is construed with the *bhāvanā* (the efficient force).

In the case of a suffix denoting the agent (*kartṛ-pratyaya*), the agent is what is connected with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*); in the case of a suffix denoting the object (*karman-pratyaya*), the object is what is connected with the productive operation. Since in both cases [the agent or the object] is expressed by a word ending in the nominative case, its status as the cause of that [number] is understood through the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*) alone, and not even as the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣyatā*), because it is taught that number is connected only to that which is connected with the productive operation.

The point is this: likewise, in expressions such as "the deer is running" (*mṛgo dhāvati*), although the deer and so forth function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the act of seeing by virtue of being its object (*karman*), they are nonetheless presented [to consciousness] as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Since they exist there [in that capacity], there is no logical inconsistency in their connection with number. Alternatively, one might object: "Granted that the presentation [of the object] through the relation of being the qualificand is the cause [of its connection with number], then in figurative usages (*lākṣaṇika-prayoga*) such as 'the rice cooks' (*taṇḍulaḥ pacati*), since the rice is presented through that same relation, it would follow that it must be connected with number because it exists there [as the qualificand]. To this he replies: "Apart from number and time," and so forth.

The meaning of the root text, "the cognition of number is the cause for the connection of number when there is a presentation produced by a word ending in the nominative case, which is related to the qualificand residing in that which is connected to the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) according to the actual state of things," is as follows: since there is no connection with the *bhāvanā* in the case of *taṇḍula* (rice), there is an absence of the presentation of it through such a relation; thus, the consequence of the connection of number does not arise there. This is the intended sense.

Now, if it is granted that the cognition of that [absence] is the cause because it is presented through the aforementioned relation, then in the case of the cognition "The absence of a jar residing on the ground exists" (*bhūtalavṛttighaṭābhāvo 'stitvāśrayaḥ*), since the number must be construed with the absence itself—given that the absence is the substratum of existence—it would follow that the sentence "Two jars do not exist on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭau na staḥ*) would be erroneous; for the singularity conveyed by the singular ending in the word "exists" (*asti*) would remain uncontradicted in respect to the absence.

Nor should it be argued that, although non-existence (*abhāva*) cannot be construed with the verb, there is no possibility of its being construed with the singular number because it is not presented by a word ending in the nominative case; for, through the recollection of the elided case-ending following the negative particle (*nañ*), its meaning is also indeed presented by a word ending in the nominative case. Otherwise, even in the case of "the jar does not exist" (*ghaṭo nāsti*), the construction of the singular number with the non-existence would be untenable.

Nor should it be argued that there is no cognition in that case of the form "the jar, which is the counter-positive of the absence, exists on the ground," and thus, since the jar is not the correlate of the verbal root (bhāvanā), its expressed number cannot be correlated with it; for in the case of "there are no two jars on the ground," the expressed singularity would be untenable due to its contradiction with the two jars that are the correlates of the verbal root. This objection is not valid, because it would result in an expectancy for a locus, namely, "where?"—but this is not the case here.

In cases where there is co-utterance with the negative particle (*nañ*), that which is the counter-positive of the absence of connection with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is the cause for the cognition of number through its occurrence in the relation of being the qualificand residing therein; likewise, in cases where there is co-utterance with the negative particle, that which is connected with the productive operation by the very nature of things is the cause for the cognition of number through its occurrence in the relation of being the qualificand residing therein.

And thus, although in the case of "the jar does not exist" (*ghaṭo nāsti*) there is the cognition that the absence of the jar exists, the jar—which is the counter-positive of that absence—is capable of being construed because its oneness can be construed with the substratum (*anvayi*). In the case of "two jars do not exist" (*ghaṭau na staḥ*), such a pair of jars cannot have oneness construed with them, and thus they are incapable of being so construed. However, in the case of "the two jars do not exist" (*ghaṭau na staḥ*), since the duality expressed by the dual ending can be construed with that pair of jars, they are capable of being so construed; therefore, the aforementioned defect does not apply.

Alternatively, in the sentence "There is no pot on the ground," the meaning of the locative case (*saptamī*) is "being described" (*nirūpitatva*); the meaning of the root *as* is "existence" (*vidyamānatva*); and the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) is "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*). Thus, in the cognition "The pot is that which lacks the substratum-ness of existence as described by the ground," the singularity conveyed by the verbal suffix is construed with the pot, thereby accounting for the grammatical correctness of that sentence. In the case of "Two pots do not exist," there is the absence of the substratum-ness of existence in the two pots.

There is no lack of logical connection because the singularity denoted by the suffix is not sublated. Nor should it be argued that the co-referential relation (*anvaya*) of the meaning of the verbal suffix with a negation has never been observed; for in cases such as "Caitra does not cook" (*na pacati caitraḥ*), the co-referential relation of the action (*bhāvanā*)—which is the meaning of the verbal suffix—with the negation is indeed observed. If it is objected: "In that case, since the pot (*ghaṭa*) lacks the status of being the correlate of the action (*bhāvanānvayitva*), and since it lacks the status of being the counter-positive of the absence of the correlate of the action (*bhāvanānvayyabhāvapratiyogitva*), how can the number conveyed by the verbal suffix be construed with it?"—we reply: No.

Since it is accepted that the cause for the cognition of the number denoted by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) as connected with the meaning of the first-case-ending-generated representation is the relation of being the qualificand of the bhāvanā—whether directly or through a common succession—and the relation of being the locus of that [number] residing in the qualificand, there is no lack of justification for the connection of number there [in the case of "ghaṭo bhavati"], because even though the jar is not the direct qualificand of the bhāvanā, it is the qualificand of the bhāvanā through the relation of being the locus of its own locus.

Nor should it be argued that even in this case, when the absence of the locus-ness of present existence as determined by the ground (bhūtala) is construed with the word delimited by "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*)—just as in the case of duality (*dvitva*)—the expression "there are not two pots on the ground" would fail to apply to a ground containing a single pot; for if the negation were construed with [the absence] being co-referential (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the duality residing in the pot, then the expression "there are not two pots" would indeed apply even to a place containing two pots, because the absence of existence on the ground would still obtain in a pot belonging to some other location.

The meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) cannot be co-referential (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the duality residing in the jar, because [the absence] is delimited by that [duality]. Even if there were co-reference of the meaning of the negative particle with a duality residing in another locus, since there is no absence of the absence of existence on this floor with respect to the duality residing in the jar that resides on this floor, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) does not arise that one could say "there are no two jars" in a place where two jars exist.

[Objection: It might be argued that in the case of "There is no jar on the ground," since absence resides in the locus (anuyogin), one must accept its residence in the counter-positive (pratiyogin) as well; thus, in the case of "Existence (sattā) does not exist in the universal (jāti)," the comprehension of the sentence would have to be that existence possesses the absence of being the substratum of residence as defined by the universal. But that is not possible. For, since existence does possess residence in the universal delimited by co-inherence (ekārthasamavāya), it is impossible to convey the absence of such residence; furthermore, because the property of "being inherent in a universal" is unestablished anywhere, it cannot be negated. [Response: This is not so.

In the view of those who accept the cognition "there is no jar on the ground" as "the absence of a jar residing in the ground is the locus of existence," although the statement "existence does not reside in the universal" (*jātau na sattā*) is logically consistent—since it can be explained as "there is an absence of existence residing in the universal"—nevertheless, the claim that "the universal does not reside in existence" (*jātir na sattāvṛttiḥ*) is untenable. This is because, regarding the relation [of residence], the absence of "residing-in-existence" as delimited by the general property of being (sāmānyatva) is impossible in the case of a universal; furthermore, since the absence of "residing-in-existence" as delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*) is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*), its negation is impossible. Thus, that prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is refuted.

[Objection: Because of the equality [of the two cases], is it not the case that the sentence "the universal (*jāti*) does not reside in existence (*sattā*)" is simply ungrammatical? Or, the word "residence" (*vṛtti*) may refer to residence delimited by a direct relation (*sākṣāt-sambandha*). Thus, what is understood there is the absence of residence delimited by a direct relation as defined by existence. And since residence delimited by a direct relation as defined by existence is well-known in terms of [properties] such as knowability (*prameyatva*), which possess their own form as a relatum, the aforementioned fault does not apply. [Reply: This is not so.

Even in the sentence "there is no existence in genus" (*jātau sattā nāsti*), the verbal root *as* (to be) must be understood through a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) characterized by its occurrence being delimited by a direct relation; thus, the cognition produced is that "existence is that which lacks the state of being a locus for an occurrence delimited by a direct relation defined by genus. This is because I, who maintain that the absence of occurrence in the correlate (*anuyogin*) is what connects with the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), am likewise able to say this. Such is the direction of the argument.

If an action (*kriyā*) were to function as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), then in such instances as "I bow to his feet as the man walks," there would be no coreferential reference (*parāmarśa*) to the man by the word *tat*. Anticipating this objection, it was argued that since usage is observed in cases such as "The leaf of the *paṭola* removes bile, but its stalk brings about phlegm," the word *tat* can indeed refer to the qualifier even when it is not the qualificand; however, that which was asserted is incorrect. In those cases, it is true that the word *tat* refers to the qualifier as well.

However, as long as that pronoun (*tacchabda*) refers to the principal element (*pradhāna*), it is not appropriate for it to refer to a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Therefore, in cases such as "the man goes" (*puruṣaḥ prayāti*), since one accepts a cognition where the meaning of the nominative-terminated word is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the pronoun refers only to that which has become the principal element; this is because it is accepted in exactly that way. With this in mind, he says: "Because in some cases there is a reference to the qualificand, and in some cases a reference to the qualifier. Thus ends the discussion.

In some cases, such as "A person goes," the pronoun refers to the substantive (*viśeṣya*); in other cases, such as "The leaf of the *paṭola* plant destroys bile," it refers to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Now, if the word "that" (*tat*) were to refer only to the qualifier, then in instances such as "This pot is its [i.e., the pot's] genus" (*tajjāti*), the word "that" would fail to refer to "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). To address this, he says: "But furthermore" (*paraṃ tu*). This refers to the qualifier that constitutes the delimitor of the word-meaning (*padārthatāvacchedaka-rūpa-viśeṣaṇa*), which is itself the delimitor of the word's denotative power (*padaśaktatāvacchedaka-rūpa-viśeṣaṇa*).

The point is this: in cases such as "the leaf of the *paṭola*," if one accepts that the word *paṭola* and so forth possess a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) toward that which is related to the *paṭola*, then even though the *paṭola* and so forth serve as the delimitors of the word-meaning (*padārthatāvacchedaka*), there would be an impossibility of referring to them by the pronoun "it" (*tat*).

Thus ends the *Vākyadīpikā*, composed by Hariyaśomiśra—the disciple of the venerable Lord Udayasiṃha, who was himself the disciple of Jīvaka—[and dedicated] to the pure Consciousness (*śuddhacit*), which is the locus of the beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*) characterized by its own specific difference (*svalakṣaṇatva*) and its concomitants, and which is devoid of the temporal priority of the visible world (*dṛśya*) produced by that [ignorance], and which is the destroyer of all contrary notions.
